teile.einleitung: Sea level rise means that the surface of the oceans is slowly getting higher. The main cause is global warming: warmer water expands, and glaciers and ice sheets on land melt. For coastal cities and low-lying island states this is a great danger.
wichtigste: Global sea level has risen by about 20 centimetres since the start of the 20th century.
The most important causes are the thermal expansion of water and melting land ice.
Melting sea ice hardly raises the sea level at all.
If the whole Greenland ice sheet melted, the sea would rise by about 7 metres.
About 58 metres of sea level rise are stored in the Antarctic ice sheet.
Since the 1990s sea level has been measured with satellites.
Low-lying atoll states such as Tuvalu and Kiribati are especially threatened.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is getting warmer because humans put a lot of carbon dioxide into the air. The oceans take up a large part of this heat. Warmer water needs more space; this is called **thermal expansion**. At the same time, mountain glaciers and the great **ice sheets** on Greenland and in Antarctica are melting, and their water flows into the sea. These two causes contribute most to today's rise.

Not all melting ice makes the sea rise. **Sea ice** is already floating and pushes aside as much water as it produces itself when it melts. You can try this with an ice cube in a glass of water: when it melts, the glass does not overflow. It is different with **land ice**, which lies on rock and brings new water into the sea when it melts. The Greenland ice sheet holds about 7 metres of possible rise, and the Antarctic ice sheet about 58 metres.

In the past, the water level was measured with **tide gauges** at harbours and coasts. Since the 1990s, satellites have been watching the sea surface without gaps. They send radar signals to the Earth and measure how long the echo takes. This method is called **satellite altimetry**. Since the start of the 20th century, sea level has risen by about 20 centimetres, and the rise is getting faster.

Low-lying **atoll states** such as Tuvalu, Kiribati or the Maldives, whose islands often rise only a few metres out of the sea, are especially threatened. Large coastal cities such as Jakarta, Miami or Venice also struggle with flooding. In Bangladesh, millions of people live in low-lying river deltas. The Netherlands has been protecting itself with dykes and storm barriers for centuries. On some coasts of Scandinavia, on the other hand, the sea is hardly rising relative to the land or is even falling, because the land has been rising since the ice-age glaciers melted.

How much the sea rises by 2100 depends on how much greenhouse gas humanity still emits. Depending on what happens, experts expect a few decimetres to about a metre, and even more in the long term. Switzerland has no coast, but meltwater from the Alpine glaciers also flows into the sea via the Rhine, the Rhône and the Inn. What is more, all Swiss height measurements refer to **sea level**. Climate protection, meaning fewer greenhouse gases, is the most important way to slow down the rise.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average height of the surface of the seas.
A huge, thick covering of ice that covers a whole land area.
A ring-shaped, flat coral island that surrounds a lagoon.
A measuring post or instrument for the water level.

gewusst: The starting point for Swiss height measurement is a boulder in Lake Geneva, the “Pierre du Niton”.
At the end of the last ice age, sea level was over 100 metres lower than today.
Venice protects itself with movable gates that rise out of the sea when the water is high.

teile.einleitung: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which computers learn from examples instead of having every rule programmed in. This is how programs recognise cats in photos, filter out spam emails or suggest suitable videos. The more good examples a program sees, the better it usually gets.
wichtigste: The basic idea of machine learning is that the computer learns from examples.
In 1959 Arthur Samuel coined the term “machine learning” with a program for the board game draughts.
In supervised learning, the correct answer is given with every training example.
In unsupervised learning, the program itself looks for groups of similar things; this is called clustering.
In reinforcement learning, a program gets rewards for good actions.
Artificial neural networks are modelled on the brain, and deep learning uses networks with many layers.
If a model only learns the examples by heart, this is called overfitting.

abschnitte.text: In normal programs a person writes down every rule exactly. In **machine learning**, instead, you show the computer many examples, and it finds the rules itself. If you want it to tell apples from pears, for example, you show it thousands of pictures with the correct answer. The finished result is called a **model**, which can then also sort new pictures.

In **supervised learning**, the program is given the correct answer with every training example. A spam filter, for example, learns from thousands of emails marked “spam” or “not spam”. Over time it recognises typical features such as certain words or senders. Weather forecasts and estimates of house prices also use this method.

In **unsupervised learning** there are no correct answers. The program looks for patterns by itself and divides data into groups of similar things; this is called **clustering**. In **reinforcement learning**, a program tries out actions and gets rewards for good results. This is how the program AlphaGo learned the board game Go so well that in 2016 it beat one of the world's best players.

Many modern methods use **artificial neural networks**, which are modelled on the brain. They consist of many connected computing units in layers. The word “deep” in **deep learning** means that the network has a great many layers. Such networks are behind voice assistants, translation programs and chatbots.

In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt presented the **perceptron**, a simple learning machine. In 1959 Arthur Samuel coined the term “machine learning” with a program that played the board game **draughts** better and better over many games. For a long time there was not enough computing power or data. Only since about 2010 has there been huge progress, thanks to fast computers and the internet.

A model can learn the training examples by heart but be poor at solving new examples; this is called **overfitting**. That is why it is always tested with data it has never seen. Another problem is one-sided data: if the examples are unfair, the model decides unfairly too. That is why it is important to check the results of programs critically.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of learning, which can judge new cases.
Examples from which a program learns.
When a model learns examples by heart instead of recognising the general pattern.
Dividing data into groups of similar things without a given answer.
Learning by trying things out and getting rewards.

gewusst: In the end, Arthur Samuel's draughts program played better than its own inventor.
In Go there are more possible positions than there are atoms in the visible universe.
When you have to click on pictures with traffic lights or bikes on websites, you are sometimes helping to create training data.

teile.einleitung: Lactic acid bacteria are tiny living things that turn sugar into lactic acid. Without them there would be no yoghurt, no sauerkraut and no sourdough bread. People have been using them for thousands of years to make food keep longer and taste good.
wichtigste: Lactic acid bacteria turn sugar into lactic acid.
In milk they break down the milk sugar, which is how yoghurt is made, for example.
White cabbage becomes sauerkraut through lactic acid fermentation.
The acid holds back the bacteria that make food rot, which is why soured foods keep for a long time.
In sourdough, lactic acid bacteria and yeasts work together.
Bacteria of the genus Lactobacillus are shaped like little rods.
Foods with living, useful bacteria are called probiotic.

abschnitte.text: Lactic acid bacteria are a group of **bacteria** that mainly produce lactic acid when they ferment. Some are rod-shaped, like the genus **Lactobacillus**, others are round, like Lactococcus or Streptococcus. They are found in milk, on plants, in the gut and in the mouth. Most of them do not need oxygen to live.

Lactic acid bacteria feed on **sugar**. In milk this is **milk sugar**, also called lactose. They turn the sugar into lactic acid and gain energy in the process. This is called **lactic acid fermentation**. The acid makes the milk thick, because the milk protein curdles.

If you add lactic acid bacteria to warm milk, **yoghurt** forms after a few hours. They are also needed for quark, soured cream, buttermilk and almost all kinds of cheese. For Emmental, propionic acid bacteria also help, and they make the holes. **Kefir** from the Caucasus forms when bacteria and yeasts work together in milk. Swiss dairy farming would be unthinkable without these helpers.

Vegetables can also be preserved with lactic acid bacteria. Finely shredded **white cabbage** is pounded down with salt and ferments into sauerkraut. The acid holds back the **bacteria that cause rotting**, so sauerkraut does not go off for a long time. In **sourdough**, lactic acid bacteria and yeasts work together: the bacteria make the dough sour and tasty, and the yeasts make it rise. Pickled gherkins, kimchi from Korea and silage for animal feed are made in this way too.

Some lactic acid bacteria also live in our **gut** and are part of the microbiome. Foods with living bacteria that are meant to be good for health are called **probiotic**. How great the benefit is is still being researched. In the mouth, however, lactic acid bacteria can also do harm, because their acid attacks tooth enamel and encourages tooth decay.

People were souring milk and vegetables thousands of years ago without knowing about the bacteria. Only in the 19th century did the French researcher Louis Pasteur show that microorganisms cause fermentation. Around 1900 the researcher Ilya Mechnikov made yoghurt known in Europe as a healthy food. Today selected **starter cultures** are bred so that yoghurt and cheese always turn out equally well.

begriffe.erklaerung: The breakdown of sugar by microorganisms without oxygen.
Another word for milk sugar.
A genus of rod-shaped lactic acid bacteria.
Selected bacteria that are added to start a fermentation.
Containing living bacteria that are meant to be good for health.

gewusst: A single pot of yoghurt can contain billions of living lactic acid bacteria.
Chocolate also needs bacteria and yeasts, because the cocoa beans are fermented before drying.
Silage, the fermented fodder for cows, is also preserved by lactic acid bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Mary Anning was an English fossil collector who lived from 1799 to 1847 in Lyme Regis on the south coast of England. Even as a girl she found skeletons of prehistoric sea creatures in the cliffs. Her finds helped the scientists of her time to understand that there used to be animals that are now extinct.
wichtigste: Mary Anning searched for and found fossils on the coast of southern England.
At about 12 she and her brother found the skeleton of an ichthyosaur.
She found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur.
She was the first person in England to find a pterosaur.
Her family lived by selling fossils.
Because she was a woman, she was not allowed to become a member of the Geological Society in London.
The English tongue-twister “She sells seashells” is said to be about her.

abschnitte.text: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in **Lyme Regis** in the county of Dorset. Her family was poor, and her father was a carpenter. On the side he collected fossils and sold them to tourists, and the children helped. After her father's early death, the family lived by **selling fossils**, and Mary soon became the best fossil hunter in the area.

abschnitte.titel: The cliffs of the Jurassic Coast
abschnitte.text: The coast around Lyme Regis is now called the **Jurassic Coast** and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Its rocks are about 200 million years old and full of fossils. After storms, parts of the cliffs break off and reveal new fossils. That is why Mary searched mainly in winter, but it was dangerous, because there were often **rockfalls**. In 1833 her dog was killed in such a rockfall, and she herself only just survived.

Around 1811 Mary's brother Joseph found the skull of an **ichthyosaur**, and Mary, at about 12, uncovered the rest of the skeleton. In 1823 she discovered the first complete skeleton of a **plesiosaur**, a marine reptile with a long neck and four paddles. In 1828 she was the first person in England to find the skeleton of a **pterosaur**. She also realised that certain stones were the fossilised droppings of prehistoric reptiles.

In the 19th century, women in England were not allowed to study or to take part in scientific societies. So Mary Anning was not allowed to become a member of the **Geological Society of London**. Many men bought her finds and described them in scientific articles, often without mentioning her name. Even so, well-known researchers came to her to learn from her knowledge.

Mary Anning's finds showed that there used to be animals that are now **extinct**. At the time this was a new and exciting idea. Today she is considered one of the most important pioneers of **palaeontology**. In 2024 a statue in her honour was put up in Lyme Regis. Many of her finds are on display in the Natural History Museum in London.

The English tongue-twister “She sells seashells by the seashore” is said to be about Mary Anning. Whether this is true is not completely certain, but the story is often told. Today there are children's books and a feature film about her life. So many children who are excited about dinosaurs and fossils know about her too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from earlier times that has turned to stone.
A fish-like marine reptile that looked like a dolphin.
A marine reptile with a long neck and four paddles.
The science of the living things of past ages of the Earth.

gewusst: As a baby, Mary Anning survived a lightning strike in which three women near her died.
Mary Anning had no schooling, but taught herself a great deal about geology and anatomy.
The rocks of Lyme Regis still reveal new fossils after every big storm.

teile.einleitung: Courage means doing something even though you are afraid. So a brave person is not someone without fear, but someone who acts anyway because something matters to them. You need courage to jump into the water just as much as to help in a difficult situation.
wichtigste: Courage means acting despite fear.
Fear is a normal feeling that protects us from danger.
Courage is not the same as recklessness.
Moral courage is the courage to help people in need, even when onlookers are there.
A very brave person is called a hero or a heroine.
In stories the lion is often seen as an especially brave animal.
Courage can be practised, best in small steps.

abschnitte.text: Courage is the ability to face a fear, a danger or a difficult task. It is brave, for example, to give a talk in front of the class even though your heart is pounding. Admitting that you have made a mistake also takes courage. The ancient Greek thinkers already counted **bravery** among the most important virtues of a person.

**Fear** is an important feeling, because it warns us of danger. The body then reacts with a fast heartbeat, sweating or wobbly knees. Courage means feeling this fear and still acting thoughtfully. On the other hand, someone who simply ignores dangers is not brave but **reckless** or overconfident.

**Moral courage** is the courage to stand up for others, for example when someone is being teased, threatened or left out. In doing so you should not put yourself in danger. You can say loudly that something is not right, speak directly to other people or get help. In Switzerland you can reach the police on 117 and the European emergency number on 112.

In the Swiss legend, **William Tell** has to shoot an apple from his son's head on the orders of the bailiff Gessler. Since then Tell has been a symbol of courage and freedom. In many fairy tales and coats of arms the lion stands for courage, which is where the expression lionheart comes from. A real example is the St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger**, who in 1938 helped hundreds of refugees, even though he lost his job for it.

Many brave people work in jobs in which they help others. Firefighters, paramedics and mountain rescuers often go to dangerous places when there are accidents. But courage is also shown by someone who stands by a friend or honestly says what they think. Such people are sometimes called **everyday heroes**.

Courage can be trained like a muscle. It is best to practise in small steps: first jump into the water from the starting block, later perhaps from the one-metre board. It helps to prepare well beforehand and to talk to someone about your fear. Every time something works, your **self-confidence** grows.

begriffe.erklaerung: The courage to stand up in everyday life for others and for what is right.
A good quality in a person, for example honesty or bravery.
Careless behaviour in which you ignore dangers.
The feeling of trusting yourself to do something.

gewusst: In old German the word Mut, courage, meant mood or spirit in general; words such as Wehmut (wistfulness), Übermut (high spirits) and Hochmut (arrogance) come from it.
The Tell legend became world-famous through the play William Tell by Friedrich Schiller from 1804.
Paul Grüninger was only fully cleared by a court in 1995, long after his death.

teile.einleitung: A mass extinction is an event in which a great many animal and plant species disappear within a short time in terms of Earth's history. Experts usually distinguish five big mass extinctions in the last 450 million years or so. The best known ended the age of the dinosaurs.
wichtigste: In a mass extinction, many species die out in a short time.
Usually five big mass extinctions are distinguished.
The first of the big five happened at the end of the Ordovician.
The biggest mass extinction happened at the end of the Permian.
The main cause then was huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia.
The extinction at the end of the Triassic, about 201 million years ago, cleared the way for the dinosaurs.
After a mass extinction, surviving groups often develop many new species.
Some researchers today speak of a sixth mass extinction, because humans are making many species disappear.

abschnitte.text: Species die out again and again; this is a normal part of **evolution**. But in a **mass extinction**, a large proportion of all species on the whole Earth disappears within a short time. In Earth's history, short often means a few thousand to a few hundred thousand years. Researchers recognise such events in rock layers in which many fossils suddenly disappear. Above them lie layers with completely new living things.

The first big mass extinction happened at the end of the **Ordovician**, about 444 million years ago, when it became very cold on Earth. In the late Devonian, about 372 million years ago, many sea creatures died, especially in reefs. At the end of the Permian, about 252 million years ago, came the biggest of all. At the end of the Triassic, about 201 million years ago, many species disappeared again. The last big mass extinction happened at the end of the **Cretaceous**, about 66 million years ago.

abschnitte.titel: The Great Dying in the Permian
abschnitte.text: At the end of the **Permian**, probably over 90 per cent of all marine species and a large part of the land animals disappeared. The main cause was huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia, which over a long time poured out enormous amounts of lava and gases. The gases warmed the climate strongly and made the seas acidic and low in oxygen. This event is also called the **Great Dying**. It took millions of years for life to recover.

After the extinction at the end of the **Triassic**, the dinosaurs had little competition and spread across the whole Earth. About 135 million years later, disaster struck them too. About 66 million years ago, an **asteroid** about 10 kilometres across struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. Dust darkened the sky, and it stayed cold for a long time. All dinosaurs except the birds died out, and afterwards the mammals spread.

Many researchers today speak of a **sixth mass extinction**. This time humans are the cause: through deforestation, hunting, pollution, introduced species and climate change. Species are disappearing much faster today than would be expected naturally. In Switzerland, too, many animals and plants are on the **Red List** of threatened species. Protected areas, wildlife-friendly gardens and less pollution can help to save species.

begriffe.erklaerung: The disappearance of a great many species in a short time.
A group of living things that are very similar and can have young together.
A remain or imprint of a living thing that has turned to stone.
A list of the animals and plants that are threatened with extinction.

gewusst: Without the extinction of the dinosaurs, humans might not exist at all.
At Monte San Giorgio in Ticino, famous fossils from the Triassic are found, and the site is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Birds are the only descendants of the dinosaurs that have survived to this day.

teile.einleitung: The Antikythera mechanism is a bronze device over 2000 years old with many gear wheels. It could be used to calculate the movements of the Sun, the Moon and probably the planets and to predict eclipses. It is considered the oldest known calculating machine in the world.
wichtigste: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient calculator for the movements of the heavens.
It was found in a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
Sponge divers discovered the wreck around 1900.
Its gear wheels are made of bronze, and about 30 of them survive.
It could be used to predict solar and lunar eclipses.
From 2005, X-ray computed tomography made hidden inscriptions readable.
Today it is kept in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

abschnitte.text: Around 1900, sponge divers from the island of Symi sheltered from a storm near the small island of **Antikythera**. It lies between Crete and the Greek mainland. On the sea floor they discovered an ancient **shipwreck** full of statues, coins and amphorae. The ship had sunk in the 1st century BC. Among the finds was an unremarkable, heavily encrusted lump of bronze.

Only in 1902 did people notice that there were **gear wheels** inside the lump. Today 82 fragments are known, in which about 30 bronze gear wheels survive. The device was about the size of a shoebox and sat in a wooden case. On the front and back there were dials with pointers. When you turned a handle, the pointers moved and showed the positions of the heavenly bodies.

The mechanism showed where the Sun and Moon stood in the sky and what phase the Moon was in. It could predict **solar eclipses** and lunar eclipses. It probably also showed the positions of the five planets known at the time. One dial even showed the dates of important contests such as the **Olympic Games**. So it was a kind of astronomical calendar.

For a long time the mechanism was a mystery. From the 1950s the physicist Derek de Solla Price studied it with X-ray images. From 2005 an international research team used **X-ray computed tomography**, which makes the inside visible layer by layer. This made it possible to read thousands of tiny letters, a kind of instruction manual on the device. To this day researchers build replicas to understand how it worked.

Such fine gearing appeared again in Europe only over a thousand years later, in **astronomical clocks**. The mechanism shows how advanced science was in ancient Greece. Nobody knows exactly who built it. Today the fragments are in the **National Archaeological Museum** in Athens. It is often called the oldest analogue computer in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with teeth round its edge that can drive another wheel.
The science of stars, planets and other heavenly bodies.
When the Sun or the Moon is hidden by another heavenly body.
An X-ray method that makes pictures of the inside of an object in thin layers.

gewusst: Because people hardly believed something so old could be so advanced, some at first thought the find was a fake or a later object.
The largest gear wheel of the mechanism has a diameter of about 13 centimetres.
The Zytglogge in Bern is also an astronomical clock, but it was built over 1500 years later.

teile.einleitung: The common swift is a fast migratory bird that spends almost its whole life in the air. In summer in Swiss towns you hear its shrill “sree” calls when groups chase around the houses. Although it looks similar, it is not closely related to swallows.
wichtigste: The swift spends almost its whole life in the air.
It has long, sickle-shaped wings and very short legs.
That is why it finds it hard to take off from flat ground.
It eats small insects that it catches in flight.
It often breeds in cracks and holes in buildings.
On migration it even sleeps while flying.
It leaves Switzerland as early as the start of August.

abschnitte.text: The swift is about 17 centimetres long and weighs about 40 grams, roughly as much as two chocolate bars. Its feathers are dark brownish black; only the throat is a little lighter. Typical are its long, **sickle-shaped wings**, which make it look like an anchor or a boomerang in flight. Its legs are very short, all four toes point forwards and have sharp claws. With them it can cling to walls, but it can hardly walk.

No other bird in Europe is so well adapted to the air. The swift eats, drinks and sleeps in flight. Researchers found that some swifts stay in the air without a break for about ten months outside the breeding season. To sleep, they climb to great heights and glide slowly along. If a swift lands on flat ground, it finds it hard to get up again because of its short legs and long wings.

The swift feeds on small **insects** and spiders carried up into the air by the wind. It catches them in flight with its wide-open beak. For its young it collects the prey in its throat pouch to make a small ball of food. Such a ball can contain hundreds of insects. In cold, rainy weather there are hardly any insects in the air, and then the birds often fly long distances to better hunting grounds.

Originally, swifts bred in cracks in rocks and holes in trees. Today they nest mainly in **buildings**, under roof tiles, in holes in walls and in roller-shutter boxes. They return to the same nest site every year. A pair usually lays two or three eggs, and the young stay in the nest for about six weeks. If food is short, the young can fall into a kind of cold torpor and survive a few days without food in this way.

Swifts arrive in Switzerland from Africa at the end of April or the beginning of May. As early as the start of August they leave again for their **winter quarters** south of the Sahara. Nest sites are often lost when houses are renovated, so the species needs help. The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach and many nature conservation groups recommend special **nest boxes** under the roof. In the Alps and in Ticino there is also the larger Alpine swift with its white belly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that flies to warmer regions in autumn and returns in spring.
The area where migratory birds spend the winter.
A stretchy skin on the throat in which the swift collects food.
An artificial breeding place that people put up for birds.

gewusst: In the course of its life, a swift flies a distance that would take it to the Moon and back several times.
Young swifts start their life in the air as soon as they leave the nest, and often do not land again for years.
If you find a swift on the ground, you should not simply throw it up into the air but ask a bird rescue centre.

teile.einleitung: Air pressure is the force with which the air presses on everything around it. Above us there is a layer of air many kilometres high, whose weight is constantly pressing on us without our feeling it. When you blow air into a balloon, the air inside presses on the skin of the balloon, and the balloon gets bigger.
wichtigste: Air pressure comes from the weight of the air above us.
At sea level, air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
The higher you go, the lower the air pressure becomes.
If you blow air into a balloon, the pressure inside rises and the balloon expands.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer.
High and low pressure areas determine our weather.
On high mountains, water boils below 100 degrees.

abschnitte.text: Air consists of countless tiny particles that are constantly flying about and bumping into everything. Air also has weight, even though it is light. So the whole layer of air above us presses on the Earth and on our bodies; this is **air pressure**. We do not feel it, because there is an equally strong counter-pressure inside our bodies. If you blow air into a **balloon**, there are more air particles inside pressing against the skin, and the balloon expands.

Air pressure is measured with a **barometer**. The first barometer was built by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli in 1643, using a glass tube full of mercury. Today air pressure is usually given in **hectopascals**, abbreviated hPa. At sea level it averages about 1013 hectopascals. That is roughly the weight of 10 tonnes on every square metre.

The higher you climb, the less air there is above you, and the air pressure falls. On the Jungfraujoch, at about 3450 metres, it is only about two thirds as high as at sea level. That is why you get out of breath more quickly there when climbing stairs. On high mountains, water boils below 100 degrees; at 3000 metres, for example, it boils at about 90 degrees. When you go up in a cable car, your ears “pop” because the pressure in your ear adjusts to the pressure outside.

Air pressure is not the same everywhere and is constantly changing. In a **high pressure area**, air sinks and the weather is usually fine and dry. In a **low pressure area**, air rises, clouds form and it often rains. The air flows from the high to the low, and this creates wind. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss measure air pressure in many places in order to forecast the weather.

In 1654 the mayor of Magdeburg, Otto von Guericke, showed the force of air pressure with a spectacular experiment. He put two metal hemispheres together and pumped out the air between them. After that, even several teams of horses could not pull the **Magdeburg hemispheres** apart. The air pressure from outside held them together. Suction cups that stick to smooth tiles use the same principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument for air pressure.
The unit in which air pressure is usually given, hPa for short.
A zone of high air pressure, which usually brings fine weather.
A zone of low air pressure, which often brings clouds and rain.

gewusst: Air pressure puts a weight of several tonnes on a child, which the child does not notice at all because of the counter-pressure in the body.
Because air pressure is low at great heights, aircraft cabins are pressurised artificially.
A sealed bag of crisps can become really puffed up on a high mountain pass, because the air pressure outside is lower.

teile.einleitung: A mutation is a change in the genetic material of a living thing. It can be tiny and affect only a single building block of the DNA, or it can change whole chromosomes. Without mutations there would be no evolution and so not the huge variety of living things on Earth.
wichtigste: A mutation is a change in the genetic material, the DNA of a living thing.
Mutations often happen by chance, for example through mistakes when the DNA is copied.
UV radiation, radioactive radiation and certain chemicals can also cause mutations.
Most mutations have no visible effect, some are harmful and a few bring advantages.
Only mutations in egg or sperm cells are passed on to offspring.
Mutations are the raw material of evolution.

abschnitte.text: The genetic material is like a huge instruction book stored in the **DNA**. In a mutation, something in this book is changed: a letter is swapped, missing or appears twice. The term comes from the Latin word “mutare”, which means “to change”. The Dutch botanist Hugo de Vries made it well known in biology around 1901.

In a **gene mutation**, only a single gene is affected, often only one building block. In a **chromosome mutation**, a piece of a chromosome is missing or put in the wrong way. In a genome mutation, the number of chromosomes is not right. A well-known example of this is trisomy 21, in which chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice.

Every time a cell divides, it has to copy all its DNA, and occasionally mistakes happen. Such spontaneous mutations happen without any outside cause. Substances or rays that cause mutations are called **mutagens**. These include the Sun's UV radiation, X-rays and substances in cigarette smoke. That is why sun protection is important, because too many mutations in skin cells can cause skin cancer.

Many mutations are neutral and are not noticed at all. Some cause diseases, for example sickle cell anaemia, in which the red blood cells have a sickle shape. Others bring advantages: thanks to a mutation, many people in Europe can digest milk well even as adults. White animals such as albino mice have a mutation that stops pigment from being made.

Viruses and bacteria multiply very quickly, so they also mutate often. This is how new variants of the **flu virus** appear every year, which is why the flu vaccine is regularly adjusted. From 2020, new variants of the coronavirus also kept appearing. Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics through mutations.

Mutations make sure that living things of the same species differ slightly. If a change is useful in a particular environment, those who carry it are more likely to survive and have more offspring. Charles Darwin called this process **natural selection**. Over many millions of years, whole new species arise from small changes in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in which the building instructions of a living thing are stored.
A section of DNA that contains the instructions for a particular characteristic.
A substance or radiation that can cause mutations.
A coiled thread of DNA; people normally have 46 of them in every body cell.

gewusst: Every person carries dozens of new mutations that neither their mother nor their father had.
Many breeds of dog and kinds of vegetable such as cauliflower go back to mutations that people deliberately went on breeding.
Blue eyes also originally arose through a mutation.

teile.einleitung: A model is a simplified picture of reality. It helps you understand something that is too big, too small, too complicated or too far away. From the globe to the atomic model to the climate model on a computer, researchers work with models all the time.
wichtigste: A scientific model is a simplified picture of reality.
Models leave out details on purpose and so are never quite complete.
A globe shows the Earth greatly reduced in size as a ball that can turn.
The Bohr model of the atom shows electrons on fixed paths around the nucleus.
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick presented the double helix model of DNA.
With computer models, researchers calculate how the climate might develop.
The particle model explains solid, liquid and gaseous substances.

abschnitte.text: A **model** shows only what matters for a particular question. A globe, for example, shows continents and seas, but not individual houses. By **leaving out** details, something complicated becomes understandable. That is why models are never quite complete; they are tools for thinking.

Some models can be touched, for example a model railway, an architectural model or a skeleton in the biology room. Many are reduced to **scale**: at 1:100, everything is a hundred times smaller than in reality. So a 15-centimetre model train at this scale stands for a real train 15 metres long. The **ball-and-stick model** shows molecules with coloured balls for atoms and sticks for the bonds.

Atoms are far too small to see directly. In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr developed the **Bohr model** of the atom, with electrons on fixed paths around the nucleus. Today we know that the picture is not quite right, but it still helps with learning. The **particle model** explains why substances are solid, liquid or gas: the tiny particles move about to different degrees depending on the state.

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick presented the model of DNA as a **double helix**, a kind of twisted rope ladder. They even built a large model out of metal parts for it. Maps, family trees and cycles in school books are also models. Each shows part of reality in an understandable way.

Many models today consist of mathematical equations on computers. **Climate models** calculate how the Earth's temperature might develop over the next few decades. Weather models predict the weather for the next few days; in Switzerland this is done by MeteoSwiss. Such models are constantly compared with real measurements and improved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified picture of something real.
States how much something has been reduced or enlarged, for example 1:100.
An idea of how an atom is built.
The shape of DNA, like a twisted rope ladder.
A model on a computer that acts out how something develops.

gewusst: A well-known saying among researchers goes roughly: all models are wrong, but some are useful.
Watson and Crick built their DNA model from small metal plates and rods.
A map is also a model, because it shows the curved Earth flat on paper.

teile.einleitung: Microplastics are tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres. Many of them are so small that you cannot see them with the naked eye. Today microplastics are found almost everywhere: in the sea, in Swiss lakes, in the soil, in the air and even in the snow of the Alps.
wichtigste: Plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres count as microplastics.
Primary microplastics are made small on purpose, for example as microbeads in scrubs.
Secondary microplastics form when larger pieces of plastic break down.
In Switzerland, wear from car tyres is the biggest source of microplastics in the environment.
Clothes made of synthetic fibres such as polyester lose fine fibres when washed.
Pollutants can build up on the surface of the particles.
The largest known garbage patch in the Pacific lies between Hawaii and California.

abschnitte.text: Plastic is made from crude oil or natural gas. If a piece of plastic breaks into pieces smaller than 5 millimetres, these are called **microplastics**. Much smaller particles still, which can only be seen with very powerful microscopes, are called **nanoplastics**. Microplastics can be beads, splinters, bits of film or fine fibres.

A distinction is made between **primary microplastics**, which are made small on purpose, and **secondary microplastics**, which form when larger pieces break down. Primary ones include microbeads, tiny plastic beads in scrubs or toothpaste. But the biggest source in Switzerland is **tyre wear**: on every journey, car tyres rub a little off on the road. Other sources are artificial turf pitches, shoe soles and rubbish thrown away that becomes brittle in the sun.

Many clothes are made of synthetic materials such as **polyester**, nylon or fleece. When washed, thousands of tiny fibres come loose from such textiles. They go with the waste water to the sewage treatment plant. Swiss sewage treatment plants hold back a large part, but some still reaches rivers and lakes.

A lot of plastic reaches the sea via rivers. Ocean currents collect the rubbish in huge **garbage patches**; the best known is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch between Hawaii and California. Plastics such as **polyethylene** and polypropylene float on the water because they are lighter than seawater. Other plastics sink and end up on the sea floor.

Fish, mussels, worms and seabirds often mistake plastic particles for food. Their stomachs then fill with something they cannot digest. In addition, **pollutants** from the water build up on the surface of the particles. Bacteria, algae and tiny organisms also settle on plastic rubbish; this community is called the **plastisphere**.

Using less throwaway plastic and disposing of rubbish properly helps. Clothes made of natural fibres such as cotton or wool do not shed microplastics. Full washing machines and lower temperatures release fewer fibres. How much microplastics harm human health is still being intensively **researched**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that is mostly made from crude oil.
Tiny plastic beads that are added on purpose to scrubs or cosmetics.
Fine rubber dust that forms when car tyres wear down on the road.
The community of bacteria, algae and tiny organisms on plastic rubbish in the sea.
A plant that cleans dirty waste water before it flows into rivers and lakes.

gewusst: Researchers have even found microplastics in the ice of the Arctic and on high mountain peaks.
A single wash load of fleece clothes can release thousands of synthetic fibres.
Plastic does not really break down in the sea; it just breaks into smaller and smaller pieces.

teile.einleitung: Margaret Mead was an American anthropologist, a researcher who studies the lives of people in different cultures. In the 1920s and 1930s she travelled to islands in the Pacific and wanted to find out how culture shapes the way children and young people grow up. She became one of the best-known scientists of her time.
wichtigste: Margaret Mead lived from 1901 to 1978.
She studied at Columbia University under Franz Boas.
In 1925 and 1926 she did research on Samoa for the first time.
Among the Manus people of the Admiralty Islands she studied childhood and returned decades later.
For decades she worked as a curator at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.
With the anthropologist Gregory Bateson, her husband, she did research on Bali.
In 1983 Derek Freeman sharply criticised her Samoa study.
In 1979, after her death, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

abschnitte.text: Margaret Mead was born in Philadelphia in the USA in 1901. Her parents were both teachers and researchers, which encouraged her curiosity early on. At Columbia University in New York she studied **anthropology** under Franz Boas, one of the founders of the subject. The anthropologist Ruth Benedict was also her teacher and became a close friend. Mead belongs to the so-called **culture and personality school**, which studied how a culture shapes people's character.

At only 23, Mead travelled alone to the island group of **Samoa** in the Pacific. There, in 1925 and 1926, she lived in villages for several months and watched how girls and young women grow up. She wanted to show that the teenage years are not equally difficult everywhere, but depend strongly on the culture. Her book about it was published in 1928 and became a bestseller. This made anthropology known to the general public.

Later Mead did research in New Guinea, today Papua New Guinea. Among the **Manus** of the Admiralty Islands she watched how children play and learn. Decades later she went back and saw how much life there had changed. With her husband Gregory Bateson she did research on **Bali** in the 1930s. The two took thousands of photos and film recordings, which was new in research at the time.

From 1926 Mead worked for decades at the **American Museum of Natural History** in New York, in the end as a curator. She wrote many books, gave lectures and spoke out in magazines and on television. She talked about family, upbringing, the environment and how different cultures live together. Many people saw her as a kind of explainer of the world. She died in New York in 1978.

Five years after her death, in 1983, the anthropologist **Derek Freeman** published a sharp criticism of her Samoa study. He claimed that Mead had misunderstood the Samoans and had jumped to conclusions too quickly. This led to a long dispute among experts that has still not been fully settled. What is undisputed is that Mead made fieldwork well known and paved the way into science for many women. In 1979, after her death, she received the **Presidential Medal of Freedom**, one of the highest honours in the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of human beings and their cultures.
Research in which you live among the people yourself and observe them.
An expert in a museum who looks after collections and plans exhibitions.
Everything a group of people has in common, such as language, customs and rules.

gewusst: On her travels Margaret Mead often carried a tall forked walking stick, which became her trademark.
Her daughter Mary Catherine Bateson also became an anthropologist.
For her research Mead always learned the language of the people she lived with.

teile.einleitung: A rain gauge, also called a precipitation gauge, is a device that measures how much rain or snow falls. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss need these measurements for weather reports and climate research. You can even make a simple rain gauge yourself.
wichtigste: A rain gauge measures how much rain falls.
The amount of rain is usually given in millimetres.
1 millimetre of rain is the same as 1 litre of water on one square metre.
A simple rain gauge has an opening at the top like a funnel.
You read off the amount of rain on a scale on the container.
You set it up outdoors, away from trees and buildings.
After reading it, you empty it so that you can measure again.

abschnitte.text: A rain gauge catches rain in a container with an exactly known opening. Experts also call it a **pluviometer**, after the Latin word pluvia for rain. It measures not only rain but all **precipitation**, including snow, hail and soft hail. Snow is melted for this and measured as water.

The amount of rain is given in **millimetres**. This means the height the water would reach on a level surface if it neither soaked in nor evaporated. 1 millimetre of rain means 1 litre of water on one square metre. In a heavy thunderstorm, 30 millimetres or more can fall in an hour, which is 30 litres on every square metre.

A simple rain gauge consists of a **funnel** and a clear container with a **scale**. The funnel collects the water and leads it into the container, where you can read off the amount. After reading it, you empty the gauge so that the next measurement starts at zero. Automatic devices have a **tipping bucket**, a small seesaw that tips over after each small amount of water and sends a signal to a computer as it does so.

A rain gauge must stand in the open, well away from trees, walls and roofs. Otherwise obstacles keep rain off, or the wind blows drops past the gauge. Usually the opening is about a metre above the ground, so that no splashes get in. In mountain areas that are hard to reach, **totalisers** are used, large collecting containers that are read only once or twice a year.

More than 2000 years ago, amounts of rain were already being measured in India in order to plan the harvest. In 1441 the Korean king Sejong had uniform metal rain gauges set up throughout his kingdom. In Europe, the Italian Benedetto Castelli built one of the first rain gauges in 1639. Today MeteoSwiss measures precipitation at many automatic stations and adds to the data with **weather radar**.

In Switzerland the amount of precipitation varies a lot. On the northern edge of the Alps and in Ticino it rains a lot, while the inner **Valais** is one of the driest areas in the country. The measurements help to forecast floods and to plan drinking water supplies. Farmers, power stations and municipalities also use the data.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that falls from the air to the Earth, for example rain, snow or hail.
The technical word for a rain gauge.
A row of lines with numbers from which you can read off a value.
A large rain collector in the mountains that measures over a long period.

gewusst: You can make a simple rain gauge from a PET bottle by cutting off the top and putting it in upside down as a funnel.
Just a few millimetres of rain an hour already counts as moderate rain.

teile.einleitung: Monte San Giorgio is a wooded mountain in the canton of Ticino on Lake Lugano. It is world-famous for its fossils from the Middle Triassic, which are about 240 million years old. Since 2003 the Swiss part has been a UNESCO World Heritage site.
wichtigste: Monte San Giorgio lies in southern Ticino on Lake Lugano, on the border with Italy.
Since 2003 the Swiss part has been a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The famous fossils come mainly from the Middle Triassic.
The mountain is known above all for marine reptiles and fish.
The fossils are so well preserved because they lay on the oxygen-poor floor of a lagoon.
Tanystropheus had an extremely long neck, which was longer than its body.
There is a fossil museum in Meride.

abschnitte.text: Monte San Giorgio is about 1100 metres high and lies between two arms of **Lake Lugano**. Part of the mountain belongs to Switzerland and part to Italy. Its slopes are densely wooded, and villages such as **Meride**, Riva San Vitale and Brusino Arsizio nestle at its foot. A cable car runs from Brusino up to Serpiano.

In the **Middle Triassic**, about 240 million years ago, there was a tropical sea with a lagoon here. At the bottom of this lagoon there was hardly any oxygen. So dead animals that sank there were not broken up by scavengers and decayed only a little. Fine mud covered them, and this is how exceptionally well-preserved **fossils** formed. Later the layers of rock were lifted up when the Alps were folded.

At Monte San Giorgio mainly **marine reptiles** and fish were found, but also crabs, insects and plants. The best known is **Tanystropheus**, a reptile with an extremely long neck that was longer than its body. **Helveticosaurus** is named after Switzerland, and the predatory land reptile **Ticinosuchus** after the canton of Ticino. Other finds are the ichthyosaur Mixosaurus and the fish Saurichthys with its long snout.

Fossils were already discovered here in the 19th century, when rock was quarried to extract oil. From the 1920s the palaeontologist **Bernhard Peyer** of the University of Zurich dug systematically on the mountain. The University of Zurich still does research there today, and many finds are in its Palaeontological Museum. In 2003 the Swiss part was declared a **UNESCO World Heritage site**, and in 2010 the Italian part was added.

In the village of **Meride** is the Monte San Giorgio Fossil Museum. The building was converted by the Ticino architect Mario Botta and shows original finds and models of the prehistoric animals. A nature trail leads through the woods to old excavation sites. But you are not allowed to collect fossils on the mountain yourself, because the area is protected.

Monte San Giorgio is important not only for fossils but also for plants and animals. Because of the mild climate, sweet chestnuts, hop hornbeams and rare orchids grow here. Many butterflies live in the meadows. So the area is also an important place for **nature conservation** in Ticino.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone.
A period of Earth's history from about 252 to 201 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs lived.
A shallow part of the sea cut off from the open sea by a barrier.
The science of the living things of past ages of the Earth.
A place that UNESCO protects because of its special importance for humanity.

gewusst: Tanystropheus had such a long neck that researchers wondered for a long time whether it was a pterosaur.
Monte San Giorgio was the first World Heritage site in Switzerland to be listed because of its fossils.
Some fish from Monte San Giorgio are so well preserved that you can still count their scales.

teile.einleitung: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a model that puts human needs into an order of importance. The psychologist Abraham Maslow presented it in 1943. It is best known as a pyramid, with self-actualisation at the top.
wichtigste: Abraham Maslow presented the hierarchy of needs in 1943.
Right at the bottom are the basic physical needs such as food, drink and sleep.
Directly above them come the needs for safety.
According to Maslow, higher needs only become important when the lower ones are met.
Maslow called the lower levels deficiency needs.
Maslow belongs to humanistic psychology.
The well-known pyramid was drawn by later authors, not by Maslow himself.
Critics say that the strict order of levels has not been proven scientifically.

abschnitte.text: Abraham Maslow was an American psychologist who lived from 1908 to 1970. He grew up in New York as the son of immigrants. Maslow was less interested in illnesses of the mind than in what makes people healthy and happy. This made him one of the founders of **humanistic psychology**. In 1943 he published an essay on human motivation in which he presented his hierarchy of needs.

Right at the bottom are the **basic physical needs**: eating, drinking, sleeping, warmth. Above them come the needs for safety, such as a roof over your head, health and an orderly life. The third level is social needs such as friendship, family and belonging. On the fourth level are recognition and esteem, meaning being praised and respected. At the very top is **self-actualisation**: developing your talents and becoming what you are capable of being.

Maslow believed that a person must first satisfy the lower needs before the higher ones become important. Someone who is very hungry hardly thinks about recognition or a hobby. He called the lower four levels **deficiency needs**, because their absence causes restlessness and a sense of lack. He called self-actualisation a growth need, which is never completely satisfied. In later writings he added self-transcendence above it, meaning working for something bigger than yourself.

A teacher knows that a child without breakfast finds it hard to learn, because a basic need is missing. Someone who feels left out in a class often has trouble concentrating on the work. Companies use the model to think about what motivates their staff. It is also used in **advertising**, because products often appeal to particular needs. In many school books in Switzerland the pyramid appears in economics or psychology.

Many experts say that the strict order of levels has not been clearly proven **empirically**, meaning through studies. People can, for example, stick closely together or create art despite poverty. Needs also have different importance in different cultures. What is more, Maslow himself never drew a pyramid; it comes from later authors. Even so, the model is popular because it is easy to understand and makes you think.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that a person requires or strongly wishes for.
An order of rank in which some things stand above others.
Developing your abilities and talents to the full.
The inner drive to do something.

gewusst: For his ideas Maslow studied the lives of famous people such as Albert Einstein, whom he considered especially self-actualised.
The word “pyramid” does not appear at all in Maslow's famous essay of 1943.
Some joke pictures today put Wi-Fi and battery as a new bottom level below the pyramid.

teile.einleitung: Natural selection is a process in nature in which the best-adapted living things have the best chance of surviving and passing on their characteristics. Over a great many generations, whole species change in this way. Charles Darwin made this idea famous in the 19th century.
wichtigste: In natural selection, the best-adapted living things pass on their characteristics most often.
A requirement is that there are differences between the living things of a species.
It is not a single animal that changes, but a population over many generations.
The phrase “survival of the fittest” comes from Herbert Spencer.
“Fittest” does not mean the strongest, but the best adapted.
When people deliberately breed animals or plants, this is called artificial selection.
Bacteria that become resistant to antibiotics show natural selection happening today.

abschnitte.text: From 1831 to 1836 the English naturalist **Charles Darwin** sailed round the world on the ship Beagle. He observed animals and plants, for example on the Galápagos Islands. In 1859 he published his famous book on the origin of species. Independently of him, the researcher **Alfred Russel Wallace** had had almost the same idea.

Living things of a species are never quite the same; they differ in **characteristics** such as size, colour or the shape of their beak. Usually more young are born than there will later be food and space for. Those that fit their environment better are more likely to survive and have more offspring. These inherit the helpful characteristics, and so over time they become more common in the **population**.

The economist **Thomas Malthus** wrote that populations can grow faster than food. This thought strongly inspired Darwin. Darwin also bred **pigeons** himself and saw how differently breeders could shape them. The phrase “survival of the fittest” was later coined by the philosopher Herbert Spencer, and Darwin took it up in later editions.

Among **Darwin's finches** on the Galápagos Islands, in dry years birds with strong beaks that can crack hard seeds are more likely to survive. In England during industrialisation, dark **peppered moths** became more common because they were harder to see on sooty tree trunks. In medicine, bacteria become resistant to **antibiotics**: if only the tough ones survive, it is exactly these that multiply. That is why you should only take antibiotics when a doctor prescribes them.

In **artificial selection**, people choose which animals or plants are allowed to breed. This is how the many breeds of dog, from the Chihuahua to the St Bernard, came from the wolf. Switzerland's breeds of cattle and many kinds of vegetable were also created by breeding. In nature, on the other hand, the environment does the choosing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Choosing; here, which living things survive and have offspring.
All the living things of a species that live in the same area.
A characteristic that helps a living thing in its environment.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
When bacteria are no longer killed by a medicine.

gewusst: Darwin waited over 20 years before publishing his theory.
All the dog breeds in the world are descended from the wolf and were created by artificial selection.
In bacteria, selection can show within a few days, because they multiply so quickly.

teile.einleitung: The Manhattan Project was a secret research programme of the USA during the Second World War, in which the first atomic bombs were built. Thousands of researchers, technicians and workers took part in it. The consequences of this project still shape the world today.
wichtigste: The Manhattan Project ran from 1942 to 1946 in the USA, with support from Great Britain and Canada.
The military head was General Leslie Groves, and the scientific head at Los Alamos was J. Robert Oppenheimer.
One trigger was the Einstein-Szilárd letter of 1939 to President Roosevelt.
In 1942 in Chicago, under Enrico Fermi, the first controlled nuclear chain reaction succeeded.
On 16 July 1945 the first atomic bomb exploded in the Trinity test in New Mexico.
In August 1945 atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
By 1945 the project had cost about 2 billion US dollars.

abschnitte.text: At the end of 1938, **nuclear fission**, which releases huge amounts of energy, was discovered in Berlin. Many researchers feared that Nazi Germany could build a weapon from it. In 1939 Leó Szilárd, together with Albert Einstein, wrote a letter to US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, the **Einstein-Szilárd letter**. It is considered one trigger for the American atomic programme, which from 1942 ran under the code name Manhattan Project.

Overall military command lay with General **Leslie Groves**. He chose the physicist **J. Robert Oppenheimer** as scientific director of the new laboratory at Los Alamos in the state of New Mexico. Many of the best-known physicists of the time worked there, including refugees from Europe. At its height, well over 100,000 people worked on the project in total, but most of them did not know what they were working on.

On 2 December 1942, under the leadership of **Enrico Fermi** in Chicago, the first controlled nuclear **chain reaction** succeeded. The reactor was made of graphite blocks and uranium and stood under a stand at one of the university's sports grounds. This proved that nuclear energy can be released in a controlled way. This experiment is also considered the birth of nuclear power stations.

The project had several large, secret sites. At **Oak Ridge** in Tennessee, uranium was enriched, meaning the share of fissile uranium-235 was increased. At **Hanford** in the state of Washington, plutonium was produced in reactors. At Los Alamos the bombs were developed. Whole towns were built for this within a few months.

On 16 July 1945, in the desert of New Mexico, the researchers set off the world's first atomic bomb; the test was called **Trinity**. On 6 August 1945 the US Air Force dropped the uranium bomb “Little Boy” on **Hiroshima**, and on 9 August a plutonium bomb on **Nagasaki**. Tens of thousands of people died at once, and many more later from injuries and radiation damage. Shortly afterwards Japan surrendered, and the Second World War ended.

After the war, an **arms race** began between the USA and the Soviet Union, which also tested an atomic bomb in 1949. Many of those involved, including Oppenheimer, later warned of the dangers of nuclear weapons. Today there are international treaties meant to limit the spread of nuclear weapons. The cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki remember the victims with memorials and campaign for a world without nuclear weapons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a great deal of energy.
A process in which each nuclear fission sets off further fissions.
The fissile form of the element uranium, used in atomic bombs and nuclear power stations.
A process that increases the share of uranium-235 in uranium.
A fissile element produced artificially in reactors.

gewusst: The name “Manhattan Project” comes from an army department that was based in Manhattan in New York at the start.
Officially the town of Los Alamos did not exist at all; post for researchers went to a post office box in Santa Fe.
The life of J. Robert Oppenheimer was told in the 2023 film “Oppenheimer”.

teile.einleitung: Nanoparticles are tiny particles that are only about 1 to 100 nanometres in size in at least one direction. Because they are so small, they often behave quite differently from the same substance in large pieces. Gold, for example, can look ruby red instead of golden yellow.
wichtigste: Nanoparticles are about 1 to 100 nanometres in size; a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
Compared with their mass, they have a huge surface and so are good catalysts.
A solution of very small gold nanoparticles is typically ruby red.
The colour comes from surface plasmon resonance.
Because of Brownian motion, nanoparticles stay suspended in liquids.
Gold particles a few nanometres across melt at a much lower temperature than solid gold.
Silver nanoparticles are used in textiles for an antibacterial effect.

abschnitte.text: A **nanometre** is a billionth of a metre. A nanometre is to a metre roughly what a hazelnut is to the whole Earth. Many nanoparticles consist of only a few hundred to a few thousand atoms. They can only be seen with special equipment such as the **electron microscope**.

If you divide a cube into smaller and smaller cubes, the total surface grows a lot. That is why nanoparticles have a great deal of surface on which chemical reactions can take place, and they make good **catalysts**. The melting point changes too: gold particles a few nanometres across melt well below the 1064 degrees of ordinary gold. In liquids they hardly sink, because the random bumps of the water molecules keep pushing them around; this is **Brownian motion**.

Very small gold nanoparticles make a liquid glow ruby red, and silver nanoparticles often yellow. The cause is **surface plasmon resonance**: the electrons at the surface vibrate in time with particular colours of light and absorb them. As early as 1857 the English researcher Michael Faraday made red gold solutions and studied them. Medieval church windows also often owe their glowing red to tiny gold particles in the glass.

Even the ancient Romans used nanoparticles without knowing it. The famous **Lycurgus Cup** from the 4th century AD contains tiny particles of gold and silver in its glass. When it is lit from outside it looks greenish, but when light shines through it from inside it glows red. Today it is in the British Museum in London.

There are two ways of making nanoparticles. In the **top-down** approach, a larger material is broken up more and more finely, for example by grinding. In the **bottom-up** approach, the particles are built up from single atoms or molecules, for example through chemical reactions in a solution. But nanoparticles also form quite naturally, for example in volcanic eruptions, forest fires or as soot from engines.

Many sun creams contain nanoparticles of **titanium dioxide** or zinc oxide, which block UV radiation without leaving a white film. Silver nanoparticles in sportswear are meant to hold back bacteria and so the smell of sweat. In car catalytic converters, nanoparticles of platinum and other metals help to clean exhaust gases. But because nanoparticles can also get into the body and the environment, their risks are being carefully researched.

begriffe.erklaerung: A billionth of a metre or a millionth of a millimetre.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself.
The jittery random movement of small particles caused by bumps from molecules.
Making something by breaking up larger material.
Making something by building it up from atoms or molecules.

gewusst: Brownian motion is named after the Scottish botanist Robert Brown, who in 1827 watched grains of pollen jittering in water.
The prefix “nano” comes from the Greek word for dwarf.
The soot in candle flames is also partly made of nanoparticles.

teile.einleitung: A majority is the larger part of a group, for example in a vote. When the majority decides, what counts is what more than half of the voters want. In Switzerland, with its many popular votes, the majority principle is especially important.
wichtigste: In a vote with two options, the majority has more than half of the votes.
In a simple vote, a proposal is accepted if there are more yes votes than no votes.
The smaller group is called the minority.
If both sides have the same number of votes, this is called a tie.
In a class of 24 children, at least 13 votes are needed for more than half.
In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden people vote by raising their hands at the Landsgemeinde.
In Switzerland, changes to the Federal Constitution need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A majority is the larger of two or more groups. If 15 children want to go to the zoo and 10 to the woods, the outing goes to the zoo if the majority decides. The smaller group is called the **minority**. Having the majority does not mean being right; it only means that more people hold that opinion. In a democracy it is therefore important to treat the minority fairly too.

An **absolute majority** means more than half of all the votes. Out of 9 children, 5 yes votes are enough, because 5 is more than 4.5. With a **relative majority**, whoever has the most votes wins, even if it is less than half. This matters when there are more than two options. For especially important decisions, a qualified majority is sometimes required, for example two thirds of the votes.

Sometimes both sides have exactly the same number of votes; this is called a **tie**. Then there has to be a rule about who decides. In many clubs and councils, the president has the **casting vote**. Otherwise, in a simple vote, a proposal counts as rejected, because there are not more yes votes than no votes. In a school class you can also discuss it again and vote once more.

In Switzerland, voters vote on factual questions several times a year. For a normal law, the **majority of the people** is enough, meaning more yes votes than no votes in the whole country. For a change to the Federal Constitution, the **majority of the cantons** is also needed: most of the cantons must agree too. This double majority makes sure that cantons with many inhabitants cannot simply outvote the small ones. It has happened that a proposal won the majority of the people but failed to win the majority of the cantons.

In the cantons of **Glarus** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden**, voters meet once a year in the open air for the Landsgemeinde. There they vote by raising their hands. The Landammann looks out over the crowd and estimates which side has the majority. If it is very close, the vote is held again or looked at more carefully. This form of direct democracy has existed in Switzerland for centuries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which many people decide on a question together.
The smaller group in a vote or in a society.
The majority of the cantons in a federal vote.
The deciding vote in a tie, usually held by the person in charge.

gewusst: At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden, men used to bring a sword or bayonet as proof of their right to vote, a custom that is partly still kept today.
Because six cantons have only half a cantonal vote, there are 23 cantonal votes in total for the majority of the cantons.
Animals such as bees or deer also sometimes make group decisions in which a kind of majority tips the balance.

teile.einleitung: A natural history museum shows and researches nature and its history: animals, plants, rocks, minerals and fossils. There you can look at stuffed animals up close, marvel at huge dinosaur skeletons and discover sparkling crystals. Behind the exhibitions, researchers work with enormous collections.
wichtigste: “Natural history” means that it is about the history of nature.
The collection includes many preserved animals, plants, rocks and fossils.
Researchers also study the finds for science.
The famous St Bernard dog Barry stands in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
In Basel, the Natural History Museum is on the cathedral hill.
In the Zurich village of Aathal there is a dinosaur museum with large skeletons.
Many fossils must not be touched, so that they are not damaged.

abschnitte.text: A **natural history museum** collects objects from nature and shows them to the public. These include **specimens** of animals, dried plants, rocks, minerals and fossils. The words natural history mean that the history of nature is told. So you find out how life on Earth has developed over millions of years.

Usually only a small part of the **collection** is on display. Storerooms often hold millions of objects, for example beetles, butterflies, bird skins and rock samples. Researchers study these finds, describe new species and compare how animals and plants have changed. So collections are like a huge archive of life.

In the **Natural History Museum in Bern** stands the most famous dog in Switzerland, the St Bernard **Barry**. He lived from 1800 to 1814 at the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass and is said to have rescued over 40 people from snow and cold. After his death he was preserved and brought to the museum. The large dioramas with animals from all over the world are also well known in Bern.

The **Natural History Museum in Basel** is in the old town near the cathedral and is one of the oldest in Switzerland. In Geneva there is a large natural history museum with many animals from all the continents. In the **Dinosaur Museum Aathal** in the canton of Zurich stand huge dinosaur skeletons, some of which come from the museum's own excavations in the USA. Many other towns such as Lucerne, Fribourg, St Gallen and Neuchâtel also have such museums.

Very well known is the Natural History Museum in **London**, whose magnificent building opened in 1881. In the Museum für Naturkunde in **Berlin** stands one of the largest mounted dinosaur skeletons in the world. The Natural History Museum in **Vienna** shows a huge collection of meteorites and minerals in a splendid building. The American Museum of Natural History in New York is also world-famous.

In many museums you can do some research yourself, for example looking at rocks and fossils under a magnifying glass or touching animal furs. Some museums offer courses, guided tours and nights at the museum for children. Real fossils, on the other hand, are often behind glass, because they are fragile and unique. If you look closely, you will discover exciting stories from Earth's history in every room.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal or part of a plant that has been preserved for a museum or research.
The remains or traces of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.
All the objects that a museum keeps and researches.
A display case that shows animals in a recreated natural setting.
A solid substance formed naturally, often as crystals.

gewusst: The famous little barrel around the neck of rescue dogs is a legend; Barry never wore one.
Some animal species were only recognised as new species decades after they were found in a museum collection.
Museum collections also keep animals that are now extinct, such as the thylacine.

teile.einleitung: Marie Curie was a Polish-French physicist and chemist and one of the most famous researchers of all time. She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, and together with her husband Pierre Curie she discovered the elements radium and polonium. She is the only person to have received Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.
wichtigste: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867 and died in France in 1934.
In 1903 she was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, in physics.
In 1911 she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry.
With Pierre Curie she discovered the elements radium and polonium in 1898.
She researched radioactivity and coined this term.
She was the first woman professor at the famous Sorbonne in Paris.
She died from the effects of the radiation she had worked with for years.

abschnitte.text: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw on 7 November 1867 as **Maria Skłodowska**. At that time Poland belonged to the Russian Empire, and women were not allowed to study at university there. Maria was an excellent pupil and first worked as a governess to save money. In 1891 she moved to Paris and studied physics and mathematics at the **Sorbonne**. There she met the physicist Pierre Curie, whom she married in 1895.

The physicist Henri Becquerel had discovered that uranium gives off invisible radiation. Marie Curie studied this radiation more closely and called the phenomenon **radioactivity**. Together with Pierre she found two new chemical elements in 1898. She named the first **polonium**, after her home country Poland. She named the second **radium**, after the Latin word for ray, because it glows and radiates strongly.

In 1903 Marie Curie, Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel jointly received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. Marie was thus the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. In 1906 Pierre died in an accident with a horse-drawn cart in Paris. Marie took over his professorship and so became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own for obtaining pure radium.

In the First World War, Marie Curie worked to help wounded soldiers. She had cars fitted with **X-ray machines**, which drove to the front. With these mobile X-ray stations, which were called “little Curies”, doctors could find bullets and broken bones in the body. Marie Curie went along herself and trained women as X-ray assistants. In this way she helped to save many lives.

At that time people did not yet know how dangerous radioactive radiation is. Marie Curie often carried radium in the pocket of her lab coat and became ill from the radiation. She died on 4 July 1934 in a sanatorium in the French Alps. Her daughter **Irène Joliot-Curie** also received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935. Today the chemical element curium is named after the Curies, and Marie's grave is in the Panthéon in Paris.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of some substances of giving off invisible, high-energy radiation by themselves.
A basic substance that consists of only one kind of atom, such as radium or oxygen.
One of the most important awards in the world for science, literature and peace.
A machine with which you can look inside the body, for example at bones.

gewusst: Marie Curie's notebooks are still so radioactive today that they are kept in lead boxes.
The Curie family won five Nobel Prizes in total, if you add together those of Marie, Pierre, their daughter Irène and their son-in-law Frédéric.
Marie Curie was the first woman to be buried in the Panthéon in Paris for her own achievements.

teile.einleitung: The neutron is a tiny particle in the nucleus of an atom. It carries no electric charge, so it is neutral, hence its name. Together with the protons, it holds together the atomic nuclei of almost all elements.
wichtigste: The neutron is a building block of the atomic nucleus.
It has no electric charge.
A neutron is almost exactly as heavy as a proton.
It was discovered in 1932 by the Briton James Chadwick.
Atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.
Neutrons play an important part in nuclear fission in nuclear power stations.

abschnitte.text: Every atom consists of a tiny **atomic nucleus** and a shell of electrons. In the nucleus sit positively charged **protons** and uncharged neutrons. Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons, meaning building blocks of the nucleus. Ordinary hydrogen is the only atom with no neutron at all in its nucleus.

A neutron is unimaginably small and light; it weighs about 0.0000000000000000000000017 grams. It is only very slightly heavier than a proton. A neutron itself is made of even smaller particles, the **quarks**, namely one up quark and two down quarks. Outside an atomic nucleus, a free neutron decays after about a quarter of an hour on average.

For a long time researchers knew only about protons and electrons. But atomic nuclei were heavier than the protons alone could explain. In 1932 the British physicist **James Chadwick** detected the missing particle. For this discovery he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935.

All the atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but not always the same number of neutrons. Such variants are called **isotopes**. Carbon usually has 6 neutrons; a rare variant has 8 neutrons and is called carbon-14. Experts can use this isotope to work out the age of old bones or wood.
