If a neutron hits a uranium nucleus, the nucleus can break into two parts and release new neutrons. This is **nuclear fission**, which provides heat for electricity in nuclear power stations such as Gösgen or Leibstadt. At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau there is a large neutron source. With its neutrons, researchers study the inside of materials, engines and even old works of art.

When a very large star explodes, a **neutron star** can be left behind. It consists almost entirely of tightly packed neutrons. Such a star is often only about 20 kilometres across, but heavier than our Sun. A teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A variant of an element with a different number of neutrons.
The breaking of a heavy atomic nucleus into smaller parts, which releases a lot of energy.

gewusst: Although the neutron has no charge, it behaves like a tiny magnet because of its quarks.
Because neutrons are uncharged, they can get deep into substances and so make their insides visible.
The word neutron comes from the Latin “neuter”, which means “neither of the two”.

t1dsekm5.t: Redefinition of the SI base units

teile.einleitung: Since 20 May 2019, all seven base units of the International System of Units, SI for short, have been defined by unchanging natural constants. Before that, the kilogram still depended on a lump of metal in a safe near Paris. With the redefinition, the metre, the kilogram and the others are the same everywhere in the world and for all time.
wichtigste: The redefinition of the SI base units came into force on 20 May 2019.
It was decided by the General Conference on Weights and Measures in November 2018.
Until 2019 the kilogram was the last unit defined by an object, the international prototype kilogram.
Since then the kilogram has been defined by the Planck constant.
Since 2019 the kelvin has been defined by the Boltzmann constant.
For the second, only the wording changed, not the content.
The gravitational constant is not one of the seven defining constants.

abschnitte.titel: What are the SI base units?
abschnitte.text: The **International System of Units**, SI, is used almost all over the world. It has seven base units: the second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. All other units, for example kilometres per hour or watts, can be derived from them. So that measurements agree worldwide, these units must be defined very precisely.

abschnitte.titel: The problem with the prototype kilogram
abschnitte.text: From 1889 the kilogram was defined by the **international prototype kilogram**, a small cylinder of platinum and iridium. It is kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris. Comparisons showed that it and its official copies had drifted apart by about 50 micrograms in roughly 100 years. That is less than a grain of sand, but too much for precise science.

In November 2018 in Versailles, the **General Conference on Weights and Measures** decided to define all the units by seven fixed numbers. These include the speed of light, the **Planck constant**, the elementary charge, the **Boltzmann constant** and the Avogadro constant. In addition there is a vibration frequency of the caesium atom and the luminous efficacy for the candela. The gravitational constant is not one of them, because it cannot be measured precisely enough.

The kilogram now depends on the Planck constant and is realised with a special balance, the **Kibble balance**. The ampere used to be defined by the force between two parallel wires carrying a current; now it is defined by the electric charge of an electron. The kelvin for temperature is defined by the Boltzmann constant. For the second and the metre only the wording changed, because they were already defined by natural constants before.

In everyday life nobody notices the change; a kilo of apples weighs exactly the same as before. It matters for very precise measurements in research and technology. In Switzerland, the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern takes care of precise measures. It has built its own Kibble balance to determine the kilogram according to the new definition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic unit from which other units are derived, such as the metre or the second.
A number in nature that never changes, for example the speed of light.
A metal cylinder that defined exactly one kilogram until 2019.
The science of accurate measuring.
A very precise balance that determines mass using electrical measurements.

gewusst: 20 May is World Metrology Day, which is why the redefinition came into force on exactly that day.
The prototype kilogram is kept under several glass bell jars in a safe.
The speed of light has been exactly fixed since 1983, which is why the metre is also defined by it.

teile.einleitung: A measuring jug is a container with a printed scale used to measure liquids. In the kitchen it helps to measure the right amount of milk, water or oil for a recipe. For the result to be right, you have to read it correctly.
wichtigste: You measure liquids with a measuring jug.
The scale usually shows millilitres, decilitres or litres.
A litre has 1000 millilitres.
You put the measuring jug on the table so that the liquid is level.
You read it at eye level.
The little spout at the rim is for pouring neatly.
In the laboratory, the narrow measuring cylinder is more accurate than a wide measuring jug.

abschnitte.text: A measuring jug is a beaker or jug made of plastic, glass or metal. A **scale** printed on the side shows how much liquid is in it. A kitchen measuring jug often holds half a litre or a whole litre. The scale usually shows **millilitres** and often decilitres too. At the top of the rim it has a little spout so that you can pour neatly.

To read it, you stand the measuring jug on a level surface such as the table. Then the liquid is level and you do not measure at a slant. Then you bend your knees and look at the scale **at eye level**. If you look from above, the amount looks bigger or smaller than it is. In narrow containers the surface of the water curves slightly at the edge; this curve is called the **meniscus**.

abschnitte.titel: Doing sums with a measuring jug
abschnitte.text: With a measuring jug you can add and subtract amounts. If you pour 200 ml and then another 150 ml into an empty jug, there are 350 ml in it. If a jug shows 400 ml and you pour away 100 ml, 300 ml are left. The conversions are important: 1 litre is 10 decilitres or 1000 millilitres. So one decilitre is 100 millilitres, which you need for many Swiss recipes.

Many measuring jugs also have scales for sugar, flour or rice in grams. These scales are different because the same amount of space weighs different amounts for different substances. A decilitre of sugar is heavier than a decilitre of flour. It is more accurate to weigh solid ingredients with **kitchen scales**. In the USA, recipes often measure in “cups”, with a capacity of about 2.4 decilitres.

In chemistry and biology laboratories, liquids are measured with special equipment. The **measuring cylinder** is narrow and tall, so the distance between two lines is bigger and you can read it more accurately. For even more precise amounts there are pipettes and volumetric flasks. Laboratory containers are often made of heat-resistant glass. Small measuring cups are also used at the pharmacy and the doctor's, for example for liquid medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: The division into lines and numbers on a measuring instrument.
A thousandth of a litre, abbreviated ml.
The slightly curved surface of a liquid in a narrow container.
A narrow, tall measuring container for accurate measurements in the laboratory.

gewusst: A millilitre of water weighs about one gram, so you can also measure water with scales.
Children's medicines often come with their own small measuring cup or syringe so that the amount is exactly right.
Cookbooks from the USA often say “cup”, which means a measuring cup used as a unit.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is the Earth's natural companion and shines brightly in the night sky. It is also called the Earth's satellite, because it constantly circles the Earth. It is the only heavenly body apart from the Earth that people have already walked on.
wichtigste: The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite.
On average it is about 384,400 kilometres away from the Earth.
The Moon does not shine by itself, but is lit by the Sun.
The phases of the Moon repeat about every 29.5 days.
Together with the Sun, the Moon causes the tides.
In 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to walk on the Moon.
There is no air to breathe and no liquid water on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The **Moon** has a diameter of about 3474 kilometres, a little more than a quarter of the Earth's. On average it is about 384,400 kilometres away; by car, without a break, it would take about half a year to get there. Its gravity is only about a sixth as strong as on Earth. That is why the astronauts could make big jumps there. The Moon has no real atmosphere, so the sky there is black even during the day.

The Moon does not shine by itself but is lit by the **Sun**. Depending on how the Sun, Earth and Moon are positioned in relation to one another, we see a different part of its lit side. This creates the **phases of the Moon**: new moon, waxing moon, full moon and waning moon. It takes about 29.5 days from one full moon to the next. Our word “month” comes from this too.

The Moon takes about 27 days to go once round the Earth, and in the same time it turns once on its own axis. That is why we always see the same side of the Moon, and the far side stays invisible from Earth. Its gravity pulls on the oceans and, together with the Sun, causes the **tides**, meaning high and low tide. When the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow, there is a **lunar eclipse**. The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year.

On the Moon you can see bright highlands and dark areas, which people used to think were seas and which are therefore called **maria**. In reality they are huge plains of solidified lava. Everywhere there are craters, made by the impact of lumps of rock. The Moon probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when a large body collided with the young Earth. The Moon then formed from the debris thrown out.

On 20 July 1969 the American mission **Apollo 11** landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon's surface, and Buzz Aldrin followed shortly afterwards. By 1972 a total of twelve astronauts had been on the Moon. As their first experiment, the astronauts set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern, which caught particles from the Sun. Today the USA, China and other countries are planning to send people to the Moon again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for the Moon, because it accompanies the Earth.
The different shapes in which we see the lit Moon, for example the full moon.
The regular rising and falling of sea level, also called high and low tide.
A bowl-shaped hollow made by the impact of a lump of rock.

gewusst: The astronauts' footprints can probably still be seen on the Moon today, because there is no wind to blow them away.
The solar wind sail from Bern was the only non-American experiment on the Apollo 11 mission.
Compared with the size of its planet, the Moon is one of the largest moons in the whole solar system.

teile.einleitung: The dandelion is one of the best-known meadow flowers in Switzerland. In spring it turns whole meadows bright yellow, and later the flower becomes the fluffy dandelion clock. It gets its name from its jagged leaves, which look like lion's teeth.
wichtigste: The dandelion grows in meadows, pastures, by paths and in gardens.
Its leaves are jagged like teeth, which is where its name comes from.
If you break the stem, a white milky sap comes out.
The flower closes in the evening and when it rains.
It has a long, deep taproot and is hard to pull out completely.
Young dandelion leaves can be eaten as salad.
Rabbits especially like to eat dandelion leaves.

abschnitte.text: The dandelion forms a flat **rosette of leaves** close to the ground. From its centre grow hollow stems, each with one yellow flower head on top. What looks like a single flower is in fact made of many small **ray florets**, often well over a hundred. That is why the dandelion belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower and the daisy.

After flowering, the flower head closes and opens again a few days later as a white ball. This **dandelion clock** is made of many fruits, each hanging from a fine little parachute of hairs. The wind carries the fruits far away like little parachutes. In this way the dandelion spreads very successfully to new areas.

A white, bitter **milky sap** flows in all parts of the plant. It makes stains on clothes that are hard to get out. Underground, the dandelion has a long **taproot** that reaches deep into the soil. If a piece of it stays in the ground when you pull it up, a new plant grows from it. Rubber can even be obtained from the milky sap of a related species.

Young dandelion leaves taste slightly bitter and are eaten as salad in spring. The flowers can be boiled with sugar into a sweet syrup, which some people call dandelion honey. In the past the roasted root was used as a coffee substitute. In folk medicine the dandelion is considered a remedy for digestion and the gall bladder.

In spring the dandelion is an important source of food for **bees**, bumblebees and butterflies. It provides plenty of nectar and pollen when little else is flowering yet. Rabbits, guinea pigs and tortoises love to eat its leaves. For farmers it is good fodder for cows, as long as it does not take over too much.

The dandelion's flowers open in the morning and close in the evening. They also stay closed in rain and dull weather. In this way the plant protects its pollen from getting wet. In Switzerland in April and May you often see whole **dandelion meadows**, especially on well-fertilised pastures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family whose flower heads are made of many small single flowers.
A long, strong main root that grows straight down into the ground.
Leaves spread out in a circle on the ground.
A white liquid that flows in some plants.

gewusst: The name dandelion comes from the French dent-de-lion, which means lion's tooth.
A single dandelion clock can carry over a hundred fruits with parachutes.
Researchers are studying the Russian dandelion because rubber for car tyres can be made from its milky sap.

teile.einleitung: Compassion means sensing how someone else is feeling and wanting to help them. If you feel compassion, you are happy with others or sad when things are going badly for them. Compassion holds families, school classes and whole societies together.
wichtigste: Compassion means sensing how others are feeling.
The technical word for being able to feel your way into others is empathy.
Without words, you can best tell how someone is feeling from their face.
Even babies often cry too when another baby nearby is crying.
Researchers have observed that chimpanzees comfort each other after a quarrel.
A sentence such as “I'm sorry that happened to you.” shows compassion.
Compassion can be practised, for example by listening and asking questions.

abschnitte.text: Compassion means noticing another person's feelings and sharing in them. This includes **empathy**, the ability to feel your way into others: you put yourself in the other person's position. But compassion also adds the wish to do the other person **good**. Other words for it are sympathy or mercy.

To feel compassion, you first have to recognise how someone is doing. The **face** reveals the most, meaning facial expressions such as tears, a lowered gaze or a smile. The voice and posture also show feelings. If you are not sure, you can simply **ask**: “How are you?”

Even **babies** react to the feelings of others; they often cry too when another baby cries. Toddlers sometimes bring a sad person their own cuddly toy. As they get older, children learn that others can feel and think differently from themselves. In psychology this ability is called **perspective-taking**.

Animals also show signs of compassion. The behavioural scientist Frans de Waal observed that **chimpanzees** comfort each other after a quarrel by hugging or kissing. Elephants look after injured members of the herd. In experiments, rats free trapped companions, even when they have to give up food to do so.

If a child falls over in the playground and cries, you show compassion by asking whether they are all right. If a **new child** joins the class, you can invite them to play. A simple sentence such as “I'm sorry that happened to you.” can make a big difference. **Listening**, without straight away giving advice, is also a form of compassion.

Compassion helps to settle quarrels and keep friendships going. It protects against **bullying**, because people who feel compassion do not look away. Many people volunteer out of compassion, for example with the Red Cross, which was founded by Henry Dunant from Geneva. It is also important to be kind to yourself; this is called **self-compassion**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to feel your way into others and put yourself in their place.
Showing that you care about what happens to others.
Being able to imagine how a situation looks to someone else.
Treating yourself in a kind and understanding way.

gewusst: Compassion can be catching: people who see helpfulness are more likely to help afterwards themselves.
Henry Dunant founded the Red Cross after he had seen the suffering of wounded soldiers after the Battle of Solferino in 1859.
Even children under two help adults of their own accord, for example by picking up something that has been dropped.

teile.einleitung: Seawater is the salty water of the oceans and seas, which covers most of the Earth's surface. On average it contains about 3.5 per cent salt, which is about 35 grams per litre. That is why it tastes salty and is not fit to drink.
wichtigste: Seawater contains on average about 3.5 per cent dissolved salts.
The most common salt in seawater is sodium chloride, which is table salt.
Most of the salt comes from rock on land, from which rivers wash it out.
Seawater only freezes at about minus 2 degrees Celsius.
If you drink seawater, you get even thirstier, because the body has to get rid of the salt again.
The Baltic Sea is only slightly salty, whereas the Red Sea and the Dead Sea are very salty.
Drinking water can be obtained from seawater by desalination.

abschnitte.text: About 97 per cent of all the water on Earth is salty seawater. It contains many dissolved substances, above all **sodium chloride**, which we know as table salt. There are also magnesium, calcium, potassium and sulphate. On average a litre of seawater contains about 35 grams of salt, which is about seven teaspoons. The salt content is called **salinity**.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the salt come from?
abschnitte.text: Over millions of years, rainwater dissolves tiny amounts of minerals from the rock on land. Rivers carry these substances into the sea. When seawater evaporates at the surface, the salt stays behind; only the water rises as vapour. In this way the salt in the sea has built up over the history of the Earth. Hot springs on the sea floor and volcanoes also release substances into the water.

Not all seas are equally salty. The **Baltic Sea** is only slightly salty, because many rivers bring fresh water and the link to the North Sea is narrow. The **Red Sea**, with about 4 per cent salt, is one of the saltiest seas connected to the world ocean, because a lot of water evaporates there. The **Dead Sea** is really a salt lake and is so salty that you can float on top without any effort. In river mouths, fresh and salt water mix to form **brackish water**.

Salt water is heavier than fresh water, which is why you float a little more easily in the sea than in a lake. Seawater only freezes at about minus 1.9 degrees Celsius. When it freezes into **sea ice**, most of the salt is given off into the surrounding water. That is why old sea ice is almost fresh. The cold, salty water below it sinks into the depths and drives great ocean currents.

Seawater is saltier than our blood. The kidneys have to get rid of the extra salt using a lot of water. As a result, the body loses more water than it has taken in, and you become even thirstier. In dry countries such as Saudi Arabia or Israel, drinking water is obtained by **desalination**. The water is evaporated or pressed through very fine filters, which is called **reverse osmosis**.

Switzerland has no sea, but it still has salt from a sea. About 200 million years ago a shallow sea lay here, which evaporated and left thick **layers of salt**. The Swiss salt works now take this salt out of the ground, for example at Schweizerhalle and Riburg on the Rhine and at Bex in the canton of Vaud. Water is pumped down deep, the salt dissolves and the brine is brought back up. Then the water is evaporated, and the salt is left.

begriffe.erklaerung: The salt content of water.
A mixture of fresh water and salt water, for example in river mouths.
A process for removing the salt from seawater.
The chemical name for table salt.
Water in which a lot of salt is dissolved.

gewusst: If you took all the salt out of the oceans, you could cover the land areas of the Earth with a thick layer of it.
The water in the Dead Sea is almost ten times saltier than in the Mediterranean.
Penguins and gulls can drink seawater, because they get rid of the salt through special glands on their heads.

teile.einleitung: Neumayer Station III is a German research station in Antarctica. It stands on stilts on the Ekström Ice Shelf and can be raised above the new snow every year. People live and do research here even during the icy, dark polar winter.
wichtigste: Neumayer Station III is run by Germany.
It opened in 2009.
The station stands on the Ekström Ice Shelf, meaning on floating ice.
Hydraulic stilts raise the building above the snow that builds up every year.
It is named after the geophysicist Georg von Neumayer.
In winter about ten people stay at the station.
An observatory continuously measures ozone and other components of the air.

abschnitte.text: The station lies on the coast of Antarctica, at the edge of the Weddell Sea. It stands on the **Ekström Ice Shelf**, a huge sheet of ice that floats on the sea and is about 200 metres thick. It is run by the **Alfred Wegener Institute** in Bremerhaven. In winter it gets very cold and stormy there, and the sun does not rise for weeks.

Earlier stations were buried under the snow, because new snow is added every year. That is why Neumayer Station III stands on **hydraulic stilts**. With these supports the whole building can be lifted so that it does not sink into the snow. Under the living and working area there is a garage in the snow, where vehicles and supplies are kept.

The station is named after **Georg von Neumayer**, a German geophysicist who strongly supported polar research in the 19th century. The first Georg von Neumayer Station was built in 1981, and the second in 1992. Both gradually sank into the ice. The third station opened in February 2009 and is planned to be used for a long time.

At the station there are observatories for weather, air chemistry and earthquake waves. They continuously measure **ozone** and other components of the atmosphere, which is important for understanding the ozone hole. With underwater microphones, whales and seals can also be heard in the sea under the ice. The series of measurements have been running for decades and help us to understand climate change.

From 2018, the greenhouse of the **EDEN ISS** project stood next to the station. Lettuce, cucumbers, tomatoes and herbs grew in it without soil, using only a nutrient solution and LED light. The project tested how astronauts might later grow fresh vegetables on the Moon or Mars. For the overwintering team, the fresh greens were a great joy.

In the Antarctic winter only about ten people stay at the station, including researchers, a doctor, a cook and technical experts. For months no aircraft can land, so the team has to solve everything by itself. In summer more people come, and ships bring fuel and supplies. Living in a small space calls for a lot of **team spirit**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thick sheet of ice that is joined to the land and floats on the sea.
When a small team spends the whole polar winter at a station.
Technology that uses liquid pressure to move heavy loads.
A gas in the atmosphere that protects us from harmful rays from the Sun.

gewusst: Because the ice shelf flows slowly towards the sea, the station moves a little with it every year.
During the polar night you can often see the southern lights in the sky at the station.
A colony of emperor penguins lives near the station.

teile.einleitung: The myelin sheath is a fatty covering around many nerve fibres, rather like the plastic insulation on an electric cable. It makes sure that nerve signals race through the body very quickly. Without it we could neither react quickly nor move skilfully.
wichtigste: The myelin sheath covers the long extensions of nerve cells, the axons.
Its main job is the electrical insulation of the nerve fibre.
In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells form the myelin sheath.
In the brain and spinal cord, oligodendrocytes take on this job.
Between the sections of myelin there are short bare spots, the nodes of Ranvier.
The signal jumps from node to node and so reaches up to about 100 metres a second.
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin sheaths.

abschnitte.text: A nerve cell passes signals on along a long extension, the **axon**. Many axons are wrapped in a covering of **myelin**, a substance made largely of fats. This covering stops electric charge from being lost on the way. In a similar way, the rubber covering of a cable protects the current in the copper wire.

The myelin sheath is formed by special helper cells that wrap themselves tightly around the axon many times. In the nerves of the arms, legs and organs these are the **Schwann cells**, named after the German researcher Theodor Schwann. In the brain and spinal cord they are called **oligodendrocytes**. A single oligodendrocyte can cover several axons at once.

The covering is not continuous but is briefly interrupted at intervals, usually of less than two millimetres. These gaps are called **nodes of Ranvier**, after the French doctor Louis-Antoine Ranvier. The signal only has to be produced afresh at these points and, as it were, jumps on in between. This **saltatory conduction** is much faster than conduction in fibres without a covering, which often manage only about 1 metre a second.

In the brain, a great many covered nerve fibres lie close together. Because myelin is fatty, these areas look pale and are called **white matter**. The areas with many cell bodies, on the other hand, look darker and are called grey matter. So the white matter connects different parts of the brain like a network of cables.

In newborn babies, many nerve fibres are not yet fully covered. This is one reason why babies only gradually learn to control their movements. Myelin goes on forming throughout childhood and the teenage years. Especially in the front part of the brain, which helps with planning, it continues into young adulthood.

In **multiple sclerosis**, MS for short, the body's own immune system attacks the myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord. As a result, signals are passed on more slowly or are disturbed. People affected may, for example, have problems with their sight, tingling or difficulty walking. MS is not infectious and today it can often be well slowed down with medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long extension of a nerve cell that passes on signals.
The fatty substance that the insulating covering is made of.
A short bare spot between two sections of myelin.
Jumping, from the Latin word for jumping or dancing.
A helper cell in the brain and spinal cord that forms myelin.

gewusst: At about 100 metres a second, a nerve signal would be faster than a car on the motorway, at over 300 kilometres an hour.
The name myelin comes from the Greek word for marrow.
Vertebrates such as fish also have myelin sheaths, but many invertebrates such as insects do not.

teile.einleitung: The molecular clock is a method that researchers use to work out from genetic material when two species or lines of descent separated. It is based on the idea that DNA changes at a roughly steady rate over time. The more differences there are, the longer ago the separation happened.
wichtigste: The molecular clock is based on the assumption that mutations build up at a roughly constant rate.
Émile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling proposed the idea in 1962.
The clock is usually calibrated with fossils of known age.
In animals, mitochondrial DNA is especially suitable for short periods, because it changes faster.
Selectively neutral sites in the DNA tick especially evenly.
The clock is not perfectly accurate, because mutation rates differ between lines.
According to molecular estimates, humans and chimpanzees separated about 5 to 10 million years ago.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing carries its genetic information in its **DNA** or in proteins. Each time it is passed on, small changes can arise, the **mutations**. If they build up at roughly the same speed, they can be used like the ticking of a clock. If you compare the DNA of two species, the number of differences shows how long they have been going their separate ways.

In 1962 the researchers **Émile Zuckerkandl** and **Linus Pauling** proposed the idea. They compared the protein haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, in different animals. They noticed that the differences grew with the time since the species separated. Later the Japanese researcher Motoo Kimura provided an explanation with his **neutral theory**: many changes are neither useful nor harmful and so build up evenly.

For the clock to show real years, it has to be **calibrated**. For this, **fossils** of known age are usually used. If you know from finds, for example, when two groups of animals separated, you can work out the mutation rate per million years. If the difference grows by 2 per cent per million years and two species differ by 10 per cent, they separated 5 million years ago.

Not all parts of the DNA tick equally fast. **Selectively neutral** sites, such as many synonymous sites where a change does not alter the protein, tick especially evenly. The **mitochondrial DNA** of animals changes faster than most nuclear DNA and is therefore suitable for short periods. For very old separations, on the other hand, slowly changing genes are used.

With the molecular clock it is estimated that the lines of **humans and chimpanzees** separated about 5 to 10 million years ago. The age of Mitochondrial Eve was also worked out in this way. Researchers also use the method to trace the origin of viruses, for example flu or Covid-19. In this way they can estimate when a new virus first appeared.

The molecular clock is not perfectly accurate. **Mutation rates** differ between lines, for example in animals with short or long generation times. The fossils used for calibration also have uncertainties. That is why researchers always give their results as a **time range** and check them with several genes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A random change in the genetic material.
To set a measuring method using known values.
The idea that many mutations are neither useful nor harmful.
A remain or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone.

gewusst: The molecular clock does not tick in seconds but in mutations over thousands or millions of years.
The method can also be used to compare species of which there are hardly any fossils.
In viruses, the molecular clock ticks so fast that changes can be seen within a few months.

teile.einleitung: Nescafé is a soluble coffee, also called instant coffee, invented by the Swiss company Nestlé. You simply put the powder into hot water and have a cup of coffee straight away, without any coffee machine. Nescafé has been on the market since 1938 and today is one of the best-known coffee brands in the world.
wichtigste: The special thing about Nescafé is that the coffee powder dissolves completely in water.
Nescafé was invented by the Swiss company Nestlé.
The name is made from the words Nestlé and café.
In 1930 Brazil asked Nestlé for help because there was far too much coffee.
The research group was led by Max Morgenthaler.
Nescafé came onto the market in 1938.
It was first sold in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Nescafé is an **instant coffee**, meaning a coffee that is ready straight away. It consists of dried coffee extract, which dissolves in hot water. Unlike ground coffee, it leaves no coffee grounds behind. The name Nescafé combines the words **Nestlé** and café.

Around 1930 **Brazil**, already the largest coffee producer in the world, had far too much coffee. Prices had collapsed after the Great Depression, and large amounts of coffee beans were in danger of spoiling. So in 1930 the Brazilian Coffee Institute asked Nestlé whether the coffee could be made to keep. The idea was a coffee powder that would store for a long time and be quick to prepare.

At Nestlé, the Swiss chemist **Max Morgenthaler** and his team took on the task. Earlier instant coffees often tasted stale, because a lot of the aroma was lost during drying. Morgenthaler spent years looking for a process that would keep the taste and smell better. After about seven years of research the powder was ready.

First, coffee beans are roasted, ground and brewed with hot water into a strong coffee extract. In **spray drying**, this extract is sprayed in fine droplets into a tower of hot air, where the water evaporates at once and powder is left. In **freeze drying**, the extract is first frozen and then the ice is removed in a vacuum, which protects the aroma even more. This produces the well-known coarse granules.

On 1 April 1938 Nescafé came onto the market in **Switzerland**, and soon afterwards in Britain and the USA too. In the Second World War, instant coffee became very popular with American soldiers because it was light and kept for a long time. After the war, Nescafé spread to many countries around the world. This made Nestlé, with its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva, even better known.

Nescafé also led to new drinks. In 1957 a Nestlé employee in Greece invented the cold, shaken **frappé** when he shook Nescafé with cold water in a beaker. Today instant coffee comes in many kinds, with milk, decaffeinated or as cappuccino powder. But because of the caffeine, coffee is not suitable for children.

begriffe.erklaerung: Soluble coffee that dissolves in water straight away.
A concentrated preparation; here, strong brewed coffee.
Drying in which a liquid is sprayed in fine droplets into hot air.
Drying in which ice turns directly into vapour in a vacuum.
A substance in coffee, tea and some drinks that keeps you awake.

gewusst: Nescafé came onto the market on 1 April of all days, but it was not an April Fool's joke.
The Greek frappé was created in 1957 at a trade fair in Thessaloniki.
One or two teaspoons of powder are enough for a cup of Nescafé.

teile.einleitung: Nicolaus Copernicus was an astronomer and scholar who lived from 1473 to 1543. He claimed that it is not the Earth but the Sun that stands at the centre, and that the Earth circles around it. This idea changed people's view of the world for ever.
wichtigste: Copernicus was born in 1473 in Thorn (today Toruń in Poland) and died in 1543 in Frauenburg.
For most of his life he worked as a canon in Warmia.
He developed the heliocentric model, in which the planets circle the Sun.
His main work “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium” was published in 1543, the year of his death.
The young scholar Georg Joachim Rheticus from Feldkirch urged him to publish.
Copernicus also wrote a well-known essay on money.
Today people speak of a “Copernican revolution” when a way of seeing things changes completely.

abschnitte.text: Nicolaus Copernicus was born on 19 February 1473 in **Thorn** on the River Vistula. His father was a merchant and died early, so his uncle, a bishop, looked after him. Copernicus studied in Kraków and later in Italy, including in Bologna and Padua. He learned astronomy, mathematics, medicine and church law. So he was a scholar with many interests, as was common at the time.

After he returned, Copernicus became a **canon** in Frauenburg in **Warmia**, a region in what is now northern Poland. A canon was a clergyman who helped to run a diocese. Copernicus looked after estates and finances and also worked as a doctor. In his free time he watched the sky and calculated the paths of the planets. So astronomy was really his hobby alongside his job.

Since ancient times, most people had believed in the **geocentric model** according to Ptolemy. In it, the Earth stands still at the centre, and the Sun, Moon and planets circle around it. Copernicus instead proposed the **heliocentric model**: the Sun stands at the centre, and the Earth is a planet that moves around it. The Earth also turns once a day on its own axis, which is why the Sun seems to rise and set. However, Copernicus still assumed that the planets move on perfect circles.

Copernicus hesitated for many years to publish his ideas, because he feared mockery and opposition. In 1539 the young mathematician **Georg Joachim Rheticus** from Feldkirch in Vorarlberg came to see him in Frauenburg. Rheticus was enthusiastic and urged him to have his work printed at last. So in 1543 the book **“De revolutionibus orbium coelestium”** was published in Nuremberg, in English “On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres”. According to legend, Copernicus only received the first printed copy on his deathbed.

Copernicus also studied **money**. In his time there were many coins that contained less and less silver. In an essay he showed that bad money drives out good money: people keep the valuable coins and pay with the bad ones. Today this idea is often named after the Englishman Thomas Gresham, but Copernicus had described it earlier.

Later researchers such as Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei built on Copernicus's ideas. Kepler found out that the planets' paths are not circles but ellipses. The idea that the Earth is not the centre of the universe was a huge step for science. Today a fundamental change in the way of seeing things is called a **Copernican revolution**. A crater on the Moon and the chemical element copernicium are named after Copernicus.

begriffe.erklaerung: A view of the world in which the Sun stands at the centre.
An old view of the world in which the Earth stands at the centre.
A clergyman who helps to run a diocese.
The science of the stars, the planets and the universe.

gewusst: Copernicus made his observations without a telescope, because it was only invented after his death.
His grave in Frauenburg Cathedral was only rediscovered in 2005 and confirmed with the help of DNA traces.
The element copernicium, with the atomic number 112, bears his name.

teile.einleitung: Measurement uncertainty states the range in which the true value of a measured quantity probably lies. Instead of just “50.0 cm”, you write for example “(50.0 ± 0.5) cm”. Then everyone can see at once how reliable a measurement result is.
wichtigste: Every measurement result consists of a value and its uncertainty.
The international guide to this is called the GUM, the “Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement”.
Type A is based on the statistical analysis of series of measurements, Type B on other information.
With the coverage factor k = 2, the stated range covers about 95 per cent of the values.
Independent contributions are added in quadrature, so 3 mg and 4 mg become 5 mg.
Systematic deviations cannot be reduced by repeating many times.
Precision describes how close repeated measured values are to each other.

abschnitte.text: No measurement result is completely exact, so you give a **range**. Writing (50.0 ± 0.5) cm means that the true value probably lies between 49.5 cm and 50.5 cm. If you divide the uncertainty by the measured value, you get the **relative uncertainty**, here 1 per cent. In this way even very different measurements can be compared.

So that all laboratories worldwide calculate in the same way, there is the **GUM**, the “Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement”. It was first published in 1993 and later revised. It is published by international organisations, including the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris. The Swiss institute **METAS** also works by these rules.

The GUM distinguishes two ways of working out uncertainties. In **Type A**, you measure several times and analyse the series of measurements statistically, for example with the standard deviation. In **Type B**, you use other information, for example manufacturer's data, a calibration certificate or experience. Both types count equally and are combined at the end.

If you measure often, the mean becomes more accurate. You get the standard deviation of the mean by dividing the standard deviation by the **square root** of the number of measurements. With 16 measurements and 0.4 mm, that gives 0.4 mm divided by 4, so 0.1 mm. Independent contributions are added in quadrature, similar to Pythagoras' theorem: 3 mg and 4 mg give a **combined standard uncertainty** of 5 mg. If you multiply by the **coverage factor** k = 2, the range covers about 95 per cent of the possible values.

People like to imagine measurements as arrows on a target. If all the hits are close together, the measurement is **precise**. If on average they are exactly in the centre, it is **true**. A measurement can be precise and still be off target if there is a systematic deviation. This does not disappear through repetition, only through calibration.

Measurement uncertainties are important wherever things have to be measured precisely. In medicine, laboratory values decide on treatments, and in industry parts have to fit together. In speed checks, the police take a **safety margin** off the measured value. That way nobody is fined unfairly because of a measurement error.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how widely measured values are spread around their mean.
The number k by which the uncertainty is enlarged to cover more values.
How close repeated measured values are to each other.
The uncertainty divided by the measured value, often as a percentage.
The international guide to stating measurement uncertainty.

gewusst: To make a measurement twice as precise, you have to repeat it about four times as often.
Measurement uncertainty also plays a part in sports records, which is why sprint times are measured to hundredths of a second.
Even the best atomic clocks have a measurement uncertainty, even if it is tiny.

teile.einleitung: Mimik is the German technical term for a person's facial expressions. With our eyes, mouth, forehead and nose we show how we feel, often without saying a single word. That is why our face is one of the most important tools for communicating with others.
wichtigste: Facial expressions are the expressions on a person's face.
With our facial expression we show our feelings.
When we are surprised, our eyebrows move upwards.
You can recognise a real, warm smile by the little wrinkles at the eyes.
If something smells disgusting, we often wrinkle our nose.
A smile is understood as friendly almost everywhere in the world.
A wink with one eye often means that something is only a joke.

abschnitte.text: **Facial expressions** are all the visible movements of the face. They are made by the **facial muscles**, of which we have more than 40. These muscles pull on the skin and so change the shape of the mouth, eyes, nose and forehead. Together with **gestures**, meaning movements of the hands, and posture, facial expressions are part of **body language**.

Every feeling has typical signs. With **surprise**, the eyebrows go up and the mouth opens. With disgust, we wrinkle our nose and pull up our upper lip. With anger, the eyebrows draw together, and with sadness the corners of the mouth droop. When thinking, many people wrinkle their forehead; this is called **frowning**.

Not every smile is the same. In a polite smile, it is mainly the mouth that moves. In a real, warm smile, the muscle around the eyes also tightens, and small **laughter lines** appear. It is called the **Duchenne smile** after the French doctor Guillaume Duchenne, who studied it in the 19th century.

As early as 1872, the naturalist Charles Darwin wrote a book about the expression of feelings in humans and animals. Later the psychologist Paul Ekman travelled to peoples who had hardly any contact with the rest of the world. He found that some **basic emotions** such as joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise are recognised in a similar way almost everywhere. A smile is understood as friendly almost everywhere. But when and how strongly you may show feelings differs from culture to culture.

Some facial expressions are signals rather than feelings. If you **wink** with one eye, you often want to say that something is only a joke. Even babies copy faces and learn in this way to understand facial expressions. Actors practise their facial expressions for a long time so that the audience understands their feelings. In text messages, **emojis** replace some facial expressions, because you cannot see the other person's face.

Animals also show feelings on their faces. Dogs have a special muscle above their eyes with which they can make “puppy-dog eyes”. When playing, chimpanzees show an open **play face** that is reminiscent of our laughter. Horses and cats show with their ears and eyes whether they are relaxed or afraid.

begriffe.erklaerung: The expressive movements of the face.
Movements of the hands and arms with which you express something.
Everything we communicate with our body without words.
Feelings such as joy, sadness, anger and fear that all people know.

gewusst: Even newborn babies can copy faces, for example sticking out their tongue.
People who have been blind from birth smile when happy just like sighted people.
A fake smile often disappears more quickly than a real one.

teile.einleitung: A food chain shows who eats whom and how energy is passed on from one living thing to the next. One example is the chain grass, grasshopper, frog. At the start there is almost always a plant, which gets its energy from sunlight.
wichtigste: A food chain describes who eats whom.
At the start there are usually green plants, which get energy from sunlight.
Plant-eaters such as the roe deer eat plants.
Meat-eaters such as the lynx hunt other animals.
Omnivores eat both plants and meat.
At the end, fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals.
In the mountains the golden eagle is often at the end of the chain.

abschnitte.text: A **food chain** is a row of living things in which each is eaten by the next. It is often written with arrows, for example leaf, caterpillar, tit, sparrowhawk. The arrows show the direction in which food and energy flow. Each link in the chain depends on the one before.

Green plants, algae and some bacteria are the **producers**. With the help of sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, they make sugar; this is called **photosynthesis**. This sugar contains the energy that is later passed on through the whole chain. So without plants there would be no food for animals.

Animals are **consumers**. Plant-eaters such as the roe deer, the hare or the grasshopper are the first consumers. Meat-eaters such as the frog, the fox or the lynx eat other animals and come further along. Omnivores such as the wild boar, the badger or humans can appear at several places in a chain.

When plants and animals die, they do not lie there for ever. Fungi, bacteria, earthworms and woodlice break them down; they are called **decomposers**. This produces nutrients that go back into the soil. The plants take up these nutrients with their roots, and the cycle starts again.

In a meadow in the Central Plateau, the grasshopper eats the grass, the frog eats the grasshopper and the grey heron eats the frog. In the forest, the roe deer eats buds and herbs, and the lynx hunts the roe deer. In the Alps, the marmot eats grasses and herbs and is caught by the **golden eagle**. In the lake, tiny crustaceans eat algae, small fish eat the crustaceans and the pike eats the small fish.

Food chains show how closely living things are linked to each other. If one link disappears, this has consequences for the others. If there are fewer insects, for example, birds and bats also find less food. That is why it is important to protect the variety of living things.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that makes its own food with sunlight, for example a plant.
A living thing that eats other living things.
A breaker-down such as fungi and bacteria, which break down dead material.
An animal that eats both plants and meat.
The process in which plants make sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.

gewusst: A single lynx eats about one roe deer or chamois a week.
In the deep sea there are food chains that do not start with sunlight but with bacteria at hot springs.
During the breeding season, a tit needs many hundreds of caterpillars a day for its young.

teile.einleitung: Maggi is a well-known brand of soups, stock and seasoning that started in Switzerland. It was founded by Julius Maggi from Thurgau, who in the 19th century wanted to develop cheap and nourishing ready-made food for working families. Many people still know the brown bottle of Maggi seasoning today.
wichtigste: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld in 1846.
His factory was in Kemptthal near Winterthur.
He made his first ready-made soups from pea and bean flour.
In 1886 he invented a liquid seasoning, Maggi seasoning.
Around 1908 the Maggi stock cube came onto the market.
With hot water, a stock cube quickly becomes soup.
Since 1947 Maggi has belonged to the food company Nestlé.

abschnitte.text: Julius Maggi was born in 1846 in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. His father came from Italy and later ran a mill in Kemptthal. Julius took over the mill, but the flour business went badly. So he looked for new products. He died in 1912 and left behind a company that was active in many countries.

In the 19th century many people worked long hours in factories and had little time to cook. The factory inspector Fridolin Schuler campaigned for better food for working families. Together with him, from 1884 Maggi developed a flour made from **pulses**, meaning peas and beans. Nourishing, protein-rich soups could be cooked from it quickly. This was one of the very first **ready-made soups**.

To make his soups taste better, Julius Maggi invented a liquid seasoning in 1886. It went on sale in a typical brown bottle with a yellow and red label. Around 1908 came the **stock cube**, a pressed cube of salt, fat and spices. If you add hot water, you get stock in a few minutes. Such cubes were practical because they keep for a long time and are easy to carry.

The factory in **Kemptthal** near Winterthur became a large industrial plant with its own railway station. As early as 1887 Maggi also opened a factory in Singen in Germany, where the brand became especially popular. In 1947 the company merged with **Nestlé**. Today the old factory site in Kemptthal is used for businesses and homes. Maggi products are now sold in many countries, for example in Germany, Africa and Asia.

Ready-made soups and stock are practical when you need something quickly. But they often contain a lot of **salt**, so you should not use them too often. Home-made soups from fresh vegetables are usually healthier. Even so, many cooks use stock as a base for risotto, sauces or soups. In this way Julius Maggi's idea lives on in many kitchens.

begriffe.erklaerung: A clear, strong broth used as a soup or as a base for cooking.
Seeds of plants such as peas, beans and lentils, which contain a lot of protein.
A substance that gives food more flavour.
A soup that is already prepared and only needs to be cooked with water.

gewusst: The herb lovage is often called “Maggi herb” in German because it smells similar, even though Maggi seasoning contains no lovage at all.
The shape of the Maggi seasoning bottle has stayed almost the same for over a hundred years.
For a time, Maggi worked on his advertising with Frank Wedekind, who later became a famous writer.

teile.einleitung: A Mars rover is a remote-controlled vehicle that explores the surface of the planet Mars. Rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance are laboratories on wheels with cameras, drills and measuring instruments. They look for traces of water and of past life on the Red Planet.
wichtigste: A Mars rover is a vehicle that explores Mars and examines rock and soil.
Robots are sent instead of people because the journey is long and dangerous.
Mars is reddish because its dust contains a lot of iron oxide, which is rust.
Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012, Perseverance in 2021.
Perseverance took a small helicopter called Ingenuity with it.
The big rovers Curiosity and Perseverance each have six wheels.
Mars rovers drive slowly and carefully, because nobody can repair them.

abschnitte.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and about half the size of the Earth. Its surface is **reddish** because the dust contains a lot of iron oxide, a kind of rust. It is very cold there, and the air is much thinner than on Earth. Researchers believe that billions of years ago there were rivers and lakes on Mars, and they wonder whether **life** once existed there.

The journey to Mars takes about seven months, and on the planet there is no air to breathe and a lot of dangerous radiation. That is why **robots** are sent instead of people. Depending on the distance, radio signals take between about 4 and 24 minutes to get from the Earth to Mars. So you cannot steer a rover like a toy car; it has to do many things by itself. Because nobody can repair it, it drives very slowly and carefully.

The first Mars rover was the little **Sojourner**, which landed in 1997 and was only the size of a microwave oven. In 2004 came the twin rovers **Spirit** and **Opportunity**, which were planned to last only three months. But Opportunity kept going for over 14 years and covered more than 45 kilometres. In 2021 the Chinese rover **Zhurong** also landed on Mars.

NASA's rover **Curiosity** landed in Gale Crater in August 2012. It is about the size of a small car, has six wheels and is powered by a radioactive battery instead of solar cells. With a laser it can examine stones from several metres away. Curiosity found evidence that there used to be a lake in the crater in which life would have been possible.

**Perseverance** landed in February 2021 in Jezero Crater, where a river once flowed into a lake. It collects rock samples in small tubes, which a later mission is meant to bring back to Earth. It took with it the small helicopter **Ingenuity**, the first aircraft to fly on another planet. It managed over 70 flights before its mission ended in 2024.

Switzerland also takes part in research on Mars. The University of Bern built the camera **CaSSIS**, which since 2018 has been taking colour pictures of the Martian surface from a European satellite. Swiss companies and universities supply parts for space missions. The European Space Agency, ESA, is planning a mission of its own with the rover **Rosalind Franklin**, which is meant to drill deep into the Martian soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remote-controlled vehicle for exploring a planet or moon.
A round hollow, often made by the impact of a meteorite.
A compound of iron and oxygen, known from rust.
A small piece of rock that is to be examined closely.

gewusst: The rover Opportunity was planned for 90 Martian days and in the end lasted over 14 years.
On its first anniversary on Mars, Curiosity sang “Happy Birthday” to itself by making notes with one of its instruments.
A day on Mars lasts only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A tape measure is a long tape that can be rolled up, with a scale on it, used to measure lengths. There are soft tape measures for dressmaking and stiff ones for tradespeople. With them you can also measure things that are round or much longer than a ruler.
wichtigste: A tape measure is used for measuring lengths.
Dressmakers use a soft tape measure that they can put around the body.
A dressmaker's tape measure is usually 150 centimetres long.
A retractable tape measure rolls back into its case by itself after being pulled out.
At its start, a retractable tape measure has a small metal hook for hooking onto an edge.
In Switzerland, the folding rule used by tradespeople is called a Doppelmeter.
You always measure from zero.

abschnitte.text: The **dressmaker's tape measure** is made of soft plastic or fabric and is usually 150 centimetres long. Because it bends, you can put it around a waist, chest or arm. This is how dressmakers measure how big a piece of clothing needs to be. Children's doctors also often use one to measure a baby's head circumference to see whether it is growing well. Many dressmaker's tape measures have an inch scale on the back.

The **retractable tape measure** is a steel tape rolled up in a case. You pull it out, and a spring then rolls it back in. The tape is slightly curved so that it stays straight for a little way even in mid-air. At the start there is a small **metal hook** that you can hook onto an edge. The hook is a little loose so that you measure accurately, whether you hook it on or press it against a wall.

Tradespeople in Switzerland often use the **Doppelmeter**, a folding rule two metres long. It consists of short sections of wood or plastic that you fold out. In Germany it is called a Zollstock. It is stiff and is good for measuring heights and widths of furniture or walls. Folded up, it fits into any trouser pocket.

You always measure from **zero**. The tape must lie straight and taut, otherwise you measure too much. When reading it, you look closely at the line where the thing you are measuring ends. For long distances, a second person helps by holding the start. If you want to be accurate, you measure twice and compare the results.

For building sites and sports grounds there are tape measures 20, 30 or 50 metres long. Experts use them, for example, to measure the distance in the long jump or the size of a plot of land. Today many tradespeople also use a **laser distance meter**, which measures distance with light. Even so, a tape measure belongs in almost every toolbox. It needs no electricity and always works.

begriffe.erklaerung: A steel measuring tape that rolls up into a case.
A measuring rule two metres long that folds up; in Switzerland it is called a Doppelmeter.
The division into lines and numbers on a measuring instrument.
The length all the way round something, for example round the head.

gewusst: The little hook on a retractable tape measure is loose on purpose: it moves by exactly its own thickness.
The word Rollmeter for a retractable tape measure is used mainly in Switzerland; in Germany people tend to say Bandmass.
A soft dressmaker's tape measure can stretch over time and then becomes inaccurate.

teile.einleitung: A law of nature is a rule that describes how nature always behaves, everywhere. A stone falls downwards, energy is never lost and planets circle the Sun on fixed paths. Unlike laws made by people, laws of nature can neither be broken nor abolished.
wichtigste: A law of nature is a rule that applies in nature without exception.
You cannot break or abolish a law of nature like a law passed by parliament.
In 1687 Isaac Newton set out the law of gravitation.
Johannes Kepler discovered that planets move around the Sun on elliptical paths.
The law of conservation of energy says that energy is neither newly created nor disappears.
Antoine Lavoisier showed that the total mass stays the same in chemical reactions.
Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance.

abschnitte.titel: What is a law of nature?
abschnitte.text: A **law of nature** describes a relationship that always applies, whether in Zurich, in Japan or on the Moon. It can often be written down as a mathematical formula. Researchers find laws of nature by observing, measuring and repeating **experiments**. If a law passes all the tests, people trust it, even though it can never be finally proven.

A law passed by parliament sets out what people should do, for example how fast you are allowed to drive. You can break it, change it or abolish it. A law of nature, on the other hand, describes what actually happens, and nobody can switch it off. If you let go of a ball, you cannot decide that it will fly upwards.

As early as the 3rd century BC, the Greek scholar **Archimedes** described the **law of the lever**: with a long lever you can lift heavy loads with little force. Around 1600 Galileo Galilei studied how bodies fall and roll. At the beginning of the 17th century, **Johannes Kepler** found out that planets move around the Sun in ellipses. This made it clear that the heavens also follow fixed rules.

In 1687 the Englishman **Isaac Newton** published his famous work on the motion of bodies. In it he described the **law of gravitation**: all masses attract each other. The same force makes an apple fall from a tree and keeps the Moon on its path around the Earth. Newton also set out three laws of motion, which are still learned at school today.

In the 18th century, using precise weighing, the Frenchman **Antoine Lavoisier** showed that no mass is lost in chemical reactions. In the 19th century, researchers such as Julius Robert Mayer and Hermann von Helmholtz discovered the **law of conservation of energy**. Energy can change its form, for example from movement into heat, but it can never arise from nothing or disappear. Around 1826 Georg Simon Ohm found Ohm's law, which applies in every electrical device.

Sometimes it turns out that a law of nature is only exactly right within a certain range. Albert Einstein, who developed some of his ideas in Bern, extended Newton's laws for very high speeds and strong gravity. But for everyday life Newton's laws are completely sufficient, even for flights to the Moon. In this way knowledge grows step by step without old findings becoming worthless.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule that describes how nature always behaves.
The force of attraction between all masses, also called gravity.
Energy is never lost; it only changes form.
An elongated, stretched circle.
A planned test used to check an idea.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a long enough lever and a fixed point he could move the Earth.
Thanks to Newton's law of gravitation, astronomers were able to find the planet Neptune in 1846 before anyone had seen it in a telescope.
According to what we know today, the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres a second, is a fixed limit that nothing can exceed.

teile.einleitung: The Milgram experiment is a famous experiment in psychology, carried out by the American researcher Stanley Milgram from 1961. He wanted to find out how far ordinary people will go when an authority gives them instructions. The result shocked many people and is still discussed today.
wichtigste: From 1961 Stanley Milgram studied obedience to authority.
The experiment took place at Yale University in the USA.
It was prompted by the trial of the Nazi criminal Adolf Eichmann.
The “learner” was really an actor who was in on it, and no real electric shocks were given.
In the basic version, about two thirds of the participants went as far as the strongest supposed shock.
Being closer to the victim clearly lowered obedience.
Today the experiment is considered ethically problematic, because the participants were deceived and put under great strain.

abschnitte.text: **Stanley Milgram** was a young psychologist at **Yale University** in New Haven, USA. His experiments began in 1961, and the first results were published in 1963. They were prompted by the trial in Jerusalem of **Adolf Eichmann**, who under the Nazis had taken part in the persecution and murder of millions of people. Eichmann claimed that he had only obeyed orders. Milgram wanted to know whether quite ordinary people obey orders even when this harms others.

The participants believed it was an experiment about learning. They were given the role of **teacher** and were to ask questions of a **learner** in the next room. For every wrong answer they were supposedly to give him an electric shock, which got stronger each time, up to 450 volts. The learner was really an **actor** and received no electricity; he only pretended to be in pain. If the teachers hesitated, an experimenter in a grey coat calmly told them they had to go on.

Before the experiment, experts had estimated that only very few people would go all the way to the end. But in the basic version, **about two thirds** of the participants did so. Many sweated, trembled and protested, but still carried on. Milgram explained this with the **agentic state**: people then see themselves only as the tool of an authority and no longer feel responsible themselves.

Milgram changed the experiment in many variations. If the learner sat in the same room or the teacher had to touch his hand, obedience clearly fell. Far fewer people obeyed when the experimenter gave instructions only by telephone. When other participants refused, it was easier for the subjects to say **no** as well. So closeness to the victim and **role models** for resistance made a big difference.

Today the experiment is considered **ethically problematic**. The participants were deceived and were under great stress. That is why today there are strict rules and **ethics committees** that check experiments on people beforehand. Some researchers also criticise the fact that not all participants really believed the experiment was genuine. But later, toned-down repetitions in several countries showed similar tendencies.

The Milgram experiment shows how strongly authority and the situation can influence our behaviour. It teaches that you are allowed to **question** instructions even from adults or bosses. If you notice that someone is being harmed, you should have the courage to refuse and to get help. That is why the experiment is often discussed in school lessons on history, ethics and psychology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person or body that is seen as having power or expert knowledge and that many people obey.
Following the instructions of others.
A state in which a person sees themselves only as the tool carrying out an authority's wishes.
A group of experts who check whether an experiment on people is acceptable.

gewusst: The electric shocks in the Milgram experiment were all just acted; the learner never received real electricity.
In 1974 Milgram wrote a whole book about his experiments.
Because the experiment would not be allowed today, researchers now carry out only greatly toned-down versions.

teile.einleitung: Lucy is the nickname of a famous fossil, the skeleton of an early prehuman about 3.2 million years old. It was found in Ethiopia in 1974 and belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis. Lucy shows that our ancestors walked upright long before their brains became large.
wichtigste: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in East Africa in 1974.
She belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis.
The skeleton is about 3.2 million years old.
The research team was led by Donald Johanson.
She got her name from a Beatles song.
Lucy was about 1.1 metres tall and walked upright on two legs.
In Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh.

abschnitte.text: Lucy was a female **prehuman** who lived about 3.2 million years ago. She belonged to the species **Australopithecus afarensis**, which means something like “southern ape from Afar”. Lucy was not a human like us, but not an ape either; she was a being somewhere in between. She was about 1.1 metres tall and weighed about as much as a schoolchild today.

On 24 November 1974, researchers near **Hadar** in the Afar region of Ethiopia discovered a bone on a slope. The team led by the American **Donald Johanson** then found many more parts of the same skeleton. Altogether about 40 per cent of the skeleton has survived, a sensation for such an old fossil. On the evening of the find, a Beatles song with the name Lucy in the title was playing in the camp, and so the skeleton got its nickname.

Lucy's pelvis and leg bones clearly show that she walked **upright** on two legs. Her brain, on the other hand, was only about as big as a chimpanzee's. This was an important discovery, because it shows that walking upright developed earlier than the large brain. Her long arms suggest that she could probably still climb trees well too.

In Ethiopia Lucy bears the name **Dinkinesh**, which means “you are marvellous” in Amharic. The real bones are kept in the National Museum in **Addis Ababa**. Visitors there usually see an exact replica, because the original is very fragile. For many people in Ethiopia, Lucy is a source of national pride.

For a long time Lucy was the oldest almost complete skeleton of a prehuman. She helped people understand that the cradle of humankind lies in **Africa**. Later more fossils of the same species were found, such as the skeleton of a child that researchers called Selam. Fossilised footprints from Tanzania also show that such prehumans walked upright.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from long ago that has turned to stone.
An early relative of humans who lived millions of years ago.
A genus of prehumans who lived in Africa about 4 to 2 million years ago.
Moving on two legs with the body held upright.

gewusst: Lucy was so famous that her bones were shown on an exhibition tour of the USA from 2007 to 2013.
A NASA space probe that flies to asteroids was named after Lucy.

teile.einleitung: The metre is the most important unit of length, abbreviated m. A metre has 100 centimetres, and 1000 metres make a kilometre. Today the metre is defined very precisely using the speed of light.
wichtigste: The metre is the base unit of length in the International System of Units.
A metre has 100 centimetres or 1000 millimetres, and 1000 metres are a kilometre.
The metre was invented in France at the end of the 18th century.
Originally it was the ten-millionth part of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
Since 1983 the metre has been the distance that light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
A long stride by an adult is about one metre.

abschnitte.text: With the **metre** you measure lengths, meaning how long, high, wide or far something is. A door in a house is about 2 metres high, and a long stride by an adult is about a metre. An Olympic swimming pool is 50 metres long. For small things you use centimetres and millimetres, and for long distances kilometres. The metre is one of the seven **base units** of the International System of Units, SI.

In the past, every region had its own measures of length such as the ell, the foot or the fathom. This made trade complicated. During the French Revolution people therefore wanted to create a measure that would apply to everyone. At the end of the 18th century, the metre was defined as the ten-millionth part of the distance from the **North Pole to the equator**. For this the researchers Delambre and Méchain laboriously measured the distance between Dunkirk and Barcelona.

In 1799 a bar of platinum was made that was meant to be exactly one metre long. Later, in 1889, a new **prototype metre** made of platinum and iridium followed. It is kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near **Paris**. Many countries received copies of it, including Switzerland. In 1875 Switzerland was one of the countries that signed the international **Metre Convention**.

A metal bar can expand slightly when warm, so it is not perfect. From 1960 to 1983 the metre was therefore defined by the wavelength of the light of **krypton-86**. Since 1983 it has been the distance that light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This gives the **speed of light** the exact value of 299,792,458 metres per second. In this way every well-equipped laboratory in the world can reproduce the metre itself.

abschnitte.titel: Measuring in everyday life and in the lab
abschnitte.text: In everyday life you measure with a folding rule, a tape measure or a ruler. Tradespeople often use laser distance meters, which measure with light to the nearest millimetre. Especially precise measurements are made with **laser interferometry**, in which light waves are overlaid. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS** for short, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for accurate measures. It makes sure that scales, petrol pumps and measuring instruments measure correctly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity with which you measure something, for example the metre or the kilogram.
A metal bar that used to serve as the official model for the length of a metre.
How fast light moves: almost 300,000 kilometres a second.
A space in which there is almost no air and no other particles.
The international system of units of measurement used by almost the whole world.

gewusst: In everyday life the United States still mainly uses feet, inches and miles instead of metres.
Light takes only about three billionths of a second to travel one metre.
The name metre comes from the Greek word “metron”, which means “measure”.

teile.einleitung: No measuring instrument measures completely exactly; every measurement has a certain inaccuracy. Measurement accuracy describes how close a measured value is to the true value. So anyone who measures should always know how accurate their result is.
wichtigste: The difference between the measured value and the true value is called the measurement deviation.
A systematic error falsifies every measurement in the same way, for example scales that always show 100 grams too much.
Random errors vary from measurement to measurement and can be reduced by taking means.
The resolution is the smallest difference that a measuring instrument can still show.
If you read a scale at a slant, you make a parallax error.
With callipers you can measure to about a tenth of a millimetre.
To get correct values, a measuring instrument is compared with a standard.

abschnitte.text: When you measure your height, you never get the exact **true value**, but a measured value. The difference between the two is called the **measurement deviation** or measurement error. Measurement accuracy says how small this deviation is. That is why in science and technology people often state how large the uncertainty of a measurement is, for example 12.2 centimetres plus or minus 0.1 centimetres.

A **systematic error** falsifies every measurement in the same direction. A set of scales that always shows 100 grams too much has such an error, and repeating does not help. **Random errors**, on the other hand, vary from measurement to measurement, for example because you do not always read exactly the same way. If you measure several times, for example 12.1, 12.3 and 12.2 centimetres, the **mean** of 12.2 centimetres gives a more reliable value.

If you read a scale at a slant instead of straight on, you make a **parallax error**, because the pointer then appears shifted. Temperature can also interfere, because metal expands when warm. A measuring instrument also has a limited **resolution**, which is the smallest difference it can still show. An ordinary ruler has a resolution of one millimetre.

With a tape measure you can measure to about one millimetre. With **callipers**, you can measure the diameter of a screw to about a tenth of a millimetre. A micrometer screw gauge can even manage a hundredth of a millimetre. For each task you choose the right instrument, because more accurate instruments are often more expensive and more delicate.

The **relative error** compares the error with the size of the measured quantity. If a distance of 1 metre is measured with an error of 2 centimetres, the relative error is 2 per cent. The way a number is written also shows its accuracy: “3.40 m” means that it was measured to the nearest centimetre, “3.4 m” only to the nearest decimetre. That is why you should not simply leave off zeros at the end.

So that a measuring instrument shows correct values, it is compared with a **standard**, an especially accurate reference measure. This process is called **calibration**. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for making sure that units are measured the same everywhere. It checks, for example, that scales in shops, petrol pumps and speed cameras measure correctly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The difference between the measured value and the true value.
An error that falsifies every measurement in the same direction.
The smallest difference that a measuring instrument can show.
A reading error when you look at a scale at a slant.
Comparing a measuring instrument with an exact standard.

gewusst: Since 2019 the kilogram is no longer defined by a metal cylinder in Paris, but by a natural constant.
Callipers have a small extra scale, the vernier, with which you can read tenths of a millimetre.
Even the most accurate atomic clock has a tiny measurement uncertainty.

teile.einleitung: A magnifying glass is a simple glass that makes small things look bigger. With it you can look closely at an ant, the veins of a leaf or the fine lines of a fingerprint. It is one of the oldest optical aids in the world.
wichtigste: A magnifying glass makes things look a little bigger.
It consists of a curved lens made of glass or plastic.
This lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge and is called a converging lens.
Magnifying glasses usually magnify about 2 to 10 times.
For stronger magnification you need a microscope.
A magnifying glass can focus sunlight and so start a fire.
Watchmakers often work with a magnifying glass in their eye.

abschnitte.text: A **magnifying glass** is a lens made of glass or clear plastic, often with a handle or in a frame. The lens bulges outwards, so it is thicker in the middle than at the edge. Such a lens is called a **converging lens**. If you hold it close to an object, the object appears bigger. Magnifying glasses usually magnify about two to ten times.

Rays of light are bent when they pass through the curved lens; we say they are **refracted**. As a result, our eye sees a magnified image of the object. The magnifying glass works best when the object is a little closer than the **focal point** of the lens. The more strongly curved the lens is, the more it magnifies. But then the image is often blurred at the edges.

A magnifying glass collects the Sun's rays in a small, bright spot, the focal point. It gets so hot there that paper or dry grass can start to burn.
