That is why a converging lens is also called a burning glass. You must never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass, because this can seriously injure your eyes. Even a magnifying glass left lying in the sun can start a fire.

As early as ancient times, people knew that curved glass or glass balls filled with water make things look bigger. In the Middle Ages, monks used so-called **reading stones**, hemispherical stones made of glass or rock crystal, which they laid on books. Spectacles, the telescope and the microscope later developed from such lenses. The magnifying glass also became the trademark of detectives such as Sherlock Holmes. To this day it is a symbol of looking closely and searching.

Many people use a **reading magnifier** to read small print. In the Swiss **watch industry**, watchmakers clamp a small magnifying glass into their eye to assemble tiny gear wheels. Stamp collectors, jewellers and doctors check details with a magnifying glass. At school and in nature, you can watch beetles and spiders in a bug viewer without hurting them. Smartphones also often offer a magnifier function using the camera.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lens that is thicker in the middle than at the edge and brings light together.
The point where a converging lens brings the rays of light together.
The bending of light when it passes from one substance into another.
A medieval magnifying glass that was laid on books.

gewusst: Even a drop of water on a leaf works like a small magnifying glass.
The German word for magnifying glass, Lupe, comes from the French “loupe”.

teile.einleitung: Niklaus Wirth was a Swiss computer scientist and one of the best-known computer pioneers in the world. Around 1970 he invented the programming language Pascal, with which millions of people learned to program. For his work he received the Turing Award in 1984, the highest honour in computer science.
wichtigste: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur in 1934 and died in 2024.
He was professor of computer science at ETH Zurich.
Around 1970 he developed the programming language Pascal.
Pascal is named after the French scholar Blaise Pascal.
The language was especially popular in programming lessons.
After Pascal, Wirth developed Modula-2 and Oberon, among others.
In 1984 he received the Turing Award.

abschnitte.text: Niklaus Wirth was born in **Winterthur** in 1934. He studied electrical engineering at ETH Zurich and gained his doctorate at the University of California at Berkeley in 1963. After that he worked at Stanford University. From 1968 he was a professor at **ETH Zurich**, until he retired in 1999. He died on 1 January 2024.

A **programming language** is a language people use to give a computer instructions. In 1970 Wirth presented the language **Pascal**, named after the mathematician Blaise Pascal, who built a calculating machine in the 17th century. Pascal was clearly structured and forced people to program tidily. That is why it was used for learning at schools and universities all over the world.

After Pascal, Wirth developed the language **Modula-2** and later **Oberon**. Together with his team at ETH he even built his own computers, such as the Lilith workstation. His aim was always to make programs simple, understandable and reliable. He also wrote famous textbooks, for example on algorithms and data structures.

In 1984 Wirth received the **Turing Award**, which is often called the Nobel Prize of computer science. This makes him one of very few winners from Switzerland. He received many other honours and several honorary doctorates from universities. Many of today's programming languages contain ideas from his languages.

An observation called **Wirth's law** is also well known. It says, in essence, that software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster. With this Wirth criticised the fact that programs keep getting bigger and more complicated. He argued for lean, well-thought-out software, an idea that is still relevant today.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial language used to give instructions to computers.
The science of processing information with computers.
The most important award in computer science, named after Alan Turing.
An exact step-by-step set of instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: The programming language Delphi, which was used to make many Windows programs, is based on Pascal.
In the 1980s Wirth built his own computer at ETH, with a mouse and a graphical screen.
His textbook on algorithms was translated into many languages.

teile.einleitung: Nanotoxicology is the branch of science that studies whether and how nanoparticles can harm people, animals and the environment. It is important because tiny particles of a substance can act differently from the same substance in coarse form. Its results help authorities set sensible rules for nanomaterials.
wichtigste: Nanotoxicology studies possible damage to health and the environment caused by nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles have more surface and can get into cells more easily than coarse particles.
Nanoparticles that are breathed in reach deep into the alveoli of the lungs.
Long, stiff carbon nanotubes are compared with asbestos fibres because of their shape.
The food colouring titanium dioxide, E171, was banned in the EU in 2022.
Soot from diesel engines is an everyday, unintended source of nanoparticles.
According to the precautionary principle, you protect yourself before harm has been definitely proven.

abschnitte.text: **Toxicology** is the study of poisons and their effects. Nanotoxicology focuses on particles in the nano range, between about 1 and 100 nanometres. It asks how such particles get into the body, where they build up and whether they damage cells. For this, cell cultures, animal experiments and measurements in the environment are used.

Nanoparticles can be breathed in, swallowed or, in rare cases, taken in through damaged skin. Breathing them in is especially worrying, because they get deep into the **alveoli** of the lungs. There they can cause inflammation, and very small particles sometimes even get into the blood. Because of their large surface, they react more easily with substances in the body than coarse particles of the same material.

Not only the substance but also the shape plays a part. Long, stiff **carbon nanotubes** are compared with **asbestos fibres**, which used to be used a lot in building and can cause serious lung diseases. Short or flexible tubes, on the other hand, are considered less worrying. That is why researchers test each nanomaterial individually.

For a long time **titanium dioxide** was used as the white food colouring E171, for example in chewing gum and sugar icing. Some of the particles are in the nano range. Because the European Food Safety Authority could not rule out damage to genetic material, E171 was banned in the EU in 2022. Titanium dioxide is still used in sun creams, because it is not eaten there.

Silver nanoparticles from sportswear can get into **waste water** during washing. There they could harm useful bacteria that clean the water in sewage treatment plants. Soot from diesel engines, wear from tyres and smoke from wood fires also put nanoparticles into the air. That is why in Switzerland many construction machines on building sites must have a particle filter.

Because a lot has not yet been researched, the **precautionary principle** often applies: protective measures are taken before harm has been definitely proven. In the EU, nanomaterials in cosmetics must be marked with “(nano)” in the list of ingredients. People who work with nano powders in laboratories or factories wear protective masks and work in areas with extraction. In Switzerland, Empa and the Federal Office of Public Health, among others, deal with the safety of nanomaterials.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of poisons and their effects.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs, where oxygen passes into the blood.
A fibrous mineral that used to be used in building and can seriously damage the lungs.
The rule of acting carefully early on when risks are uncertain.
Very small particles in the air that can be breathed in.

gewusst: Nanoparticles are also produced when toasting bread, grilling and burning candles.
Nanoparticles have always existed in nature, for example in the smoke of forest fires and in volcanic ash.
A gram of nano powder can have a much larger surface than a gram of the same substance as a coarse powder.

teile.einleitung: Curiosity is the wish to find out new things and to understand things you do not yet know. It makes children keep asking “Why?” and makes researchers work on a question for years. Without curiosity there would be no science, no inventions and no voyages of discovery.
wichtigste: Curiosity is the urge to know or experience something new.
It is one of the most important qualities that makes people do research.
You can recognise curious children by the many questions they ask.
Albert Einstein said of himself that he was only “passionately curious”.
A curious person looks it up or tries it out when they do not know an answer.
NASA's Mars rover is called Curiosity.
In Switzerland you can let your curiosity run free, for example at the Technorama in Winterthur.

abschnitte.text: **Curiosity** is an inner feeling that drives us to explore the unknown. Experts also speak of the **thirst for knowledge**. Curiosity arises when we notice that a piece of knowledge is missing, much as hunger arises when we are missing food. When we find the answer, it feels good and the brain rewards us.

Even babies are curious: they grab things, put them in their mouths and watch everything closely. Toddlers go through a **questioning phase**, in which they ask “Why?” very often. By trying things out, they learn how the world works. Animals such as cats, ravens and monkeys also explore their surroundings with curiosity.

Many great discoveries began with a curious question. In a letter in 1952, Albert Einstein wrote that he had no special talents, he was only passionately curious. Researchers ask a question, make observations and test their ideas with **experiments**. Curiosity also helps you not to give up when an experiment fails.

NASA named its big **Mars rover** “Curiosity”. The vehicle is about the size of a car and landed in Gale Crater on Mars in August 2012. There it examines rocks and soil and looks for signs of whether there used to be water. The name was suggested by a schoolchild in a competition.

If you are curious, you will find many exciting places in Switzerland. At the **Technorama** in Winterthur you can try out hundreds of experiments yourself. In the natural history museums, for example in Bern, Basel or Geneva, you can see stuffed animals, rocks and dinosaur bones. A walk in the woods, quietly watching animals, also awakens curiosity.

Ask questions and write them down in a notebook. Look for answers in books or an encyclopaedia, or ask experts. Try out simple experiments at home, for example what floats in water and what sinks. **Caution** is important too: curiosity is great, but you only try out dangerous things such as fire or electricity with adults.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wish to know or discover something new.
A planned test used to check an idea.
A remote-controlled vehicle that drives around on another heavenly body.
The time when small children ask especially many why-questions.

gewusst: In their questioning phase, toddlers sometimes ask dozens of questions an hour.
The English saying “curiosity killed the cat” warns against too much curiosity.
When learning, you remember things better if you were really curious about them beforehand.

teile.einleitung: The lungs are the organ we breathe with. They take oxygen from the air into the blood and give off carbon dioxide again. Without our lungs we could survive for only a few minutes.
wichtigste: The lungs are the human organ of breathing.
They consist of two lungs in the chest.
In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood.
At the same time, carbon dioxide from the blood is breathed out.
The most important breathing muscle is the diaphragm.
The lungs contain hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs.
Smoking does serious harm to the lungs.

abschnitte.text: The lungs lie well protected in the **chest** behind the ribs. There are two **lungs**, a right one and a left one. The right lung has three lobes and the left only two, because the heart needs room there. The lungs are soft and spongy like a sponge. They are covered by a smooth, moist skin so that they can glide well when we breathe.

When you breathe in, air flows through the nose or mouth into the throat and then into the **windpipe**. The windpipe divides into two branches, the bronchi, which branch out finer and finer like the branches of a tree. At the ends there are tiny sacs, the **alveoli**. An adult has about 300 million of them. Spread out, they would cover an area of about 100 square metres, as much as a large flat.

The alveoli are surrounded by the finest blood vessels. **Oxygen** from the air passes through their wafer-thin walls into the blood. The heart then pumps the oxygen-rich blood around the whole body. In the other direction, the blood gives off **carbon dioxide** to the alveoli, and we breathe it out. This process is called gas exchange.

The lungs have no muscles of their own. The work is done mainly by the **diaphragm**, a flat muscle below the lungs. When it tightens, the space in the chest gets bigger and air flows in. At rest, adults breathe about 12 to 16 times a minute, and children a little more often. During sport we breathe faster and more deeply, because the muscles need more oxygen.

The lungs clean the air with mucus and fine hairs that carry dust upwards. Coughing helps to get rid of foreign bodies and mucus. **Smoking** damages the lungs very badly and can lead to lung cancer and other serious illnesses. In **asthma**, the bronchi narrow and breathing becomes difficult. Exercise in the fresh air and smoke-free rooms keep the lungs healthy, and the Swiss Lung League advises people with lung diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchi, where oxygen passes into the blood.
The branches of the windpipe that distribute air in the lungs.
A flat muscle below the lungs that helps with breathing.
The passing of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of the blood.

gewusst: The left lung is a little smaller than the right, because the heart lies beside it.
A person breathes more than 10,000 litres of air in and out in a day.
The lungs of a healthy person contain so much air that a piece of lung tissue floats on water.

teile.einleitung: Most people whose ancestors did not come only from Africa carry a small piece of Neanderthal genetic material. This shows that our ancestors met these early humans tens of thousands of years ago. This was discovered by researchers who can read ancient DNA from bones.
wichtigste: In people today outside Africa, about 1 to 2 per cent of the genetic material comes from Neanderthals.
According to current knowledge, the gene flow took place mainly in the Middle East or western Asia.
East Asian populations carry on average a little more Neanderthal DNA than Europeans.
The first draft of the Neanderthal genome was published in 2010.
The Denisovans were discovered through DNA from a finger bone in a cave in the Altai.
A Denisovan gene variant called EPAS1 helps people in Tibet to live at high altitude.
Because different people carry different sections, a much larger part of the Neanderthal genome survives altogether.

abschnitte.text: The **Neanderthals** were close relatives of humans today. They lived for hundreds of thousands of years in Europe and western Asia and died out about 40,000 years ago. They get their name from the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf, where bones were found in 1856. They made tools, used fire and hunted large animals such as mammoths.

The Swedish researcher **Svante Pääbo** developed methods for decoding tiny remains of DNA from old bones. He worked at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. In 2010 his team published a first draft of the whole Neanderthal **genome**. For this Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2022.

Modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, arose in Africa and later moved to Asia and Europe. Probably mainly in the Middle East, these people met Neanderthals, and genetic material passed from one group to the other. Experts call this **gene flow**. That is why people today outside Africa have about 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA, on average a little more in East Asia than in Europe.

In 2010 researchers studied a tiny finger bone from **Denisova Cave** in the Altai Mountains in Siberia. The DNA showed that there had been a previously unknown group of humans, the Denisovans. Some people today also carry genetic material from them, especially in Oceania. The Denisovan gene variant **EPAS1** helps Tibetans to live with little oxygen in the highlands.

Today some Neanderthal genes influence, for example, the skin, the hair or the **immune system**. In 2020 researchers described a Neanderthal section on chromosome 3 that increases the risk of severe **Covid-19**. Other sections, on the other hand, can protect. African populations also have small traces, because people from Eurasia later partly moved back to Africa.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the hereditary information of a living thing, stored in the DNA.
The complete genetic material of a living thing.
When hereditary information passes from one group into another.
The scientific name of humans today.
An extinct group of humans known mainly through their DNA.

gewusst: The Denisovans were discovered almost entirely through their DNA, before more of their bones were known.
Taken together, all people today still carry a large part of the Neanderthal genome, spread across many people.
Neanderthals had, on average, a slightly bigger brain than people today.

teile.einleitung: The MOSAiC expedition was the largest research journey ever into the central Arctic. From autumn 2019 to autumn 2020, the German research ship Polarstern let itself drift with the sea ice for a whole year. This allowed researchers to observe the climate of the Arctic closely through all the seasons for the first time.
wichtigste: MOSAiC stands for a drifting observatory for studying the Arctic climate.
The research ship Polarstern let itself be frozen into the sea ice and drift for about a year.
The expedition was led by the Alfred Wegener Institute in Bremerhaven.
It was modelled on the famous drift of the polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen with the ship Fram.
The measurements from the winter, when it is dark all the time during the polar night, are especially valuable.
On the ice floe beside the ship, the researchers set up a camp with many measuring stations.
Switzerland also took part, above all the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos.

abschnitte.text: In September 2019 the **Polarstern** set off from Tromsø in Norway. In October 2019, north of Siberia, the researchers chose a thick, stable **ice floe** and let the ship freeze fast to it. After that the Polarstern switched off its engines and drifted slowly with the ice towards the North Pole and the Atlantic. In October 2020 the ship returned to Bremerhaven in Germany.

The idea is over 125 years old. From 1893 to 1896 the Norwegian **Fridtjof Nansen** let his wooden ship **Fram** freeze into the ice and drift across the Arctic Ocean. He wanted to prove that the ice moves across the Arctic like a huge conveyor belt. MOSAiC used the same idea, but with modern technology.

Beside the ship, a **research camp** grew up with tents, measuring masts and power cables. There, air, clouds, snow, ice, seawater and tiny living things were studied. A network of further measuring stations was spread out on the ice up to several dozen kilometres away. Researchers from about 20 countries took turns on board during the year.

In winter, the sun does not rise for months in the central Arctic; this is called the **polar night**. Then it is often colder than minus 30 degrees, and icebreakers can hardly get through. That is why there had been almost no measurements from this time before. MOSAiC filled this gap and provides data for better **climate models**.

In spring 2020 the **Covid-19 pandemic** made the planned change of crew difficult. Flights were cancelled, and researchers first had to go into quarantine. So the Polarstern briefly left the floe and exchanged crews off Svalbard with other ships. In summer 2020 the first floe broke up, and the team carried on at a new floe near the North Pole.

The **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in Davos mainly studied the snow on the sea ice. Snow acts like a blanket that protects the ice from the cold and reflects sunlight. The researchers measured how thick, how dense and how salty the snow was. These values help to understand how fast the Arctic ice is melting.

begriffe.erklaerung: Frozen seawater that floats on the ocean as a layer of ice.
Slowly being carried along by wind and current, without your own power.
The time in winter near the poles when the sun does not rise all day.
A computer program that calculates how the climate might develop.
A large, freely drifting sheet of sea ice.

gewusst: The Arctic is warming much faster than the rest of the Earth.
During MOSAiC, polar bears kept coming near the camp, so armed guards kept watch.
During the expedition, the Polarstern travelled over a thousand kilometres in the ice without using its own engines.

teile.einleitung: The Montreal Protocol is an international agreement to protect the ozone layer, signed in 1987. It gradually bans substances such as CFCs, which destroy the ozone in the atmosphere. It is considered one of the most successful environmental agreements in the world.
wichtigste: The Montreal Protocol was signed in Montreal in Canada in 1987.
It mainly regulates substances that damage the ozone layer, such as CFCs.
It was preceded in 1985 by the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer.
The ozone hole over Antarctica was first described by a team from the British Antarctic Survey.
Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 for their work on ozone depletion.
By 2009 all UN member states had ratified the protocol.
With the Kigali Amendment of 2016, hydrofluorocarbons were also regulated.

abschnitte.text: At a height of about 15 to 35 kilometres lies the **ozone layer**. Ozone is a form of oxygen whose molecules consist of three oxygen atoms. The ozone layer absorbs a large part of the Sun's dangerous **UV radiation**. Without it there would be far more sunburn, skin cancer and damage to plants and animals.

**CFCs**, chlorofluorocarbons, used to be used in spray cans, fridges and foams. In 1974 Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland warned that high up these substances release chlorine, which destroys ozone. Paul Crutzen had shown earlier that nitrogen oxides also break down ozone. For this work the three received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1995.

In 1985 researchers from the **British Antarctic Survey** reported a strong loss of ozone over Antarctica during the southern hemisphere spring. This phenomenon became known as the **ozone hole**. The discovery alarmed the world. In the same year the **Vienna Convention** for the Protection of the Ozone Layer was agreed, which formed the framework for further rules.

On 16 September 1987 the protocol was signed in Montreal, and it came into force in 1989. The countries committed themselves to gradually ending the production and use of CFCs and similar substances. The rules were later tightened several times. In 2009 it became the first environmental agreement ever to be ratified by **all UN member states**. With the **Kigali Amendment** of 2016, hydrofluorocarbons were added; they do not destroy ozone, but they strongly warm the climate.

Switzerland signed the Montreal Protocol and has adopted its rules into Swiss law. **Arosa** in the Grisons plays a special role: in 1926 the world's longest series of measurements of total ozone began there. The measurements are continued today by MeteoSwiss. Thanks to such long series, you can see exactly how the ozone layer is changing.

Since the agreement, the amount of ozone-damaging substances in the atmosphere has fallen. Experts expect the ozone layer to largely recover by about the middle of the 21st century, and a little later over Antarctica. Because many CFCs are also strong **greenhouse gases**, the agreement has also protected the climate. Today 16 September is the **International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas made of molecules with three oxygen atoms.
Chlorofluorocarbons, substances that destroy the ozone layer.
An area with a greatly thinned ozone layer, especially over Antarctica.
To officially accept an agreement as binding for your own country.
Invisible, high-energy radiation from the Sun that causes sunburn.

gewusst: If the whole ozone layer were squeezed together at sea level, it would be only about three millimetres thick.
A single chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules in the atmosphere.
Former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan called the Montreal Protocol perhaps the most successful international agreement.

teile.einleitung: Nature conservation covers everything people do to preserve plants, animals and their habitats. This includes large protected areas such as the Swiss National Park, but also small things such as a nest box in the garden. Everyone can help to protect nature.
wichtigste: Nature conservation preserves plants, animals and habitats.
In nature reserves you are not allowed to pull up plants.
The edelweiss is protected in Switzerland.
In winter wild animals need peace and quiet, which is why there are wildlife rest areas.
Toad fences in spring stop toads being run over on roads.
Nest boxes and insect hotels help birds and wild bees in the garden.
You always take your own rubbish back out of nature with you.

abschnitte.text: Nature conservation aims to preserve **biodiversity**, the variety of species and habitats. Many animals and plants are threatened because meadows have been built on, streams straightened or moors drained. Threatened species are listed on the **Red List**. In Switzerland, about a third of the species studied are considered threatened.

The **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps. There nature is allowed to develop without any interference, and you must not leave the paths. There are also moorland landscapes, floodplains, game reserves and many small **nature reserves**. Since 1987 moors in Switzerland have been protected by the Federal Constitution.

Many plants are protected in Switzerland, for example the **edelweiss** with its white, felty stars and some kinds of gentian. You are not allowed to pick them or dig them up. Animals such as the beaver, the lynx, the golden eagle and all amphibians are also protected. The ibex was once completely wiped out in Switzerland and was successfully reintroduced from 1911.

abschnitte.titel: Help for toads and wild animals
abschnitte.text: In spring, common toads migrate to the waters where they spawn and often have to cross roads on the way. Volunteers then put up **toad fences**, collect the animals in buckets and carry them safely across the road. In winter, chamois, red deer and black grouse need peace and quiet to save energy, which is why there are **wildlife rest areas**. In spring, dogs should be kept on a lead in the woods, because wild animals have young then.

You can also do a lot in your own garden or on your balcony. A **nest box** gives tits or sparrows a place to breed. An **insect hotel** and flowering native plants help wild bees and butterflies. A pile of branches, a hedge or a small pond quickly becomes a home for hedgehogs, lizards and dragonflies.

Since 1966 the federal Nature and Cultural Heritage Act has regulated the protection of landscapes, plants and animals. Organisations such as **Pro Natura**, founded in 1909, WWF Switzerland and BirdLife Switzerland work for nature. For everyone the rule is: stay on the paths, do not pull up plants, do not disturb animals and take your own rubbish home with you. Small actions by many people together have a big effect.

begriffe.erklaerung: The variety of species, habitats and genes in nature.
A list of threatened species of animals and plants.
An area where wild animals must not be disturbed in winter.
An area with special rules to protect nature.
Animals such as frogs, toads and newts that live on land and in water.

gewusst: Pro Natura was originally founded to raise money for the new national park.
All the ibex in Switzerland are descended from animals brought from Gran Paradiso in Italy.
A chamois that is startled several times in winter can lose so much energy that it does not survive the winter.

teile.einleitung: Neuroplasticity means that the brain changes through experience and practice. Nerve cells make new connections, strengthen those that are used often and remove those that are rarely used. So the brain is not a fixed machine but stays changeable throughout life.
wichtigste: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change through experience.
The brain stays changeable throughout life.
In 1949 Donald Hebb described how nerve cells that are active together become more strongly connected.
Connections that are rarely used become weaker or are removed.
In London taxi drivers, part of the hippocampus was enlarged.
After a stroke, other areas of the brain can take over tasks.
In blind people, the visual cortex often helps with reading Braille.

abschnitte.text: The human brain consists of about 86 billion **nerve cells**, also called neurons. These are connected to each other through tiny points of contact, the **synapses**. Neuroplasticity means that these connections are constantly changing. The word comes from “neuron” and the Greek “plastikos”, which means mouldable.

In 1949 the Canadian psychologist **Donald Hebb** put forward an important idea. When two nerve cells are often active at the same time, their connection gets stronger. This is often summed up in the phrase: cells that fire together wire together. On the other hand, connections that are rarely needed become weaker or are removed altogether, like a footpath that becomes overgrown.

Around the year 2000, researchers in London studied taxi drivers, who have to know thousands of streets by heart. In them, part of the **hippocampus**, which is important for finding your way, was larger than in other people. In another study, adults practised juggling for three months. Afterwards certain areas of the brain for seeing movement had grown in volume, and after a break they shrank a little again.

In a **stroke**, areas of the brain are damaged, and people lose, for example, the ability to speak or to move an arm. Through a lot of training in therapy, other areas of the brain can take over some of these tasks. That is why rehabilitation after a stroke is so important. Plasticity can also be seen in blind people: the **visual cortex** is often also used when feeling Braille.

Every time you learn something new, your brain changes a little. If you practise regularly, for example the piano, a language or mental arithmetic, you strengthen the matching connections. **Repetition**, breaks and enough sleep are especially effective, because what you have learned is strengthened while you sleep. The brain is especially mouldable in children, but adults and older people can also still learn a great deal.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that passes on electrical signals.
The point of contact where one nerve cell passes a signal on to another.
An area of the brain that is important for memory and finding your way.
Training and therapy so that sick people regain lost abilities.

gewusst: People used to believe that the adult brain could hardly change any more.
Just a few weeks of practice can cause changes that are visible in a brain scanner.
New nerve cells probably still form in the hippocampus even in adults.

teile.einleitung: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre and therefore unimaginably small. Atoms, molecules and viruses are in this range. Nanotechnology uses the special properties that substances have at this tiny size.
wichtigste: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre.
A millimetre has 1,000,000 nanometres.
The prefix nano comes from the Greek word for dwarf.
Nanotechnology works with structures of about 1 to 100 nanometres.
A hair 80 micrometres thick is 80,000 nanometres thick.
You cannot see nanostructures with an ordinary light microscope, because the wavelength of light is much bigger.
The smaller you divide up a substance, the larger its surface becomes.

abschnitte.text: The nanometre, abbreviated **nm**, is a unit of length. A metre has a billion nanometres, and a micrometre has 1000 nanometres. The prefix **nano** comes from the Greek word nanos for dwarf. A nanometre is to a metre roughly what a hazelnut is to the whole Earth.

A single atom is about a tenth of a nanometre in size. The double strand of **DNA**, our genetic material, is about 2 nanometres thick. Many **viruses** measure between 20 and 300 nanometres. A hair, on the other hand, at about 80,000 nanometres, is a giant. Visible light also has wavelengths of about 380 to 780 nanometres.

A **light microscope** cannot show structures that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. For the nano world you therefore need electron microscopes, which use electrons instead of light. Even more precise is the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, which can even show individual atoms. It was invented by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich, for which they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

If you divide a substance into tiny particles, its **surface** grows enormously. If you cut a cube with edges 1 centimetre long into little cubes with edges 1 micrometre long, the total surface becomes 10,000 times bigger. In nanoparticles, therefore, a great many atoms are at the surface. This can change the colour, strength or reactivity of a substance.

**Nanotechnology** uses these special properties. In computer chips, the tiny switching elements are now only a few dozen nanometres in size. Some sun creams contain nanoparticles that block UV rays. Coatings modelled on the lotus plant make water and dirt bead off; this is called the **lotus effect**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny basic building block from which all substances are made.
Technology that works with particles and structures in the nanometre range.
The distance between two wave crests; for light it decides the colour.
A microscope that uses electrons instead of light and can show much smaller things.

gewusst: Your fingernails grow about one nanometre a second.
As early as the Middle Ages, glassmakers coloured church windows red with nano-sized gold particles without knowing it.
A sheet of paper is about 100,000 nanometres thick.

teile.einleitung: METAS is the Federal Institute of Metrology, Switzerland's top authority on measuring. It makes sure that a kilogram, a metre or a second in Switzerland is exactly the same as everywhere else in the world. You notice this in everyday life more than you might think: at the shop scales, at the petrol pump and in the time of day.
wichtigste: In German, METAS stands for Eidgenössisches Institut für Metrologie, the Federal Institute of Metrology.
The institute is based in Wabern near Bern.
It belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police.
Measuring in Switzerland is governed by the Federal Act on Metrology, the Measurement Act for short.
METAS produces the Swiss time scale UTC(CH) and runs the atomic clock FoCS.
It checks the police's speed measuring devices and breath alcohol testers.
Shop scales and petrol pumps are usually checked by cantonal inspectors under the supervision of METAS.
METAS is a member of EURAMET, the European organisation of metrology institutes.

abschnitte.text: **Metrology** is the science of measuring. METAS is Switzerland's national metrology institute and is based in **Wabern** near Bern. Its roots go back to the 19th century, when the young federal state introduced uniform measures and weights. Since 2013 METAS has been an independent federal institute belonging to the **Federal Department of Justice and Police**.

Worldwide, the **International System of Units**, SI for short, applies, with units such as the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. METAS realises these units for Switzerland as accurately as possible and passes them on to laboratories and companies. To do this it regularly compares its measurements with other countries. In Europe it works in the organisation **EURAMET**, and worldwide with the International Bureau of Weights and Measures near Paris.

METAS produces Switzerland's official time scale, **UTC(CH)**, the Swiss version of Coordinated Universal Time. For this it runs several atomic clocks. A special one is **FoCS**, an atomic clock with a continuous caesium fountain, which was developed in Switzerland. In it, caesium atoms are cooled with laser light and shot upwards as in a fountain. The exact time is important for the railways, the telephone network, banks and satellite navigation.

The **Measurement Act** requires measuring instruments used in trade to show correct values. When apples are weighed for you at the till or your parents fill up the car, the amount must be right. Shop scales and petrol pumps are usually checked on site by the **cantonal inspectors of weights and measures**, under the supervision of METAS. Water meters, electricity meters and taxi meters are also among the instruments checked.

METAS checks measuring instruments whose results can matter in court. These include the police's **speed measuring devices**, meaning radar and laser devices. **Breath alcohol testers** must also be approved and checked by METAS. METAS also measures radiation, for example from X-ray machines in hospitals. In this way everyone can rely on a fine or a diagnosis being based on a correct measurement.

As well as doing checks, METAS researches new measuring methods. Experts work on even more accurate clocks, on measuring the tiniest lengths and on measurements for medicine and the environment. For example, instruments for measuring air pollutants and fine dust are checked. Many Swiss companies, for example from the watch and precision industries, have their own measuring instruments **calibrated** at METAS.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of accurate measuring.
An expert who checks scales, petrol pumps and other measuring instruments used in trade.
Coordinated Universal Time, which the clocks of the world follow.
A clock that measures time very accurately using the vibrations of atoms.
The International System of Units, with the metre, kilogram, second and other units.

gewusst: A good atomic clock does not go wrong by even one second in millions of years.
The pump at a petrol station also has a seal showing that it has been officially checked.
If the police catch you on a speed camera, METAS has checked the device beforehand.

teile.einleitung: A mummy is the dead body of a person or animal that has not decayed but has survived for a long time. The most famous are the mummies from ancient Egypt, which were wrapped in linen bandages. But mummies can also form quite naturally through ice, dryness or bogs.
wichtigste: A mummy is a body that has not decayed because of drying out or cold.
The ancient Egyptians made mummies for life after death.
They dried out the bodies with the salt natron.
Then they wrapped the mummies in linen bandages.
In Egypt, mummification took about 70 days.
Some mummies lay in a large stone coffin, the sarcophagus.
The Egyptians also mummified animals, for example cats.
Mummies can also form naturally through ice or great dryness.

abschnitte.text: Normally a dead body decays because bacteria and fungi break it down. But these living things need water and warmth. If it is very dry, very cold or there is no air, the body survives and a **mummy** forms. A distinction is made between **natural mummies**, which formed by themselves, and artificial mummies, which people made on purpose.

The ancient Egyptians believed in **life after death**. For this, the body was meant to be preserved so that the soul could return to it. Mummification was carried out by special priests and took about 70 days. For about 40 days the body was covered with the salt **natron**, which drew the water out of it. Then it was treated with oils and resins and wrapped in many metres of **linen bandages**.

The Egyptians often placed protective amulets between the bandages. For rich people, a painted mask was put over the face. The mummy was laid in one or more coffins, and for kings also in a large stone coffin, the **sarcophagus**. Food, furniture and jewellery for the afterlife were placed in the burial chamber. The most famous tomb discovery is the tomb of the pharaoh **Tutankhamun**, which Howard Carter found in 1922.

The Egyptians also mummified many animals, especially **cats**, ibises, falcons and crocodiles. Some animals were beloved pets that were buried with their owners. Many others were offered as gifts to gods who were imagined with animal heads. Researchers have found thousands of such animal mummies in Egypt.

In very cold regions, ice can preserve a body for thousands of years. The best-known **glacier mummy** is Ötzi, who was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps on the border between Italy and Austria. He lived about 5300 years ago and is now on display in a museum in Bolzano. Bodies are sometimes also preserved in deserts and in bogs; these are called **bog bodies**.

Mummies tell researchers a lot about the lives of people in the past. With X-ray machines and computed tomography, you can look inside without opening the bandages. In this way you find out what people ate, what illnesses they had and how old they lived to be. In the Abbey Library of **St Gallen** you can even see a real Egyptian mummy called Shepenese.

begriffe.erklaerung: To treat a dead body so that it does not decay.
A natural salt with which the Egyptians dried out bodies.
A large, often decorated coffin made of stone.
The world in which, according to the beliefs of many people, you go on living after death.

gewusst: The oldest artificial mummies do not come from Egypt but from the Chinchorro culture in Chile, and are over 7000 years old.
Ötzi had over 60 tattoos on his skin.
Sometimes hundreds of metres of linen bandages were used for a single Egyptian mummy.

teile.einleitung: Ladybirds are small, round beetles, usually red or yellow with black spots. They are seen as lucky charms and are very popular with gardeners because they eat aphids. There are thousands of species worldwide.
wichtigste: Ladybirds like eating aphids best.
The number of spots does not show the age but the species.
The red colour warns enemies that the beetle tastes bad.
When in danger it gives off a yellow, bitter liquid.
Its wings for flying are hidden under the hard wing cases.
Ladybirds spend the winter hidden away, often in groups.
The harlequin ladybird is now common in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: Ladybirds have a body shaped like half a ball and are usually only a few millimetres long. Their hard **wing cases** are often red, yellow or black and have spots. The number of spots depends on the species and does not change during its life. The best known is the **seven-spot ladybird**, with seven black spots on a red background. Under the wing cases lie the thin, folded wings with which it flies.

Most ladybirds are predators and eat **aphids**. A single beetle can eat dozens of aphids a day. The larvae, which look like little grey crocodiles with spots, are also keen aphid hunters. Some species, on the other hand, eat fungal coatings such as mildew, or plants.

The bright colours are a **warning colour**, which signals to birds that the beetle is not good to eat. If a ladybird is threatened, it squeezes a yellow, bitter liquid out of its leg joints. This trick is called **reflex bleeding**. Ladybirds also often play dead and simply drop.

Ladybirds go through a complete **metamorphosis**. From the yellow eggs stuck to leaves hatch larvae, which shed their skin several times. Then they pupate on a leaf, and after about a week the adult beetle hatches. At first it is pale; the colours and spots only appear after a few hours.

In autumn, ladybirds look for sheltered hiding places, for example under bark, in fallen leaves or in cracks in walls. Often many beetles gather in one place. In a kind of winter rest they wait for spring. Sometimes they also spend the winter in houses, for example on window frames.

Many native ladybird species live in Switzerland. For several decades the **harlequin ladybird**, which was brought to Europe for pest control, has been spreading. It is very adaptable and partly pushes out native species. You can often recognise it by a black marking shaped like an M or W behind its head. By the way, the German name Marienkäfer goes back to the Virgin Mary, because the beetle was seen as a gift from heaven, and the English “lady” also refers to Our Lady.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hard front wings that protect the thin flying wings of beetles.
A striking colour that shows enemies that an animal is poisonous or not good to eat.
Giving off a bitter liquid from the leg joints for defence.
An animal that helps people, for example by eating pests.

gewusst: A ladybird larva can eat several hundred aphids while it is developing.
There are also ladybirds with 22 spots and ones with no spots at all.
In many countries it is considered lucky when a ladybird lands on your hand.

teile.einleitung: Niklaus Riggenbach was a Swiss engineer and inventor who greatly improved the rack railway. The Vitznau-Rigi Railway, the first mountain railway in Europe, was built in 1871 using his system. Thanks to his idea, trains can climb even very steep mountains.
wichtigste: Niklaus Riggenbach is known for his rack railway.
He lived from 1817 to 1899.
The Vitznau-Rigi Railway, Europe's first mountain railway, was built using his system.
The railway up the Rigi opened in 1871.
His rack looks like a ladder.
In Olten he ran the workshop of the Swiss Central Railway.
A cog wheel on the locomotive grips the rack between the rails.

abschnitte.text: Niklaus Riggenbach was born in Alsace in 1817 and grew up in Basel. He first trained as a mechanic and then went on to become an **engineer** in Paris and Karlsruhe. In Karlsruhe he built locomotives. In 1853 he became head of the workshop of the **Swiss Central Railway** in Olten, where he lived until his death in 1899.

abschnitte.titel: How does a rack railway work?
abschnitte.text: On very steep routes, smooth iron wheels would **spin** on the rails, because there is not enough grip. That is why a **rack** lies between the rails. A cog wheel under the locomotive grips this rack and pulls the train upwards. When going down, the cog wheel brakes the train safely.

Riggenbach's rack looks like a **ladder** lying flat. Two iron sections are joined by many cross bolts, and the teeth of the cog wheel grip the gaps. Riggenbach patented his idea in France in 1863. At about the same time, the American Sylvester Marsh built a similar railway up Mount Washington in the USA.

On 21 May 1871 the **Vitznau-Rigi Railway** opened, first as far as Staffelhöhe and from 1873 to Rigi Kulm. It is considered the first mountain railway in Europe. In some places the gradient is 25 per cent. As a result, the Rigi became one of the most popular mountains for outings in Switzerland, and tourists came from all over the world.

After the success on the Rigi, rack railways using Riggenbach's system were built in many countries. Later other engineers, such as Roman Abt and Eduard Locher, developed their own systems. The **Pilatus Railway**, with the Locher system, is considered the steepest rack railway in the world. Many rack railways still run in Switzerland today, for example up the Rigi, to the Kleine Scheidegg or to the Gornergrat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A railway on which a cog wheel on the locomotive grips a toothed rack.
A rail with teeth or rungs between the ordinary rails.
How steep a route is, given as a percentage.
A right that protects an inventor's invention.

gewusst: The first locomotive of the Rigi Railway had an upright boiler, so that the water did not lie at a slant on the steep slope.
An original locomotive of the Rigi Railway is now in the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.
Riggenbach wrote down his memories in a book.

teile.einleitung: In statistics, the mode is the value that occurs most often in a set of data. It is also called the modal value. It is the simplest kind of average and even works for data without numbers, such as favourite colours or favourite animals.
wichtigste: The mode is the value that occurs most often.
Another word for mode is modal value.
In the list 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3 and 2, the mode is 3.
The mode also works for data without numbers, such as favourite animals.
A list can have several modes: for 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 4 they are 2 and 3.
As well as the mode, there are the mean and the median as kinds of average.
To find the mode, you simply count how often each value occurs.

abschnitte.text: The word **mode** comes from the Latin “modus”, which means “measure” or “manner”. In statistics it means the value that occurs most often in a set of data. It is also called the **modal value**. Along with the **mean** and the **median**, it is one of the three best-known averages.

To find the mode, you count how often each value occurs. It is best to make a **tally chart** for this. With the shoe sizes 37, 38, 38, 39, 40, 38 and 37, size 38 occurs three times, more often than any other size. So 38 is the mode. If you roll 6, 2, 4, 6, 1, 6 and 3 on a dice, 6 is the mode, because it appears three times.

A big advantage of the mode is that it also works for data you cannot calculate with. If in a class 8 children name red, 12 blue and 5 green as their favourite colour, the mode is **blue**. But you cannot work out an average of colours or animals. Such data are called **categorical data**.

Sometimes two values occur equally often as the most common. In the list 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 4, 2 and 3 are both modes, and the list is then **bimodal**. If every value occurs only once, there is no meaningful mode. This is a disadvantage compared with the mean, which always gives exactly one value.

Shoe shops want to know which **size** sells most, so that they have enough of it in stock. In surveys, the mode shows which answer is most popular. In elections and votes, too, people are interested in which answer was chosen most often. Clothing manufacturers often plan their production around the most common sizes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for mode, the most common value.
A list in which you make a mark every time a value occurs.
A set of data with two top values that are equally common.
Data that consist of names or groups instead of numbers.

gewusst: The mode is the only one of the three well-known averages that you can also find for favourite foods or hair colours.
With a fair dice there is no clear mode in the long run, because each number comes up about equally often.
In charts you can see the mode at once from the tallest bar.

teile.einleitung: A food web forms when you link together the many food chains of a habitat. In nature hardly any animal eats only one kind of food, and most animals have several enemies. So a food web shows much more accurately than a single chain how living things depend on one another.
wichtigste: A food web consists of many food chains linked together.
A food chain almost always begins with a plant or alga.
Only about 10 per cent of the energy gets from one level to the next.
That is why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.
An apex predator is a predator with no natural enemies.
Poisons such as mercury build up along the chain; this is called biomagnification.
If a predator disappears, its prey animals often multiply strongly.

abschnitte.text: A **food chain** such as grass, grasshopper, frog, grey heron is only a small part of the picture. The frog also eats flies and beetles, and it is eaten not only by the grey heron but also by grass snakes. If you draw in all these links, you get a **food web**. It looks like a spider's web with many threads.

In the food web, living things are arranged in **trophic levels**. On the lowest level are plants and algae as producers. Above them come plant-eaters, then smaller and larger meat-eaters. At the very top is the **apex predator**, for example the wolf in the forest or the pike in many Swiss lakes.

Animals use most of their food to breathe, move and stay warm. Only about **10 per cent** of the energy is then stored in the body and can be passed on to the next level. So 1000 kilograms of plants produce only about 100 kilograms of plant-eaters, and these in turn only about 10 kilograms of meat-eaters. That is why there are far more mice than foxes, and rarely more than four or five levels.

Some pollutants such as **mercury** or the old insecticide DDT are hardly broken down in the body. A small fish takes in a little poison with many tiny organisms, and a predatory fish takes in more with many small fish. So the amount rises with each level; this is called **biomagnification**. That is why animals at the very top, such as birds of prey or large predatory fish, carry especially high levels.

A food web is like a finely tuned balance. If a predator is missing, its prey animals often multiply strongly, and they then eat more plants. A well-known example is Yellowstone National Park in the USA, where after wolves returned in 1995 the deer browsed young trees less heavily. In Switzerland, too, there is discussion about how the lynx and the wolf affect the numbers of roe deer and red deer.

A web with many species is usually more stable than one with few. If one food source fails, animals can switch to another. That is why **biodiversity**, the variety of life, is so important. Protecting hedges, flower meadows and ponds strengthens the whole food web.

begriffe.erklaerung: A level in the food web, for example producers or plant-eaters.
A predator at the very top that has no natural enemies itself.
The build-up of poisons from level to level in the food web.
The variety of all living things and their habitats.
A habitat with all its living things and their relationships.

gewusst: Because of the insecticide DDT, peregrine falcons and white-tailed eagles used to lay eggs with shells so thin that they broke during incubation.
In the sea, tiny plankton forms the basis of food webs that reach all the way to whales and sharks.
The blue whale, the largest animal on Earth, eats mainly tiny crustaceans called krill and so is fairly low down in the web.

teile.einleitung: Mendel's laws describe how characteristics are passed on from parents to their offspring. They were discovered by the monk Gregor Mendel, who crossed thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden in the 19th century. They form the basis of the study of heredity, genetics.
wichtigste: There are three Mendel's laws.
The law of uniformity says that the first generation of offspring from pure-bred parents is all alike.
According to the law of segregation, the characteristics split up in the second generation in a ratio of 3 to 1.
The law of independent assortment gives a ratio of 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 for two characteristics.
In a crossing diagram, P stands for the parent generation and F1 for the first generation of offspring.
Red and white four o'clock flowers produce pink offspring; this is intermediate inheritance.
A test cross is used to check an unknown genotype.

abschnitte.text: Gregor Mendel lived from 1822 to 1884 and was an Augustinian monk at the monastery in **Brünn**, today's Brno in the Czech Republic. Between 1856 and 1863 he crossed thousands of **pea plants** in the monastery garden. He paid attention to clearly visible characteristics, such as whether the seeds were yellow or green, smooth or wrinkled. He counted the offspring carefully and calculated with the numbers. In 1866 he published his results, but hardly anyone took any notice.

The first law is called the **law of uniformity**. If you cross two pure-bred plants that differ in one characteristic, all the offspring of the first generation are the same. If you cross peas with yellow seeds and peas with green seeds, for example, all the offspring are yellow. Here yellow is **dominant**, meaning it covers the other, and green is recessive, meaning it steps back. In the crossing diagram, the parent generation is called P and the first generation of offspring F1.

The second law is called the **law of segregation**. If you cross the F1 plants with each other, both characteristics appear again in the second generation, F2. With dominant-recessive inheritance, about three quarters are yellow and one quarter green, so the ratio is 3 to 1. The green characteristic was only hidden in the F1, not lost. Each plant carries two hereditary factors for a characteristic, which today are called **alleles**.

The third law is called the **law of independent assortment**. It says that different characteristics are inherited independently of each other. If you look at two characteristics at once, such as the colour and shape of the seeds, you get a ratio of 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 in the F2. New combinations also appear that the parents did not have. However, this law only applies to genes that do not lie close together on the same chromosome.

abschnitte.titel: Other kinds of inheritance and importance
abschnitte.text: A characteristic is not always dominant. If you cross red and white **four o'clock flowers**, the offspring are pink; this is called intermediate inheritance. To find out whether a plant is pure-bred or mixed, you cross it with a pure-bred recessive plant; this is called a **test cross**. Only around 1900 did three researchers rediscover Mendel's work independently of each other. Today plant and animal breeders use his laws, for example when breeding new varieties of cereals or apples.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of heredity.
A characteristic that wins over another and becomes visible.
A characteristic that is covered by a dominant one and can stay hidden.
A plant that carries two identical hereditary factors for a characteristic.
One of several forms of a hereditary factor.

gewusst: Mendel knew nothing yet about genes or chromosomes; he only concluded from his counting that there were invisible hereditary factors.
Gregor Mendel later became abbot of his monastery and after that had hardly any time for his experiments.
Peas were ideal for Mendel's experiments, because they grow quickly and have many characteristics that are easy to tell apart.

teile.einleitung: A culture medium is a mixture of nutrients on or in which bacteria, fungi or cells are grown in the laboratory. It can be liquid like a broth or firm like a jelly in a glass dish. Culture media are among the most important tools of microbiology and medicine.
wichtigste: A culture medium provides microorganisms with everything they need to grow.
Solid media are usually made with agar, a substance from red seaweed.
In Robert Koch's laboratory, Fanny Hesse suggested using agar instead of gelatine.
Gelatine was unsuitable because it melts at body temperature.
Julius Richard Petri introduced the flat glass dish with a lid.
A selective medium lets only certain microorganisms grow.
On blood agar you can see whether bacteria break down red blood cells.

abschnitte.text: To grow, bacteria and fungi need water, sugar or other sources of energy, nitrogen, salts and often vitamins. A **culture medium** provides these substances. There are **liquid media**, in which the microbes multiply evenly, and solid **media plates**. On solid media, a single cell grows into a visible little heap, a **colony**.

The most important substance for solid media is **agar**, which is obtained from red seaweed. Agar only becomes liquid at about 85 degrees and sets again when it cools to about 40 degrees. So an agar plate stays solid even in an incubator at 37 degrees. What is more, most bacteria cannot break down agar.

Around 1881 the German doctor **Robert Koch** first worked with gelatine, but it melted at body temperature and some bacteria turned it liquid. **Fanny Hesse**, the wife of his colleague Walther Hesse, knew agar from the kitchen, where she used it to set jellies and puddings. She suggested using agar for the media, and the idea caught on. In 1887 Koch's assistant **Julius Richard Petri** described the flat dish with a lid that is now called a Petri dish.

A **synthetic medium** has an exactly known chemical make-up. A complex medium, on the other hand, contains ingredients such as meat extract or yeast extract, whose contents are not exactly known. A **selective medium** contains substances that hold back unwanted microbes, so that only certain kinds grow. Blood agar has blood mixed in, and some bacteria form a clear halo on it because they break down red blood cells.

With media plates you can count how many living germs a sample contains. You dilute the sample strongly and spread a small amount on a plate. Each colony counts as one **colony-forming unit**, CFU for short. If, for example, 45 colonies grow from 0.1 millilitres of a sample diluted ten thousand times, 1 millilitre of the original sample contained 4.5 million CFU.

In hospital laboratories, samples from patients are put on culture media to find the germ causing an infection. Then it is tested which antibiotic works against it. Food and drinking water are also checked for harmful germs in this way. In research, even human cells are grown in culture media, for example to test new medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gelling agent from red seaweed that makes culture media firm.
A visible little heap of millions of identical microbes that grew from one cell.
A flat, round dish with a lid for culture media.
A culture medium on which only certain microorganisms can grow.
A heated cabinet in which cultures grow at a constant temperature.

gewusst: In Japan, agar has been used for centuries as an ingredient in desserts, where it is called kanten.
Some artists paint colourful pictures with bacteria on culture media, which become visible after a few days.
Many kinds of bacteria from nature still cannot be grown on any culture medium in the laboratory.

teile.einleitung: The Nobel medal is a gold medal that every winner of a Nobel Prize receives. It is one of the most famous awards in the world. On it you can see Alfred Nobel's face and skilful pictures with Latin inscriptions.
wichtigste: Every Nobel Prize winner receives a medal, a diploma and prize money.
Since 1980 the medals have been made of 18-carat gold.
The front usually shows a portrait of Alfred Nobel.
The Swedish artist Erik Lindberg designed the medals for physics, chemistry, medicine and literature.
The medal for the Nobel Peace Prize is by the Norwegian sculptor Gustav Vigeland.
A Latin inscription on several medals comes from Virgil's Aeneid.

abschnitte.text: The **Nobel medal** is awarded together with the **Nobel Prize**. The prize was set up by the Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel in his will, and the first prizes were given in 1901. The award ceremony takes place every year on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. Most prizes are presented in Stockholm, and the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.

The medals for physics, chemistry, medicine and literature were designed by the Swedish artist **Erik Lindberg**. The back of the medal for physics and chemistry shows Nature as a goddess whose veil is being lifted by Science. On it is the Latin sentence “Inventas vitam iuvat excoluisse per artes”, which comes from Virgil's **Aeneid**. It means roughly that inventions make life more beautiful.

The medal for the Nobel Peace Prize looks different from the others. It was designed by the Norwegian sculptor **Gustav Vigeland**. On the back are three men with their arms around each other's shoulders, as a sign of brotherhood. The Peace Prize is awarded by a committee in Norway, because Sweden and Norway were joined together during Nobel's lifetime.

Since 1980 the medals have been made of **18-carat gold** mixed with other metals. In the Second World War, in Copenhagen in 1940, the chemist **George de Hevesy** wanted to hide two medals belonging to German physicists from the occupying forces. He dissolved them in **aqua regia**, a strong mixture of acids that can even break down gold. After the war the gold was recovered, and the Nobel Foundation had new medals struck from it.

Some prize winners have sold or given away their medal. In 2022 the Russian journalist **Dmitry Muratov** auctioned his Nobel Peace Prize medal for over 100 million dollars. The money went to a programme to help children from Ukraine who had been driven from their homes by the war. It was the highest price ever paid for a Nobel medal.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very famous award for great achievements in science and literature and for peace.
A measure of how much pure gold is in a mixture. 24 carat is pure gold.
A very strong mixture of two acids that can even dissolve gold.
Text that is engraved or stamped into metal or stone.

gewusst: Before 1980 the medals were made of even purer gold than today.
The dissolved gold of the two medals stood unnoticed in a bottle on a shelf in Copenhagen throughout the war.
Swiss researchers have also won many Nobel medals, for example in chemistry and physics.

teile.einleitung: A micrometre is a tiny measure of length: a thousandth of a millimetre. Micrometres are used to measure things so small that you can usually only see them under a microscope, such as bacteria or blood cells. The micrometre is abbreviated µm.
wichtigste: A millimetre has 1000 micrometres.
A micrometre is a millionth of a metre.
The sign µ is the Greek letter mu and stands for micro.
A human hair is about 50 to 100 µm thick.
A red blood cell has a diameter of about 7 µm.
Bacteria such as Escherichia coli are only a few micrometres in size.
The micrometer screw gauge is also simply called a micrometer and measures to 0.01 mm.

abschnitte.text: The micrometre is a unit of length in the International **System of Units**. A metre has a million micrometres, and a millimetre has 1000 micrometres. The prefix **micro** comes from Greek and means small. It is abbreviated with the Greek letter **µ**, which is called mu. The micrometre used to be called a micron.

A sheet of ordinary printer paper is about 100 µm thick, which is a tenth of a millimetre. A human hair measures about 50 to 100 µm, depending on the person. A **red blood cell** has a diameter of about 7 µm. Bacteria such as Escherichia coli are only a few micrometres long. You can no longer see such things with the naked eye; you need a **light microscope**.

In connection with air quality, people talk about **fine dust**, which is tiny particles in the air. PM10 fine dust means particles smaller than 10 µm, which can get deep into the lungs. Pollen grains, which cause hay fever, are usually a few dozen micrometres in size. The thickness of cling film or tin foil is also given in micrometres.

With an ordinary ruler you can measure to the nearest millimetre at most. For finer measurements there is the **micrometer screw gauge**, which is also simply called a micrometer. It has a fine screw that moves forward only a small amount with each turn. With it you can measure to 0.01 millimetres, which is 10 µm, for example the thickness of wires or metal sheets in workshops.

In precision engineering and the watch industry, which are very important in Switzerland, parts often have to fit to within a few micrometres. The micrometre is also important in medicine, for example for measuring cells and germs. Parts of computer chips used to be measured in micrometres. Today they are much smaller still and are given in **nanometres**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity with which you measure, for example the metre or the kilogram.
A device that lets you see very small things enlarged.
Tiny particles in the air that you cannot see but breathe in.
A precise measuring instrument with a screw that measures to a hundredth of a millimetre.

gewusst: About 140 red blood cells fit side by side in one millimetre.
A micrometre is to a metre what a metre is to 1000 kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The marshmallow test is a famous experiment in psychology. Children could eat a sweet straight away or wait a little and get two for it. Researchers wanted to find out how well children can put off their wishes.
wichtigste: The psychologist Walter Mischel developed the marshmallow test.
The children could have one sweet straight away or two later.
Distracting themselves or looking away helped the children to wait longer.
Mischel's follow-up studies reported that waiting longer went together with better achievements later on.
A large study in 2018 found a weaker link, which depended on family background.
If the researcher had broken promises beforehand, children waited much less long.
Mischel spoke of a hot and a cool system in the mind.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 1960s, Walter Mischel at Stanford University in California invited children aged about four to five to play a game. A child sat alone in a room in front of a plate with a sweet, such as a marshmallow. It was allowed to eat it straight away. But if it waited until the researcher came back, it got two. This waiting for a bigger reward is called **delayed gratification**.

The researchers watched what the children did to hold out. Some covered their eyes, sang, turned away or played with their feet. Those who **distracted** themselves could usually wait much longer. Children who stared at the sweet often gave up sooner. It also helped to imagine the marshmallow as something else, for example as a cloud.

Mischel explained the behaviour with two systems in the mind. The **hot system** reacts quickly and emotionally; it shouts: I want that now. The **cool system** thinks things over and plans for the future. If you switch on the cool system, you can resist temptation better. This ability is called **self-control**.

Years later, Mischel asked how the former children were getting on. In his follow-up studies he reported that children who had waited longer had, on average, better school results later. But a large **replication study** in 2018, with many more and more varied children, found the link to be much weaker. It depended strongly on family background, for example on how safe and reliable a child's life was. So a single test says little about a person's future.

One version of the test showed something exciting: if the researcher had broken promises to the children beforehand, they waited much less long. For these children it made sense to take the sure offer straight away. Waiting is only worth it if you can **trust** that the reward will really come. Walter Mischel, who lived from 1930 to 2018, had already become known in 1968 with his book “Personality and Assessment”. With it he started the so-called person-situation debate, about whether behaviour depends more on personality or on the situation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Waiting for a reward in order to get a bigger one later.
The ability to manage your own wishes and feelings.
An experiment that repeats an earlier one in order to check the result.
The science of human experience and behaviour.

gewusst: In the first experiments, not only marshmallows were offered but also biscuits or pretzels.
Walter Mischel was born in Vienna and as a child fled from the Nazis to the USA.
Self-control can be practised, for example by distracting yourself on purpose or making a plan.

teile.einleitung: Mineral water is water from an underground spring that has taken up minerals on its way through the layers of rock. It comes with a lot of fizz, a little or none at all. Switzerland has many well-known mineral springs, especially in the Lower Engadine.
wichtigste: Mineral water comes from an underground spring.
Its minerals come from the layers of rock in the ground.
There are especially many natural mineral springs in the Lower Engadine.
The gas in naturally sparkling water comes from deep inside the Earth.
Mineral water without fizz is often called still water.
The bubbles like to form on tiny scratches and specks of dust in the glass.
A shaken bottle often foams over when you open it.

abschnitte.text: Mineral water starts as rain or snow that seeps into the ground. There it often flows slowly through **layers of rock** for many years. As it does so, it dissolves substances from the rock, for example **calcium**, magnesium and sodium. That is why every mineral water tastes a little different, depending on the rock.

Natural mineral water must come from a protected **underground spring**. It must be pure and may hardly be changed. In Switzerland and the EU such a spring must be officially **recognised**. The water is bottled directly at the spring.

The bubbles are made of the gas **carbon dioxide**; dissolved in water it forms **carbonic acid**. Some springs sparkle naturally, because the gas rises from deep inside the Earth. But for many brands, the fizz is only added during bottling. In the closed bottle the gas is under pressure; when you open it, the gas escapes and forms bubbles.

The bubbles form mainly on tiny **scratches** and specks of dust in the glass. Because gas is much lighter than water, they rise to the top. On the way they collect more gas and so get bigger and bigger. If you shake a bottle, many small bubbles form, which foam out all at once when you open it.

Well-known Swiss springs are, for example, in Vals in the Grisons, in Henniez in Vaud and in Aproz in Valais. In the **Lower Engadine** around Scuol, especially many natural mineral springs bubble up, and some taste of iron. Centuries ago, guests already came there to take drinking cures. By the way, Swiss **tap water** is also of very good quality and much cheaper.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances such as calcium or magnesium that the body needs in small amounts.
Carbon dioxide dissolved in water, which forms bubbles.
A place where groundwater comes out of the ground by itself.
Mineral water with no or almost no fizz.

gewusst: Some mineral springs in the Lower Engadine taste so strongly of iron that the water leaves reddish marks.
Rainwater can spend many years travelling through rock before it comes back to the surface as mineral water.
In a completely clean glass with no scratches, far fewer bubbles form.

teile.einleitung: The mycelium is the fine, branching network of threads of a fungus, which usually grows unseen in the soil or in wood. The mushroom we see and pick in the woods is only the fruiting body, a small part of the whole living thing. Some mycelia are among the largest living things on Earth.
wichtigste: The mycelium is the fine network of a fungus in the soil or in wood.
It consists of countless fine threads, the hyphae.
The visible mushroom in the woods is only the fruiting body.
The mycelium of many woodland fungi joins up with the roots of trees.
Fungi are not plants but form their own group of living things.
Unlike green plants, they cannot make food with sunlight.
A giant honey fungus with a very large mycelium lives in the Swiss National Park.

abschnitte.text: If you pick a cep, you are only holding the **fruiting body** in your hand. The actual fungus lives on in the soil as a **mycelium**, often for many years. The fruiting body only grows to form **spores**, with which the fungus spreads. You can compare it with an apple, while the mycelium is like the whole apple tree.

The mycelium consists of **hyphae**, threads that are often thinner than a hair. They grow at their tips and keep branching. This creates a dense network that runs through soil, leaves or wood. A handful of woodland soil can contain fungal threads with a total length of many metres.

Many woodland fungi live in a close partnership with trees, called **mycorrhiza**. The mycelium wraps around the fine roots and takes water and nutrient salts such as phosphorus from the soil. In return the fungus gets sugar from the tree, which the tree makes using sunlight. The fly agaric and the birch, or the larch bolete and the larch, are well-known pairs.

Fungi cannot carry out **photosynthesis**; they have to take in their food. Many fungi break down dead leaves, needles and wood and turn them into fertile soil. In doing so they release digestive substances outside themselves and take in the dissolved nutrients. Without fungi, huge piles of leaves and dead branches would build up in the forest.

abschnitte.titel: A giant in the National Park
abschnitte.text: Near the Ofen Pass in the **Swiss National Park**, researchers from the WSL discovered a giant **dark honey fungus**. Its mycelium stretches over about 800 by 500 metres, which is about 35 hectares. Its age is estimated at over 1000 years. The honey fungus attacks trees and can weaken them, but it is part of the natural cycle of the forest.

Important substances come from fungi, for example the antibiotic **penicillin**, which is obtained from a mould. The mycelium of edible mushrooms such as button mushrooms is grown on straw or compost. Today researchers are also testing building materials and packaging made of mycelium, which later break down again. When picking mushrooms, it is important never to tear out the mycelium and always to have unknown mushrooms checked at a mushroom inspection point.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single fine thread of a fungus; the plural is hyphae.
The visible part of the fungus, which forms spores.
A partnership between a fungus and plant roots that benefits both.
A tiny grain from which a new fungus can grow.
A living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals.

gewusst: A honey fungus in Oregon in the USA, covering almost 10 square kilometres, is considered one of the largest living things in the world.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
The rings of mushrooms on meadows, called fairy rings, form because the mycelium grows outwards in a circle.

teile.einleitung: A mass balance is a calculation that shows whether something has gained or lost mass over a certain period. It is especially important in glacier research: it reveals whether a glacier is growing or shrinking. Because Swiss glaciers have been losing ice for decades, their mass balance is watched closely.
wichtigste: The mass balance of a glacier is the difference between the gain and the loss of mass over a period.
The gain is called accumulation, and the loss ablation.
The glaciological year in the Alps usually runs from 1 October to 30 September.
The specific mass balance is given in metres of water equivalent.
Stakes in the ice are used to measure melting in the ablation zone.
In the geodetic method, elevation models from different years are compared.
The tongue of a glacier reacts only with a delay, because the ice takes years to decades to flow.

abschnitte.text: A **mass balance** is like an account book for mass: you count what is added and subtract what is lost.
