The principle applies in chemistry, physics and environmental research, because mass does not simply disappear. For a **glacier**, you ask how much snow and ice it has gained in a year and how much it has lost. If the balance is positive, the glacier grows; if it is negative, it shrinks.

The gain in mass is called **accumulation**. This includes mainly snowfall, but also avalanches and snow blown in by the wind. The loss is called **ablation**: ice and snow melt, evaporate or break off, for example when ice calves into a lake. In the upper part of the glacier, the **accumulation zone**, gain is greater; in the lower part, the ablation zone, loss is greater.

The specific mass balance is given in **metres of water equivalent**, as if all the ice had melted to water and been spread evenly over the glacier. If a glacier gains 1.2 metres from snow and loses 2.0 metres from melting, its annual balance is -0.8 metres of water equivalent. If a glacier of 10 square kilometres has a balance of -1 metre, it has lost 10 million cubic metres of water. The calculation is usually for a year running from 1 October to 30 September.

In the **glaciological method**, researchers drill stakes into the ice and read off in autumn how much of the stake has melted free. In spring they measure in snow pits how much snow has fallen. In the **geodetic method**, elevation models of the glacier surface from different years are compared, for example from aerial photographs or lidar data. The two methods complement each other.

The length of a glacier tongue reacts only with a delay to a changed mass balance. This is because the ice takes years to decades to flow from the accumulation zone to the **tongue**. A large glacier such as the Aletsch Glacier therefore reacts more slowly than a small one. The mass balance shows changes much faster than the length does.

The Swiss glacier monitoring network **GLAMOS** measures the mass balance of many glaciers; some series of measurements, such as on the Clariden Firn, have been running for over 100 years. For decades the balance has been clearly negative almost every year. In the record year 2022, Swiss glaciers lost about 6 per cent of their volume, and in 2023 a further 4 per cent or so. The main reason is **global warming**, with hotter summers and less snow.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glacier's gain in mass, mainly through snow.
A glacier's loss of mass through melting, evaporation or breaking off.
The height of the layer of water that would form if ice or snow melted.
The upper part of a glacier, where more snow is added than melts away.
The lower part of a glacier, where more melts than is added.

gewusst: One metre of water equivalent corresponds to about 1.1 metres of ice, because ice is lighter than water.
The stakes on Swiss glaciers are often drilled into the ice with steam drills.
In 2022 and 2023 together, Swiss glaciers lost about as much ice as in the 30 years from 1960 to 1990.

teile.einleitung: The Natural History Museum Bern is one of the oldest and best-known nature museums in Switzerland. It shows animals from all over the world, minerals, fossils and meteorites. Its most famous resident is the St Bernard Barry, who rescued people from the snow.
wichtigste: The museum is in the city of Bern, in the Kirchenfeld district.
The famous rescue dog Barry is on display here.
Barry was a St Bernard and rescued people from the snow in the mountains.
The museum is known for its dioramas, display windows with animals in front of painted landscapes.
The animals are preserved by taxidermists.
The museum shows large rock crystals from the Alps.
Skeletons, the bony frames of animals, can also be seen.

abschnitte.text: The Natural History Museum Bern is on Bernastrasse in the **Kirchenfeld district**, very close to other museums. It was founded in 1832. Since the 1930s it has been in its present building. Today many families and school classes visit it every year.

The most famous exhibit is **Barry**, a dog from the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass. Barry lived from 1800 to 1814 and is said to have saved the lives of over 40 people. He tracked down people who had got lost in snow or fog. After his death he was preserved and has been on view in Bern ever since. He is considered an ancestor of the **St Bernard** breed, which is named after the pass.

The museum is especially well known for its **dioramas**. These are large display cases in which preserved animals stand in front of a painted landscape. It looks as if you were looking into a real habitat. They show animals from Switzerland, such as ibex, chamois and marmots, but also lions, zebras and gorillas from Africa.

The animals in the museum are real and have been preserved by **taxidermists**. These experts treat the skin of a dead animal and stretch it over a model body. Glass eyes are put in, and the pose is meant to look as lifelike as possible. For other animals the museum shows the **skeleton**, the bony frame.

In the earth sciences department, minerals and gemstones sparkle. Especially impressive are huge **rock crystals** from the Swiss Alps, for example from the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri. Such crystals are searched for in clefts in the rock by **Strahler**, Swiss crystal hunters. The museum also shows fossils and meteorites from space.

Behind the exhibition rooms, the museum is also a place of **research**. Millions of objects are kept in the collections, from insects and bird skins to rocks. Scientists use them, for example, to study how the animal life of Switzerland is changing. Changing special exhibitions take up exciting topics from nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A display case with animals in front of a painted landscape that recreates a habitat.
An expert who preserves dead animals for museums.
The bony frame of an animal or a person.
A person who searches for crystals in the Alps.

gewusst: Barry probably never wore a little barrel of brandy around his neck; that was invented in later pictures.
Barry's preserved body was reworked in 1923 and since then has looked more like a modern St Bernard than the original.

teile.einleitung: An mRNA vaccine is a modern kind of vaccination that gives the body building instructions for a protein from a germ. The body's cells briefly make this protein themselves, and the immune system learns to recognise it. mRNA vaccines became known worldwide from the end of 2020 in the fight against Covid-19.
wichtigste: An mRNA vaccine contains building instructions for a protein from the germ.
The “m” in mRNA stands for the English word messenger.
From the end of 2020, mRNA vaccines were approved widely for the first time, against Covid-19.
The first Covid-19 vaccines contained the building instructions for the coronavirus's spike protein.
The mRNA does not get into the nucleus and does not change the genetic material.
Tiny fatty coatings protect the mRNA and carry it into the cells.
The injection is usually given into the muscle of the upper arm.

abschnitte.text: In every cell, the **DNA**, the genetic material with all the building plans, lies in the nucleus. When the cell needs a particular protein, it copies the matching building plan onto a short molecule, the **mRNA**. This messenger travels out of the nucleus to the cell's protein factories, the **ribosomes**. There the protein is assembled according to the instructions.

With an mRNA vaccine, such a messenger is injected from outside into the muscle of the upper arm. The cells there read the instructions and build a harmless piece of the germ, which for the coronavirus is the **spike protein**. The immune system notices this foreign protein and makes **antibodies** and defence cells against it. If the real virus comes later, the body recognises it more quickly and can defend itself better.

mRNA is very delicate and breaks down easily. That is why it is packed into tiny fatty coatings called **lipid nanoparticles**. They protect the mRNA and help it get into the cells. The first Covid-19 vaccines therefore had to be stored very cold, one of them at about minus 70 degrees.

A common question is whether the vaccination changes your genetic material. The answer is no, because the mRNA does not get into the **nucleus**, where the DNA is. What is more, the body breaks the mRNA down again after a short time, usually within a few days. All that remains is the immune system's memory.

People had been researching the idea since the 1990s. The biochemist **Katalin Karikó** and the immunologist **Drew Weissman** found out how to change mRNA so that it does not trigger too strong a defence reaction. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023. The companies BioNTech with Pfizer, and Moderna, brought out the first vaccines in 2020; in Switzerland the first was approved in December 2020.

A big advantage is that the building instructions can quickly be adapted to a new germ. That is why the Covid-19 vaccines were updated several times for new variants of the virus. Researchers are also working on mRNA vaccines against flu and other diseases. It is also being tested whether the technology can help in treating cancer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger molecule that carries building instructions for a protein in the cell.
A spike-like protein on the surface of the coronavirus.
The body's defensive substances, which recognise and mark germs.
A tiny protein factory in every cell.
Very small fat droplets that protect and transport active substances.

gewusst: The building instructions for the spike protein could be designed only a few days after the virus's genetic material was published at the beginning of 2020.
A dose of vaccine contains only tiny amounts of mRNA, usually far less than a thousandth of a gram.
Katalin Karikó researched mRNA for decades, even though for a long time her idea found hardly any support.

teile.einleitung: A moraine is a pile or ridge of rock debris that a glacier carries with it and leaves behind. In it, large and small stones, sand and clay lie all mixed up. In Switzerland you come across moraines everywhere, not only in the Alps but also in the Central Plateau, where glaciers used to lie.
wichtigste: A moraine consists of rock debris that a glacier carries and leaves behind.
At the edge of a glacier lies the lateral moraine.
In front of the glacier tongue, the terminal moraine forms.
Where two glaciers flow together, a medial moraine often forms.
Under the glacier lies the ground moraine.
Old moraines show how big a glacier used to be.
A moraine across a valley can dam up a lake.

abschnitte.text: A glacier is a huge stream of ice that flows slowly down the valley. As it does so, it carries **rock debris** with it, from fine sand to blocks as big as houses. Where it leaves this material behind, **moraines** form. Because the ice does not sort anything, large and small stones lie all mixed up. This makes a moraine easy to tell apart from deposits left by a river, which are sorted by size.

At the edge of a glacier, debris falling from the valley sides collects and forms the **lateral moraine**. In front of the glacier tongue, the ice pushes together a ridge, the **terminal moraine**. Where two glaciers flow together, two lateral moraines join to form a **medial moraine**, which lies on the ice as a dark stripe. Under the glacier, the **ground moraine** forms from finely ground rock.

On the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais you can see several dark medial moraines like the lanes of a motorway. On many Alpine glaciers you can make out high lateral moraines far above today's ice. They show how big the glaciers still were around 1850, at the end of the so-called **Little Ice Age**. Since then the glaciers have melted a great deal.

abschnitte.titel: Traces of the ice age in the Central Plateau
abschnitte.text: During the last ice age, the glaciers reached far out into the Central Plateau. The city of Zurich lies on a terminal moraine of the former Linth Glacier. The causeway between Rapperswil and Hurden also stands on a moraine. Huge boulders that the ice carried a long way are called **erratic boulders**. Some terminal moraines dammed up lakes, and many lakes in the Central Plateau owe their shape to the glaciers.

After many years, trees and meadows grow on old moraines. The soil is often stony but fertile, and many hills in the Central Plateau are wooded moraines. Moraine material is an important raw material: in **gravel pits** it is dug out for gravel for concrete. Fresh moraines by melting glaciers, on the other hand, are loose and can slide down as a debris flow in heavy rain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large mass of ice that moves slowly down a valley.
The lower end of a glacier.
A large boulder that a glacier has carried far from where it came from.
A time when large parts of the Earth were covered in ice.
A fast stream of water, mud and stones that flows down a slope.

gewusst: The word moraine comes from the French dialect of the Savoy Alps.
Some erratic boulders in the Central Plateau come from the Valais Alps and were carried over a hundred kilometres by the ice.
Because glaciers are melting, many lateral moraines now stand high above the ice like the rims of an empty bath.

teile.einleitung: Messenger RNA, mRNA for short, is a messenger molecule in every living cell. It carries a copy of the building instructions of a gene from the genetic material to the ribosomes, where a protein is built from it. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, many people also know mRNA from vaccines.
wichtigste: mRNA delivers the building instructions of a gene to the ribosome.
It is made during transcription as a copy of a section of DNA.
Every three bases of the mRNA form a codon, which stands for a particular amino acid.
In eukaryotes, a 5' cap with 7-methylguanosine protects the start of the mRNA.
At the 3' end, most eukaryotic mRNAs carry a poly-A tail.
During splicing, introns are removed and exons are joined together.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman received the Nobel Prize in 2023 for work that made mRNA vaccines possible.

abschnitte.text: mRNA is a **ribonucleic acid**, a long thread made of many building blocks. Its four bases are called adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil. Unlike DNA, it is usually single-stranded and much shorter-lived. You can imagine it like a **copy** from a valuable cookbook: the book, the DNA, stays safely in the nucleus, while the copy goes to the cell's kitchen.

First an enzyme called RNA polymerase reads a gene and builds the matching mRNA; this is called **transcription**. Then the mRNA goes to the ribosomes, the protein factories of the cell. There it is read in groups of three, the **codons**. Each codon stands for an amino acid, and the amino acids are linked into a chain. This second step is called **translation**.

In plants, animals and fungi, the freshly copied precursor mRNA is processed further. A **5' cap** with 7-methylguanosine is added to its 5' end, which protects it and serves as a start signal for the ribosome. A **poly-A tail** made of many adenine building blocks is attached to the 3' end. During splicing, the cell cuts out sections without building information, the introns, and joins the exons together. Through **alternative splicing**, a single gene can even produce several different proteins.

After a while an mRNA is broken down again. In bacteria it usually lasts only a few minutes, so that **protein production** can quickly adapt to new conditions. In humans many mRNAs last for a few hours. In this way the cell can control exactly how much of a protein is made. So mRNA is a kind of throwaway message.

An **mRNA vaccine** contains building instructions for a piece of the virus; for Covid-19 it is the so-called spike protein. The body's cells briefly build this harmless piece, and the immune system learns to recognise it. So that the mRNA does not cause too strong an inflammation, uridine is replaced by the modified nucleoside **N1-methylpseudouridine**. This idea goes back to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it in 2023. The first mRNA vaccines against Covid-19 were approved at the end of 2020, including in Switzerland.

mRNA was detected around 1961 by several research groups, including Sydney Brenner, François Jacob and Matthew Meselson. Soon afterwards people began to crack the **genetic code**. Today experts are researching how mRNA can also be used against cancer and other diseases. In Valais, the company Lonza in Visp produced the active ingredient for an mRNA vaccine against Covid-19.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny protein factory in the cell that reads the mRNA.
A group of three bases on the mRNA that stands for an amino acid.
Copying a gene from the DNA into an mRNA.
A section of precursor mRNA without building information, which is cut out.
A section that stays in the finished mRNA after splicing.

gewusst: The mRNA in a vaccine is broken down in the body after a short time and does not enter the nucleus.
Katalin Karikó fought for her mRNA research for decades, even though for a long time she got hardly any funding.
A single ribosome can add several amino acids per second to a protein chain.

teile.einleitung: Nanomedicine uses tiny particles and tools only a few billionths of a metre in size to detect and treat diseases. Such nanoparticles can carry medicines straight to a tumour or make organs visible in images. It is one of the most exciting fields of research, between physics, chemistry, biology and medicine.
wichtigste: Nanomedicine works with particles about 1 to 100 nanometres in size.
Liposomes are tiny bubbles with a double layer of fat that carry drugs.
Through the EPR effect, nanoparticles build up passively in tumour tissue.
In active targeting, nanoparticles carry recognition molecules such as antibodies.
Iron oxide nanoparticles are used as contrast agents and for magnetic hyperthermia.
The red test line of many rapid tests is made by gold nanoparticles.
In the blood, a layer of proteins forms around nanoparticles, the protein corona.

abschnitte.text: A **nanometre** is a millionth of a millimetre. A human hair is about 50,000 to 100,000 nanometres thick. Many nanoparticles are as big as a virus or a large protein. Because they are so tiny, they can move about in the body where larger particles cannot get to.

One important aim is to deliver medicines exactly where they are meant to work. For this, active substances are packed, for example, into **liposomes**, small balls with a double layer of fat. As early as 1995 a cancer drug in liposomes was approved in the USA. The mRNA vaccines against Covid-19 also use tiny fat droplets, the **lipid nanoparticles**.

Blood vessels in tumours are often leaky, and drainage through the lymph works poorly. So nanoparticles collect there by themselves; this is called the **EPR effect**. In **active targeting**, the particles also carry recognition molecules such as antibodies, which dock onto particular cancer cells like a key. The aim is to spare healthy cells.

**Iron oxide nanoparticles** are magnetic and are used as contrast agents in magnetic resonance imaging. In **magnetic hyperthermia**, they are put into a tumour and heated with an alternating magnetic field, so that the tumour tissue is damaged. Gold nanoparticles are reddish in colour and gather at the test line in many antigen rapid tests. This makes the line visible when the substance being looked for is in the sample.

The brain is protected by the **blood-brain barrier**, which does not let many substances from the blood through. Researchers are trying to use nanocarriers to smuggle medicines for brain diseases through this barrier. Another hurdle is the **protein corona**, a layer of blood proteins that attaches to nanoparticles. It can change where the particles travel in the body and how the immune system reacts to them.

In Switzerland, for example, ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and Empa do research on nanomedicine. Like all medicines, new nanomedicines must be tested for a long time; in Switzerland this is done by the authority Swissmedic. It is also investigated whether the particles can cause harm in the body. Nanotoxicology deals with this question.

begriffe.erklaerung: A millionth of a millimetre.
A tiny bubble made of fat molecules that can carry active substances.
Deliberately aiming at particular cells, for example cancer cells.
A substance that makes organs or tissue easier to see in medical images.
A protective layer that shields the brain from many substances in the blood.

gewusst: Many thousands of nanoparticles fit side by side on the tip of a pin.
The test line of a coronavirus rapid test owes its colour to tiny particles of gold.
Some nanoparticles are so small that they leave the body again through the kidneys in the urine.

teile.einleitung: Ocean currents are huge movements of water in the oceans that act like rivers in the sea. They carry heat, nutrients and even plastic rubbish around the whole world. Without the warm Gulf Stream, Europe would be much colder.
wichtigste: Surface currents are driven mainly by the wind.
The thermohaline circulation is caused by differences in temperature and salt content.
Cold, salty water sinks into the depths because it has a higher density.
The Coriolis force deflects currents to the right in the northern hemisphere.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current is the ocean current carrying the most water in the world.
Plastic rubbish collects in large ocean gyres.
If the currents in the Pacific change, El Niño can develop off Peru.

abschnitte.text: Ocean currents are lasting movements of huge masses of water in the oceans. Some flow at the surface, others deep down at the sea floor. The **Gulf Stream** in the Atlantic, for example, carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico towards Europe. It carries much more water than all the rivers in the world put together.

Surface currents are driven mainly by the **wind**, especially by steady winds such as the trade winds. Because the Earth turns, the currents are deflected, to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere. This deflection is called the **Coriolis force**. As a result, huge circular **ocean gyres** form in the big oceans, in which plastic rubbish also collects.

As well as the wind there is a second driving force: differences in temperature and salt content. Cold, salty water has a higher **density** and sinks into the depths, for example in the North Atlantic near Greenland. It then flows slowly along the sea floor through all the oceans and rises again elsewhere. This worldwide current is called the **thermohaline circulation** or the global conveyor belt; a single round trip can take about 1000 years.

The **Antarctic Circumpolar Current** flows around Antarctica and is considered the ocean current carrying the most water in the world. The cold **Humboldt Current** flows northwards off the west coast of South America. When cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the surface there, this is called **upwelling**. In such areas there is especially plenty of plankton and fish.

Ocean currents spread heat between the equator and the poles. Thanks to the Gulf Stream and its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, western Europe is milder than areas at the same latitude in Canada. If the currents in the Pacific change, the water off Peru becomes unusually warm; this is called **El Niño**. Then there is unusual weather worldwide, such as droughts in Australia and heavy rain in South America.

abschnitte.titel: Plastic ducks on a world tour
abschnitte.text: In 1992, in a storm in the Pacific, containers fell off a cargo ship into the sea. They contained thousands of **plastic bath toys** such as ducks, turtles and frogs. Over the years they were washed up on coasts in Alaska, Hawaii and elsewhere. Researchers used the finds to show how ocean currents spread floating objects over long distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A warm ocean current in the Atlantic that makes the climate in Europe mild.
An apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation, which deflects currents.
A worldwide ocean current driven by differences in temperature and salt content.
The rising of cold, nutrient-rich deep water along a coast.
A weather event in which the sea off Peru becomes unusually warm.

gewusst: Some of the plastic bath toys from 1992 were still being found on coasts many years later.
The name El Niño means “the Christ child” in Spanish, because the warm water often appears around Christmas.
In the great garbage patch in the North Pacific, plastic floats over an area much larger than Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A metallic glass is a metal whose atoms do not lie neatly in a lattice but are jumbled, as in window glass. It is made by cooling liquid metal extremely quickly. This gives it amazing properties: it is very strong, very elastic and hardly rusts.
wichtigste: In metallic glasses the atoms are disordered; this is called amorphous.
Traditionally they are made by cooling a metal melt extremely quickly.
They have no grain boundaries and are therefore often especially resistant to corrosion.
Very high strength and elasticity are typical.
Soft magnetic metallic glasses are used for transformer cores.
The critical cooling rate needed limits the size of parts.
Between the glass transition and crystallisation, they can be shaped much like plastics.

abschnitte.text: In an ordinary metal, the atoms sit in a regular pattern, the **crystal lattice**. A piece of metal consists of many small crystals, the grains, which meet at **grain boundaries**. In a metallic glass this order is missing: the atoms lie jumbled up like marbles in a shaken bag. This state is called **amorphous**. Because there are no grain boundaries, corrosion cannot easily attack there either.

If a metal melt cools slowly, the atoms arrange themselves into crystals. But if you cool it extremely quickly, they stay **frozen** in their disordered positions. The first metallic glasses needed cooling rates of about a million degrees per second. That is why at first only very thin ribbons could be made, by spraying the melt onto a fast-spinning, cooled roller. The **critical cooling rate** needed still limits how thick a part can be.

The first metallic glass was made in 1960 by the researcher Pol Duwez at the California Institute of Technology, from a mixture of gold and silicon. In the following decades, alloys of several metals were found that turn into glass more easily. Since the 1990s there have been so-called **bulk metallic glasses**, which can be a few centimetres thick. They contain, for example, zirconium, titanium, copper, nickel or palladium.

Metallic glasses are often two to three times stronger than comparable crystalline metals. They are very **elastic** and spring back into shape after being deformed. When they do fail at room temperature, they deform in narrow **shear bands** and often break suddenly. If you heat them to a temperature between the glass transition and crystallisation, they become soft and can be pressed into moulds like plastic.

Soft magnetic metallic glasses based on iron are found in the cores of **transformers**, because they waste less energy there. They are also found in anti-theft tags on goods in shops. Because of their springiness, they have been used for golf clubs and tennis rackets. In medicine and precision engineering, they are being tested for tiny gear wheels and implants.

Swiss universities also research metallic glasses, for example ETH Zurich. There, among other things, researchers study how the materials can be used for medicine and precision technology. The Swiss watch industry is also interested in such materials, because they are strong, can be shaped and hardly rust.

begriffe.erklaerung: Without a regular arrangement of atoms, as in glass.
A regular arrangement of atoms in a solid substance.
The boundary between two small crystals in a metal.
A mixture of several metals or of metal and other substances.
A narrow zone in which a metallic glass suddenly deforms.

gewusst: A metallic glass is not see-through, even though it is called “glass”; the name only refers to the disordered atoms.
A steel ball bounces for an especially long time on a plate of metallic glass, because hardly any energy is lost.
The first metallic glasses were thinner than a hair.

teile.einleitung: Mass-energy equivalence says that mass and energy are equivalent and can be turned into each other. Albert Einstein described this in 1905 with the famous formula E=mc², when he was living and working in Bern. It explains why the Sun shines and why nuclear power stations produce so much energy.
wichtigste: Mass and energy are equivalent, meaning of equal value.
Mass can be turned into energy and the other way round.
The formula for this is E=mc².
Albert Einstein published it in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern.
Even a tiny mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy.
The Sun and nuclear power stations get their energy from this principle.
E=mc² is the best-known formula in physics.

abschnitte.text: In the formula, **E** stands for energy, **m** for mass and **c** for the speed of light. The speed of light is about 300,000 kilometres a second. In the formula it is also multiplied by itself, which means it is “squared”. That is why the energy contained in a small mass is unimaginably large. So mass is a very dense, packed-up form of energy.

From 1902 Albert Einstein worked as a technical expert at the **Federal Patent Office** in Bern. In his free time he thought about the big questions of physics. In 1905 he published several groundbreaking papers, including the special theory of **relativity**. In a short addition to it he showed that mass and energy are equivalent. That is why 1905 is also called Einstein's “miracle year”, and his flat at the time on Kramgasse in Bern is now a museum.

abschnitte.titel: How much energy is in mass?
abschnitte.text: If a single gram of mass were turned completely into energy, about 90 trillion joules would be produced. That is roughly as much electricity as a large nuclear power station such as Gösgen produces in a whole day. In everyday life we notice nothing of this, because mass is almost never completely converted. In theory, even a hot cup of tea is a tiny bit heavier than a cold one. But this change is so small that it cannot be measured.

In the **Sun**, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei; this is called **nuclear fusion**. The new nucleus is slightly lighter than the starting nuclei, and the difference in mass is released as light and heat. In this way the Sun loses about four million tonnes of mass every second. In nuclear power stations, on the other hand, heavy uranium nuclei are split, and here too a little mass turns into energy. This small loss of mass is called the **mass defect**.

The formula E=mc² fundamentally changed our understanding of energy and matter. It is the basis of nuclear energy and explains how stars shine. In particle accelerators such as at CERN near Geneva, energy of motion is even turned into new particles, that is, into mass. The principle also plays a part in medicine, for example in certain examinations using radiation. Hardly any other formula is so famous or so often printed on T-shirts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Being of equal value, when two things mean the same in a certain way.
The speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres a second.
Einstein's theory of space, time, motion and gravity.
The small amount of mass that is missing after nuclear reactions because it has become energy.

gewusst: Einstein wrote his famous paper in Bern when he was not yet a professor but an employee at the patent office.
In Einstein's original paper of 1905, the formula did not yet appear in the short form E=mc² that is known today.

teile.einleitung: McMurdo Station is a research station of the USA in Antarctica. It is the largest settlement on the icy continent and seems almost like a small town. From here scientists study ice, climate, animals and space.
wichtigste: McMurdo Station is run by the USA.
It is the largest station in Antarctica.
It lies on Ross Island.
In summer over 1000 people live there.
Many supply flights start in Christchurch in New Zealand.
New Zealand's Scott Base is only a few kilometres away.
The active volcano Mount Erebus rises nearby.
From 1962 to 1972 a small nuclear reactor supplied part of the electricity.

abschnitte.text: McMurdo Station lies at the southern tip of **Ross Island** on McMurdo Sound. This is a bay at the edge of the Ross Sea, about 1300 kilometres from the South Pole. Close by, the active volcano **Mount Erebus**, almost 3800 metres high, gives off smoke. A few kilometres away is Scott Base, New Zealand's research station. The station was named after the British officer Archibald McMurdo, after whom the sound is also named.

The USA built the station in 1955 and 1956 as part of Operation Deep Freeze. At that time many countries were preparing for the International Geophysical Year of 1957 and 1958. Around 1902 the polar explorer Robert Falcon Scott had already built a wooden hut nearby, which still stands today. From 1962 to 1972 a small **nuclear reactor** supplied part of the electricity. It was shut down and dismantled because of technical problems.

In the Antarctic summer over 1000 people live at McMurdo, in winter only a few hundred. The station has over a hundred buildings, including laboratories, living quarters, workshops, a canteen and a small church. Many residents are not researchers themselves but cooks, mechanics, pilots or doctors. In winter it is dark for months, and in summer the sun shines round the clock. Drinking water is made from seawater.

Almost everything the station needs has to be brought from far away. Many aircraft start in **Christchurch** in New Zealand and land on runways of ice and snow. Once a year ships bring fuel and materials, when an **icebreaker** clears a path through the sea ice. Rubbish is carefully sorted and taken back out of Antarctica. The Amundsen-Scott Station right at the South Pole is also supplied from McMurdo.

At McMurdo and from there, glaciers, sea ice, volcanoes and climate are studied. Biologists research seals, penguins and fish that survive in the icy water. Space is also observed with balloons and telescopes. Antarctica is protected by the **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959, which allows only peaceful use and research. Researchers from Switzerland also work in international projects in Antarctica, for example on ice drilling.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area around the South Pole with the ice-covered continent.
A base where scientists live and work.
A powerful ship that breaks a channel through thick ice.
An agreement between many countries to protect Antarctica for peaceful research.

gewusst: McMurdo has a cash machine, which is a great rarity in Antarctica.
Near the station are the Dry Valleys, which are among the driest places on Earth.
The residents gave McMurdo's nuclear reactor the nickname “Nukey Poo”.

teile.einleitung: A microscope is a device that lets you see very small things greatly enlarged. It makes cells, bacteria and other tiny structures visible that you would never be able to see with the naked eye. The microscope completely changed biology and medicine.
wichtigste: A microscope greatly enlarges very small things.
Light microscopes magnify up to about 1000 times or a little more.
Electron microscopes can magnify much more strongly.
In 1665, after looking through a microscope, Robert Hooke coined the term cell.
Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to see bacteria.
The scanning tunnelling microscope was invented in Rüschlikon near Zurich.
Microscopes are essential in medicine, research and industry.

abschnitte.text: A **microscope** is a device that shows tiny objects much bigger than they are. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “looking at small things”. A magnifying glass magnifies only a few times, but a microscope magnifies a hundred or a thousand times. In this way you can see, for example, the cells in onion skin or single-celled creatures in a drop of water. The field is called microscopy.

abschnitte.titel: How a light microscope is built
abschnitte.text: A **light microscope** has two lens systems: the **objective** close to the object and the **eyepiece**, through which you look. Their magnifications are multiplied together; for example 40 times by 10 times gives 400 times. The sample lies thinly on a small glass plate, the slide. A lamp usually lights it from below. You focus the image with knobs.

Around 1600, spectacle makers in the Netherlands built the first microscopes with several lenses. In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at a slice of cork and saw small chambers, which he called “cells”. The Dutch cloth merchant **Antoni van Leeuwenhoek** built tiny microscopes with only one lens, which magnified very strongly. With them, around 1676, he discovered bacteria and other tiny creatures. He called them “little animals” and so became a pioneer of microbiology.

You cannot magnify as strongly as you like with light, because light itself has a certain size. That is why from 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed the **electron microscope**, which works with electrons instead of light. It can magnify more than a million times and even shows viruses. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer invented the scanning tunnelling microscope at the IBM research laboratory in **Rüschlikon** near Zurich. For the first time it made single atoms visible, and the two received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986.

In hospitals, experts examine blood and tissue samples under the microscope to identify diseases. Biologists use them to study cells, plants and tiny creatures. In industry, tiny parts such as computer chips or watch movements are checked. The police also use microscopes to compare traces such as hairs or fibres. In many schools children are allowed to look through a microscope themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens of a microscope that is closest to the object.
The lens through which you look into the microscope with your eye.
A thin glass plate on which you place the sample.
A microscope that works with electrons instead of light and magnifies extremely strongly.

gewusst: Among other things, van Leeuwenhoek examined the plaque on his own teeth and found countless bacteria in it.
With a scanning tunnelling microscope you can not only see single atoms but even move them.

teile.einleitung: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in all the world's oceans. It lies in the western Pacific near the island of Guam and at its deepest point reaches almost 11,000 metres down. If you stood Mount Everest in it, its summit would still be more than 2000 metres below the surface of the water.
wichtigste: The Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean trench on Earth.
Its deepest point is called the Challenger Deep and is almost 11,000 metres deep.
It lies in the Pacific east of the Mariana Islands, near Guam.
The deeper you dive, the greater the water pressure becomes.
In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh were the first people to reach the bottom.
In 2012 the film director James Cameron dived to the bottom alone.
Even at the bottom there are animals, for example small amphipods.

abschnitte.text: The Mariana Trench lies in the western **Pacific**, east of the Mariana Islands, whose largest island is **Guam**. It is about 2500 kilometres long but only about 70 kilometres wide, like a huge gorge in the sea floor. The deepest point is called the **Challenger Deep**, after the British research ship Challenger. Depending on the method, measurements give almost 11,000 metres.

The Earth's surface consists of large plates that move slowly. At the Mariana Trench, the **Pacific Plate** pushes under another plate and sinks into the Earth's interior. This process is called **subduction**. It causes earthquakes and volcanoes, from which the Mariana Islands have grown.

With every ten metres of water depth, the pressure rises by about as much as all the air above us presses on the Earth. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the **water pressure** is therefore over a thousand times as strong as on land. It is as if the weight of a car were resting on a thumbnail. On top of that it is completely dark down there and only a few degrees warm.

On 23 January 1960 the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** and the American Don Walsh became the first people to reach the bottom, in the bathyscaphe **Trieste**. The vessel had been developed by Jacques Piccard's father, Auguste Piccard. In 2012 the film director **James Cameron** dived down alone in the submersible Deepsea Challenger. In 2019 the American Victor Vescovo became the first person to reach the deepest points of all five oceans.

Despite the darkness, cold and pressure, there is life in the trench. At the bottom, small **amphipods**, sea cucumbers and bacteria have been found. A few thousand metres higher up there are still fish, such as the see-through snailfish. The animals feed mainly on scraps that slowly sink down from above.

Most of the deep sea is still hardly explored today. Researchers send robots and measuring instruments down to study rock, water and living things. Sadly, plastic rubbish has been found even in the Mariana Trench. Since 2009, part of the area has been designated a marine protected area by the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, narrow and very deep channel in the sea floor.
The sinking of one of the Earth's plates under another into the Earth's interior.
The force with which water presses from all sides; it increases with depth.
A small, very strong vessel in which people travel to great ocean depths.

gewusst: The first dive in 1960 took almost five hours to go down, and the two men stayed at the bottom for only about 20 minutes.
During the descent in 1960 one of the Trieste's windows cracked, but the vessel withstood the pressure.
The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is high.

teile.einleitung: A metamorphosis is a transformation in which an animal completely changes its shape during its life. The best-known example is the caterpillar that turns into a butterfly. Frogs, beetles and dragonflies also go through a metamorphosis.
wichtigste: Metamorphosis means transformation and comes from Greek.
A butterfly develops from the egg through caterpillar and pupa to the adult.
Inside the pupa, the caterpillar's body is completely rebuilt.
A freshly hatched butterfly first has to let its wings dry.
After hatching, a butterfly does not grow any more.
The caterpillars of the peacock butterfly live on stinging nettles.
Tadpoles also turn into frogs through a metamorphosis.

abschnitte.text: The word **metamorphosis** comes from Greek and means reshaping or transformation. In biology it describes the development of an animal from a **larva** to an adult. The larva and the adult often look completely different and live in very different ways. A caterpillar, for example, eats leaves, while a butterfly sucks nectar.

A butterfly goes through four stages: **egg, caterpillar, pupa and adult**. The caterpillar eats almost non-stop and grows quickly. Because its skin does not grow with it, it has to moult several times. When it is fully grown, it looks for a sheltered place and turns into a pupa.

From the outside, the **pupa** looks still and lifeless. But inside, the caterpillar's body is almost completely broken down and put together again. Wings, long legs, antennae and a sucking proboscis develop. After a few days to weeks, the pupal case splits, and the butterfly hatches. It pumps liquid into its crumpled wings and lets them dry before flying off.

A well-known example in Switzerland is the **peacock butterfly**. On each of its reddish-brown wings it has a large, colourful eye pattern meant to frighten enemies. Its black, spiny caterpillars live in groups on **stinging nettles**. So if you leave nettles standing in the garden, you are also helping butterflies.

In butterflies, beetles, bees and flies, this is called **complete metamorphosis**, because there is a pupal stage. Grasshoppers, dragonflies and bugs have no pupa; their larvae already look like the adults, and this is called incomplete metamorphosis. Amphibians also transform: the tadpole with its tail and gills becomes a frog with legs and lungs. This is controlled by **hormones**, special messenger substances in the body.

For a long time people believed that insects simply arose from mud or rotting meat. In the 17th century the painter and researcher **Maria Sibylla Merian** watched caterpillars and butterflies very closely. She drew the transformation of insects and even travelled as far as Suriname in South America to do so. Her pictures helped people understand metamorphosis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal, which looks different from the adult.
A resting stage in which an insect larva is rebuilt into the adult.
Shedding the old skin so that an animal can keep growing.
The fully developed winged insect, the last stage of the metamorphosis.

gewusst: In a few weeks, a caterpillar can increase its weight many times over.
Some butterflies spend the winter as a pupa and only hatch the following spring.
Small and large butterflies are not young and old; they are simply different species or came from caterpillars that were fed differently well.

teile.einleitung: Milk chocolate is a chocolate made of cocoa, sugar and milk. It was invented in Switzerland, by Daniel Peter from Vevey. Today it is the most popular kind of chocolate in the world.
wichtigste: Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, the cocoa beans.
Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate in Switzerland.
He was born in Moudon in the canton of Vaud.
He married into the Cailler chocolate family.
His friend Henri Nestlé helped him with his first experiments with milk.
In the end Peter used thickened condensed milk.
From 1887 he sold his fine milk chocolate under the name Gala Peter.

abschnitte.text: Milk chocolate consists of **cocoa mass**, cocoa butter, sugar and milk powder. Because of the milk it tastes milder and sweeter than dark chocolate. The **cocoa beans** come from the cacao tree, which only grows in warm, damp areas near the equator. Today most cocoa comes from West Africa, above all from Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.

Daniel Peter was born in 1836 in **Moudon** in the canton of Vaud. He first worked in candle-making in Vevey. When he married Fanny Cailler, the daughter of the chocolate pioneer François-Louis **Cailler**, he came to chocolate. He founded his own chocolate factory and wanted to invent something completely new.

For years Peter tried to combine milk and chocolate. The problem was the **water** in milk, because it makes chocolate crumbly and makes it go off quickly. His neighbour in Vevey, **Henri Nestlé**, was making a milk powder for baby food at the time and helped him with his knowledge. In the end Peter succeeded in making a milk chocolate that would keep by using thickened **condensed milk**.

From 1887 Peter sold his milk chocolate under the name **Gala Peter**. It quickly became popular and was also sold abroad. Later his company merged with the companies Cailler and Kohler, and in 1929 it became part of Nestlé. At almost the same time, Rodolphe Lindt in Bern invented the **conche**, a machine that makes chocolate melt smoothly in the mouth.

Thanks to inventions such as milk chocolate, Switzerland became world-famous for chocolate. Well-known brands such as Cailler, Lindt, Frey, Camille Bloch and Villars come from Switzerland. On average, people in Switzerland eat about 11 kilograms of chocolate per person per year (around 2023). In Broc in the canton of Fribourg you can visit the chocolate factory Maison Cailler.

begriffe.erklaerung: A seed from the fruit of the cacao tree, the basic ingredient of every chocolate.
Milk from which a large part of the water has been removed, so that it becomes thick.
A stirring machine that keeps chocolate moving for a long time, making it fine and smooth.
The fat of the cocoa bean, which makes chocolate melt on the tongue.

gewusst: Daniel Peter experimented for about eight years before milk chocolate really worked.
The chocolate the Aztecs drank was bitter and spiced with chilli, not sweet.
Among the Aztecs, cocoa beans were even used as money.

teile.einleitung: Michael Faraday was an English scientist who lived from 1791 to 1867. Although he never went to a secondary school, he became one of the most important physicists and chemists in history. Without his discoveries there would be no electric motors, no generators and no electricity from the socket today.
wichtigste: Faraday was born in London in 1791 and first trained as a bookbinder.
In 1813 the famous chemist Humphry Davy took him on as an assistant at the Royal Institution.
In 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction, on which all generators are based.
He imagined magnetic force as lines of force.
In 1825 he discovered the substance benzene in the residues of gas used for lighting.
The unit of electrical capacitance is called the farad in his honour.
He became very well known through his Christmas Lectures for young people.

abschnitte.text: Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 near London. His family was poor, and he went to school for only a few years. At 14 he began an apprenticeship as a **bookbinder** and read many of the books he bound. He went to lectures by the chemist **Humphry Davy** and sent him his careful notes. In 1813 Davy took him on as an assistant at the **Royal Institution** in London.

In 1831 Faraday made his most important discovery, **electromagnetic induction**. He showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric current in a wire. If you move a magnet in a coil of wire, for example, a current flows. All **generators** are based on this principle, for example in the hydroelectric power stations of the Swiss Alps. As early as 1821 he had built a simple forerunner of the electric motor.

abschnitte.titel: Lines of force and the Faraday cage
abschnitte.text: Faraday knew hardly any mathematics, but he thought in pictures. He imagined the force around a magnet as **lines of force**, which can be made visible with iron filings. He also found that a closed metal shell shields its inside from electric fields. Today this shell is called a **Faraday cage**. That is why you are fairly safe during a thunderstorm in a car with a metal body or in an aircraft.

Faraday was also a great chemist. In 1825 he discovered the substance **benzene** in the residues of lighting gas. He studied how an electric current breaks down substances and in 1834 introduced terms such as **anode**, **cathode** and electrolyte. He also managed to turn gases such as chlorine into liquids by pressure.

Faraday wanted to share knowledge with everyone. In 1825 he founded the **Christmas Lectures** for children and young people at the Royal Institution, which still take place today. His series of lectures on the chemical history of a candle became famous. In it he used simple experiments to show how a flame works.

Faraday died on 25 August 1867 at Hampton Court near London. The physicist James Clerk Maxwell built his equations of electromagnetism on Faraday's ideas. The unit of electrical capacitance is called the **farad** in his honour. Albert Einstein is said to have had a picture of Faraday in his study.

begriffe.erklaerung: The production of an electric current in a wire by a changing magnetic field.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
An imaginary line that shows how a magnetic or electric force acts.
A metal shell that protects its inside from electric fields.
The unit of electrical capacitance, named after Faraday.

gewusst: Faraday refused to be knighted and wanted simply to remain Mr Faraday.
The Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures are shown on television today.
Faraday kept precise laboratory notebooks in which thousands of experiments are numbered.

teile.einleitung: Maria Sibylla Merian was an artist and naturalist of the 17th century. She watched caterpillars and butterflies closely and painted them in beautiful pictures. When she was over 50 she even travelled to South America to study insects there.
wichtigste: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in Frankfurt in 1647.
Her father's family came from Basel.
At home she kept caterpillars to watch how they developed.
She always painted insects together with their food plants.
At that time many people believed that insects came from mud.
From Amsterdam she travelled with her daughter to Suriname.
She was pictured on the German 500-mark note.

abschnitte.titel: Childhood in a family of artists
abschnitte.text: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in 1647 in **Frankfurt am Main**. Her father was the well-known copper engraver Matthäus Merian the Elder, whose family came from **Basel**. He died when she was three. Her stepfather, the flower painter Jacob Marrel, taught her to paint. Even as a girl she collected caterpillars and painted them.

In Merian's time, many people believed that insects simply arise from mud or rotting things. Merian kept caterpillars in boxes at home and fed them with fresh leaves. In this way she saw how a caterpillar becomes a pupa and how a butterfly hatches from it. This change is called **metamorphosis**. In 1679 she published a book about caterpillars and their food plants.

Merian never painted the animals on their own, but always together with the plants they feed on. In one picture you often see the egg, caterpillar, pupa and butterfly on the same plant. In this way she showed the whole **life cycle** and the connections in nature. She made her pictures as **copper engravings**, which were then coloured by hand. They were both works of art and scientific illustrations.

Later Merian lived in **Amsterdam**, where she saw exotic insects in collections. In 1699, at the age of 52, she travelled with her daughter Dorothea to **Suriname** in South America. Such a journey was very unusual and dangerous for women at that time. For almost two years she watched and painted insects, spiders, frogs and plants there. An illness forced her to return in 1701.

In 1705 her famous book about the insects of Suriname was published, with 60 large plates. It made her known throughout Europe. Merian died in Amsterdam in 1717. Today she is considered a pioneer of **entomology**. In Germany she was pictured on the 500-mark note, and schools and a research ship also bear her name.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change of an animal, for example from caterpillar to butterfly.
A picture scratched into a copper plate and then printed on paper.
The resting stage in which a caterpillar turns into a butterfly.
The science of insects.

gewusst: Some of the animals and plants that Merian painted in Suriname had been completely unknown in Europe before.
Her father Matthäus Merian is known for his detailed views of towns, including Swiss towns.
A German research ship is called “Maria S. Merian”.

teile.einleitung: A measurement error is the difference between the measured value and the true value of a quantity. No measuring instrument and no person measures perfectly accurately. But if you know where errors come from, you can keep them small and judge measurements better.
wichtigste: Every measured value differs a little from the true value.
A systematic error always works in the same direction, for example with wrongly set scales.
Random errors sometimes go up and sometimes down.
Measuring several times and taking the mean reduces random errors.
When reading a scale you must look exactly at eye level, otherwise you make a reading error.
A measured value that differs greatly from all the others is called an outlier.
Experts today usually speak of measurement deviation rather than measurement error.

abschnitte.text: If you measure a pencil with a ruler, you might get 12.5 cm. But the **true value** could be 12.48 cm. The difference is the measurement error. Every measuring instrument has limited **accuracy**, so no measured value is perfectly exact. That is why scientists state for every result how accurate it is.

A **systematic error** shifts all measured values in the same direction. One example is a set of scales that already shows 2 g with nothing on it. If you put an apple on it and it shows 152 g, the apple really weighs only 150 g. Such errors do not disappear if you measure several times; you have to **calibrate** the instrument or take the error into account in your calculation.

**Random errors** come from small fluctuations, for example from wind, a shaking hand or inaccurate reading. They are spread out, sometimes upwards, sometimes downwards. That is why you measure several times and take the **mean**. If you measure a length four times and get 12.4 cm, 12.6 cm, 12.5 cm and 12.9 cm, this gives a mean of 12.6 cm.

A common error happens when reading a scale. If you look at a measuring cylinder at a slant from above or below, you see the level of the liquid shifted. This effect is called **parallax**. So you should always read at exactly eye level, and with water at the lowest point of the curved surface.

Sometimes a value does not fit with the others at all, because you wrote it down wrongly or miscounted. Such a value is called an **outlier**. You should check where it comes from rather than simply crossing it out. Choosing the measuring instrument is also important: for the thickness of a thin wire, **callipers** are much better than a ruler. In Switzerland, the institute METAS makes sure that measuring instruments used in trade measure correctly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The exact value of a quantity, which you never know completely exactly.
An error that shifts all measurements in the same direction.
A small, unpredictable fluctuation upwards or downwards.
To check a measuring instrument against an exact reference and set it correctly.
An apparent shift when you look at a scale at a slant.

gewusst: Temperature can also cause measurement errors, because a metal ruler expands a little when warm.
If you measure ten times instead of once, you reduce random errors, but not a wrongly set zero point.
In science, a measurement without a statement of its accuracy is considered incomplete.

teile.einleitung: Motivation is the inner force that gets us to do something and keep at it. It explains why we learn, train or finish a difficult puzzle. Psychology researches where this force comes from and how it can be strengthened.
wichtigste: Motivation is the drive to reach a goal or to do something.
Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoying the thing itself.
Extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or punishments from outside.
Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in a pyramid.
At the bottom are basic physical needs, and at the top self-actualisation.
In the state of flow, you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time.
Concrete and challenging goals increase performance the most.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **movere**, which means to move. So motivation is what sets us in motion. It decides which goal we choose, how hard we try and how long we keep going. Without motivation, even an easy task is often left undone.

If you like drawing because it is fun, you are **intrinsically motivated**. If you learn for a good mark, money or praise, you are **extrinsically motivated**. Both kinds can help, but intrinsic motivation usually lasts longer. Researchers have observed that regular rewards for something you enjoy doing anyway can even reduce your pleasure in it.

From 1943 the American psychologist **Abraham Maslow** described an order of needs that is often shown as a pyramid. At the bottom are food, drink and sleep, above them safety, then friendship and belonging, and after that recognition. At the very top is **self-actualisation**, meaning developing your own talents. The idea is that someone who is hungry thinks first about food and only later about big goals.

The psychologist **Mihály Csíkszentmihályi** studied a special state that he called **flow**. You are so absorbed that you forget time and your surroundings, for example when climbing, making music or programming. Flow is most likely when a task is neither too easy nor too hard. Then ability and challenge fit together exactly.

According to the **goal-setting theory** of Edwin Locke and Gary Latham, concrete and challenging goals work best. “I'll read two chapters this week” motivates more than “I'll read something sometime”. It also helps to split big goals into small steps. Each step you manage gives you a good feeling and new energy.

According to **self-determination theory**, people need three things for strong motivation: freedom of choice, the feeling of being able to do something, and good relationships with others. That is why it helps to have a say yourself when learning, for example about the order of tasks. Learning together with friends can also spur you on. Short breaks and visible progress, such as a checklist, also help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Coming from inside, from your own enjoyment of something.
Coming from outside, for example through reward, praise or punishment.
Something that a person requires or strongly wishes for.
The happy feeling of being completely absorbed in an activity.
Developing your own abilities and wishes to the full.

gewusst: Maslow himself never drew his theory as a pyramid; this picture only appeared later.
Even looking forward to a goal can release the messenger substance dopamine in the brain, which drives us on.
If you tell someone about your goal and report back regularly, you often stick at it better.

teile.einleitung: The human microbiome is all the tiny living things that live on and in our body. These are mainly bacteria, but also fungi and viruses. Most of them are not germs that cause disease but useful lodgers that help us digest food and protect us from illness.
wichtigste: The microbiome is all the microorganisms that live on and in a person.
Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.
According to recent estimates, there are about as many bacterial cells in the body as human cells.
Gut bacteria make vitamin K, which is important for blood clotting.
From dietary fibre they make short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, which nourish the lining of the gut.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce the variety of gut bacteria.
Prebiotics are food for bacteria, while probiotics are living bacteria.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of “micro” for small and “bios” for life. The **microbiome** includes bacteria, fungi, viruses and other microorganisms. They live on the skin, in the mouth, in the nose and above all in the **gut**. Every person has a slightly different mixture, almost like a fingerprint. Animals and plants also have their own microbiome.

It used to be said that there were ten times more bacteria in the body than human cells. More recent estimates from 2016 show that the two numbers are **roughly the same**, a few dozen trillion each. Because bacteria are very small, together they weigh only a few hundred grams. The vast majority live in the **large intestine**, where they find enough food and moisture.

Our body cannot break down all parts of our food by itself. Gut bacteria ferment **dietary fibre** from vegetables, fruit and wholegrain foods. This produces **short-chain fatty acids** such as butyrate, which feed the cells of the gut lining. Some bacteria also make **vitamin K**, which is important for blood clotting. So if you eat plenty of fibre, you are feeding your little helpers.

A healthy microbiome takes up the space in the gut and on the skin, so that dangerous germs find it harder to get a foothold. It also trains the **immune system**, especially in childhood. Researchers are investigating whether a disturbed microbiome is linked to allergies, being overweight or inflammation of the gut. Many of these questions have not yet been finally answered.

**Antibiotics** kill germs that cause disease, but they also hit useful bacteria. Broad-spectrum antibiotics in particular reduce the variety of gut bacteria, which often recovers only slowly afterwards. Then the germ Clostridioides difficile can multiply strongly and cause severe diarrhoea. For repeated infections, a **faecal transplant** helps, in which healthy gut bacteria from a donor are transferred.

**Probiotics** are living bacteria that are meant to be good for health, for example in yoghurt or sauerkraut. **Prebiotics**, on the other hand, are food for bacteria, for example certain types of fibre in leeks, onions or oat flakes. A varied diet with plenty of vegetables is considered good for a varied microbiome. Exercise and enough sleep also seem to play a part.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing so small that you can only see it under a microscope.
An older name for the bacteria that live in the gut.
Plant fibres that we cannot digest ourselves, but which feed gut bacteria.
Foods or products containing living, useful bacteria.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

gewusst: Hundreds of different kinds of bacteria live in a person's gut.
A large part of faeces is made up of bacteria.
Pets such as dogs can influence the skin microbiome of their family.

teile.einleitung: Max Planck was a German physicist who is considered the founder of quantum physics. In 1900 he realised that energy does not flow in any amount you like, but is given off in tiny portions, the energy quanta. This idea changed physics for ever.
wichtigste: Max Planck lived from 1858 to 1947.
He is considered the founder of quantum physics.
In 1900 he introduced the idea of energy quanta.
The natural constant h is named after him: Planck's constant.
In 1918 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He supported the young Albert Einstein.
The Max Planck Society for research is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Max Planck was born on 23 April 1858 in **Kiel** in northern Germany. He was very musical and played the piano excellently, but he chose physics. One teacher even advised him against it, because supposedly almost everything in physics had already been discovered. Planck became a professor at the university in **Berlin** and was one of the most respected scientists of his time. He died in Göttingen on 4 October 1947.

At that time physicists were trying to explain what light hot bodies give off, for example a glowing piece of iron. The known formulas did not match the measurements. In 1900 Planck found a solution: he assumed that energy is given off only in small portions, the **energy quanta**. You can imagine it like money that you can only pay in whole coins and not in amounts as small as you like. This day is considered the birth of **quantum physics**.

For his formula Planck needed a new natural constant, which he labelled with the letter **h**. Today it is called **Planck's constant** and is a tiny number. It decides how big a packet of energy is for a particular colour of light. Since 2019 even the kilogram has been defined with the help of this constant. So Planck's discovery is part of every precise set of scales.

For the discovery of energy quanta, Planck received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for 1918. He recognised the talent of the young Albert Einstein early on and brought him to Berlin in 1914. From Planck's idea, researchers such as Einstein, Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg later developed **quantum mechanics**. It explains how atoms and light work. Without it there would be no lasers, computer chips or LED lamps.

Planck's life was marked by many tragedies. Several of his children died young, and his son Erwin was executed in 1945 because he had links to the resistance against Hitler. During the Nazi period Planck tried to help persecuted colleagues. After the war the newly founded **Max Planck Society**, which today runs many research institutes, was named after him. A European space telescope also bore his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smallest packet of energy that cannot be divided any further.
The part of physics that describes the behaviour of atoms, light and the smallest particles.
A number in nature that stays the same everywhere and always.
The natural constant h discovered by Planck, which decides the size of energy quanta.

gewusst: At first Planck himself thought his quanta were only a mathematical trick and did not believe they really existed.
As a young man Max Planck even composed a small operetta.

teile.einleitung: The Neanderthals were a kind of human who lived long ago in Europe and western Asia and died out about 40,000 years ago. They were skilled hunters, made fine stone tools and buried their dead. They are named after the Neander Valley in Germany, where the first known bones were found in 1856.
wichtigste: The Neanderthal is named after a valley in Germany.
The bones that gave them their name were found in the Neander Valley in 1856.
Neanderthals lived mainly in Europe and western Asia.
They died out about 40,000 years ago.
Their strong, stocky body was adapted to the cold of the ice age.
The Mousterian stone tool culture is typical of them.
Their brain was the same size as ours or a little bigger.

abschnitte.titel: The find in the Neander Valley
abschnitte.text: In the summer of 1856, workers in a limestone quarry in the **Neander Valley** near Düsseldorf came across old bones. The teacher **Johann Carl Fuhlrott** realised that they belonged to a primitive human. At first many scholars did not believe him and thought the bones belonged to a sick person. In 1864 this kind of human was given the scientific name Homo neanderthalensis.

Neanderthals lived for several hundred thousand years in Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia. Sites range from Spain and France to Siberia. During this time, cold periods and warm periods alternated, and large parts of Europe were covered by glaciers. About **40,000 years ago** the Neanderthals disappeared, at roughly the time when modern humans were spreading through Europe.

Neanderthals were a little shorter than us, but very strong and **stocky**, with a broad chest and short arms and legs. Such a body loses less heat, which was an advantage in the **ice age**. Typical features were a long, flat skull, strong brow ridges and a broad nose. Their brain was the same size as, or even a little bigger than, that of people today.

Neanderthals made scrapers, points and blades out of flint; this tool culture is called the **Mousterian**. It is named after the site of Le Moustier in France. They hunted large animals such as reindeer, wild horses, bison and even mammoths. They could use fire and probably wore clothes made of hides.

Finds of carefully made graves show that Neanderthals **buried** their dead. Some skeletons show severe injuries that had healed, which suggests that the group looked after the sick. Neanderthals also used pigments and jewellery, such as eagle talons. Whether they had a language like ours has not yet been settled, but their bodies would probably have allowed them to speak.

There are also traces from the time of the Neanderthals in Switzerland. In the cave of **Cotencher** in the canton of Neuchâtel, part of a Neanderthal's jaw was found. In the **Wildkirchli** cave in the Alpstein, stone tools and many cave bear bones from this time were discovered. The Swedish researcher Svante Pääbo decoded the Neanderthals' genetic material and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it in 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: The scientific name of the Neanderthal.
The stone tool culture of the Neanderthals, named after Le Moustier in France.
A long cold period in which glaciers covered large parts of the Earth.
The remains of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.
A very hard stone that forms sharp edges when it is broken.

gewusst: The Neander Valley is named after the 17th-century hymn writer Joachim Neander.
The name Neander is the Greek form of the surname Neumann and so means new man.
Neanderthals made glue from birch tar to fix stone points onto wooden shafts.

teile.einleitung: “Nature” is one of the most famous scientific journals in the world. It has been published every week since 1869 and publishes new research results from all the natural and life sciences. Anyone who manages to publish an article in it has achieved something special in science.
wichtigste: “Nature” was founded in London in 1869.
Its founder and first editor was the astronomer Norman Lockyer.
The journal comes out weekly.
It covers all the natural and life sciences.
In 1953 the famous article by Watson and Crick on the structure of DNA appeared here.
Today the journal is published by Springer Nature.
Its open-access sister journal covering all subjects is called Nature Communications.

abschnitte.text: “Nature” is a **scientific journal**, a magazine in which researchers publish their discoveries for other experts. It covers topics from physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, astronomy, geology and many other fields. As well as research articles, there are news items, comments and book reviews. Together with the American journal “Science”, it is considered the most important science journal of all.

The first issue appeared on 4 November 1869 in **London**. “Nature” was founded by the English astronomer **Norman Lockyer**, who had helped to discover the element helium in the light of the Sun. He ran the journal for about 50 years, until 1919. For a long time it was published by Macmillan; today it belongs to **Springer Nature**.

Before an article appears, it is checked closely by other experts; this is called **peer review**. These reviewers look for mistakes and ask critical questions. Only a small share of the papers submitted is finally published. That is why an article in “Nature” is considered a great honour for researchers.

On 25 April 1953 **James Watson and Francis Crick** described the double helix, the shape of DNA, in “Nature”. In 1932 James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron appeared here. In 1985 British researchers reported in “Nature” on the ozone hole over Antarctica. Dolly the cloned sheep was also presented in this journal in 1997.

A large family of journals has grown out of “Nature”. These include specialised titles such as “Nature Physics”, “Nature Medicine” and “Nature Climate Change”. Since 2010 there has been the sister journal covering all subjects, **Nature Communications**. Its articles are **open access**, meaning anyone can read them free on the internet.

Researchers from Switzerland also publish regularly in “Nature”. A famous example is the article by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from Geneva in 1995 on the first planet around a Sun-like star. For this the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. Results from CERN near Geneva also keep appearing in major journals like this one.

begriffe.erklaerung: A magazine in which researchers publish new results for experts.
The checking of a research article by other experts before it is published.
Free access to scientific articles on the internet.
A person or publisher responsible for a journal.
The shape of DNA, which looks like a twisted rope ladder.

gewusst: Watson and Crick's article on DNA was only a little more than one page long.
Norman Lockyer ran “Nature” for about 50 years.
The German word for nature is Natur, very close to the journal's name.

teile.einleitung: Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and the first person to walk on the Moon. On 21 July 1969, on the Apollo 11 mission, he set foot on the Moon's surface. About 600 million people followed the event on television at the time.
wichtigste: Neil Armstrong was born in Ohio in the USA in 1930 and died in 2012.
He was the first person on the Moon.
The landing succeeded with the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969.
Buzz Aldrin landed with him, while Michael Collins stayed in the spacecraft in orbit around the Moon.
Before that he was a fighter pilot and a test pilot for rocket planes.
His words at the first step became world-famous.
On the Moon the astronauts also set up an experiment from the University of Bern.

abschnitte.text: Neil Alden Armstrong was born on 5 August 1930 in Wapakoneta in the US state of Ohio. Even as a child he loved aeroplanes, and at 16 he had a **pilot's licence**, even before he was allowed to drive a car. He studied aeronautical engineering and flew as a US Navy pilot in the Korean War. After that he worked as a test pilot and flew, among others, the rocket plane X-15.

In 1962 Armstrong was chosen by **NASA** as an astronaut. In 1966 he flew into space for the first time on the Gemini 8 mission. During it he achieved the first docking of two spacecraft in space. Shortly afterwards the capsule began to spin out of control, but Armstrong stayed calm and brought it back safely.

On 16 July 1969 Apollo 11 launched from Florida on the huge Saturn V rocket. On 20 July the lunar module **Eagle**, with Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, landed in the Mare Tranquillitatis, the “Sea of Tranquillity”. A few hours later, in the early morning of 21 July European time, Armstrong was the first to climb out. As he did so, he said: “That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.”

Armstrong and Aldrin stayed outside the lunar module for about two and a half hours. They collected about 21 kilograms of moon rock and set up measuring instruments. Even before the American flag, they set up the **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern, a sheet of aluminium foil that caught particles from the Sun. On 24 July 1969 all three astronauts landed safely in the Pacific.

After Apollo 11, Armstrong never flew into space again. He worked at NASA for a while and then became a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati. He was a modest man who spoke little about his fame. Neil Armstrong died on 25 August 2012 at the age of 82.

The Moon landing is considered one of humanity's greatest technical achievements. It was also a high point in the **space race** between the USA and the Soviet Union. By 1972 a total of twelve people had walked on the Moon. With the Artemis programme, NASA wants to bring people to the Moon again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person trained for flights into space.
The space agency of the USA.
A small spacecraft that flies down from the main spacecraft to the Moon and back up again.
A pilot who is the first to try out new aircraft.

gewusst: Because there is no wind on the Moon, Armstrong's footprints have probably survived to this day.
The lunar module's computer was much less powerful than a mobile phone today.
A crater on the Moon and an asteroid bear the name Armstrong.

teile.einleitung: A medal is a metal disc, usually round, with pictures or writing on it, which serves as an award or a souvenir. You get one for winning in sport, for special achievements in science or to remember an event. Unlike a coin, you cannot pay with a medal.
wichtigste: A medal is usually round.
It is often hung around the neck on a ribbon.
The name of the competition is often written on the back of a winner's medal.
The Nobel Prize medal is made of gold.
Alfred Nobel's face can be seen on the front of it.
The Fields Medal is often called the “Nobel Prize of mathematics”.
It is awarded every four years to mathematicians under 40.

abschnitte.text: A medal is a piece of metal, usually round, with a picture or an inscription. The front is called the **obverse** and the back the **reverse**.
