Unlike a coin, a medal has no money value that you could spend in a shop. Medals are made of gold, silver, bronze or other metals, often struck or cast. The word comes from the Italian “medaglia”.

In competitions the top three often receive a gold, silver and bronze medal. It is usually hung around the neck on a **ribbon**. The back often shows the name of the competition, the year and the sport. By the way, at the Olympic Games the gold medal is mostly made of silver and only coated with gold. At Swiss wrestling festivals, ski races and fun runs there are also medals as souvenirs.

Anyone who wins a **Nobel Prize** receives a gold medal with Alfred Nobel's face on the front. With it come a certificate and prize money. There is no Nobel Prize in mathematics, so the **Fields Medal** is considered the highest award. It has been awarded since 1936, now every four years to two to four people under 40. In 2022, for example, it went to the Frenchman Hugo Duminil-Copin, who does research at the University of Geneva.

There are also commemorative medals that recall a special event, such as an anniversary. In the past, soldiers received medals for their service; these are called decorations. Rescuers are also sometimes honoured with a medal. Many people collect medals, and this hobby belongs to **numismatics**, the study of coins. Some medals are small works of art, designed by well-known artists.

In ancient Rome there were already large struck pieces that were handed out as gifts. But the medal as we know it developed in the **Renaissance** in Italy, in the 15th century. At that time princes had medals made with their portrait in order to become well known. An early master was the painter Pisanello. Since the 19th century, medals have been widespread as prizes in sport and science.

begriffe.erklaerung: The front of a coin or medal.
The back of a coin or medal.
The study and collecting of coins and medals.
Pressing a picture into metal with great force.

gewusst: The Olympic gold medal is made mostly of silver and is only gold-plated.
The ancient scholar Archimedes is pictured on the Fields Medal.
Some Nobel Prize winners have later auctioned their medal and given the money away.

teile.einleitung: Measuring spoons are small spoons in fixed sizes that let you measure ingredients accurately. You need them in the kitchen, when baking and sometimes for medicines. With them a recipe always turns out equally well.
wichtigste: Measuring spoons are used to measure small amounts accurately.
In German recipes, “EL” stands for tablespoon and “TL” for teaspoon.
A tablespoon is bigger than a teaspoon.
About 3 teaspoons fit into a tablespoon.
“Msp.” means a pinch on the tip of a knife, a very small amount.
You fill flour into the measuring spoon level.
If you double a recipe, you also double all the spoon amounts.

abschnitte.text: A measuring spoon is a spoon with an exactly fixed **capacity**. Often several spoons come in a set, held together by a ring. They are made of plastic or stainless steel. The amount is written on each spoon, for example 1 tbsp, 1 tsp or ½ tsp. Ordinary cutlery spoons, on the other hand, are different sizes depending on their shape.

In cookbooks you often read abbreviations. In German recipes, **EL** means tablespoon, **TL** means teaspoon and **Msp.** means a knife tip. A measuring tablespoon usually holds 15 millilitres, and a teaspoon 5 millilitres. So about 3 teaspoons fit into a tablespoon. A knife tip is only as much as fits on the tip of a knife, for example with cinnamon or nutmeg.

Powders such as flour, sugar or baking powder are measured **level**. You fill the spoon and scrape the back of a knife across the rim. A **heaped** spoon contains a lot more. Liquids are poured right up to the rim. Accuracy is especially important in baking, because too much baking powder or salt can spoil the cake.

With measuring spoons you can easily adjust recipes. If a pancake batter needs 2 tablespoons of sugar and you make **double the amount**, you need 4 tablespoons. For half the amount you take 1 tablespoon. If you have no tablespoon to hand, you take 3 teaspoons. In this way you practise multiplying and dividing along the way.

In the USA and Britain, recipes are often given in **cups** and spoons instead of grams. An American tablespoon holds just under 15 millilitres, while in Australia it is 20 millilitres. In Switzerland and Germany, larger amounts are usually weighed with **kitchen scales**. Medicine syrups often come with their own dosing spoon or measuring cup.

begriffe.erklaerung: A spoon measure of usually about 15 millilitres, abbreviated EL in German.
A spoon measure of usually about 5 millilitres, abbreviated TL in German.
A very small amount that fits on the tip of a knife.
A spoon filled to the brim and scraped smooth on top.

gewusst: A heaped tablespoon of flour can contain almost twice as much as a level one.
In Australia a tablespoon is bigger than in Europe, namely 20 millilitres.
Many sets of measuring spoons have a ring so that you do not lose a spoon.

teile.einleitung: The mean, often also called the average, is a number that sums up a whole list of numbers. You add up all the numbers and divide the total by how many there are. In this way you can work out, for example, the average temperature of a day or the average mark in a test.
wichtigste: In everyday life the mean is usually called the average.
First you add up all the numbers.
Then you divide the total by how many numbers there are.
The average of 2 and 4 is 3.
The average of 3, 5 and 7 is 5.
If all the numbers are the same, the average is that number, so for 4, 4 and 4 it is 4.
As well as the average, there are other kinds of middle value such as the median and the mode.

abschnitte.text: The mean is a single number that shows roughly where the middle of a list of numbers lies. In mathematics the ordinary average is called the **arithmetic mean**. It answers the question: how much would everyone get if everything were shared out fairly? If Lea has 2 sweets and Max has 4, after sharing fairly they each get 3.

The mean is worked out in two steps. First you add up all the numbers, which gives the **total**. Then you divide the total by **how many** numbers there are. For 3, 5 and 7 the total is 15, and 15 divided by 3 is 5. For 10 and 20 the total is 30, and 30 divided by 2 is 15.

If a team scores 1, 2 and 3 goals in three matches, that is an average of 2 goals per match. If it is 6 degrees in the morning, 8 degrees at midday and 10 degrees in the evening, the **average temperature** is 8 degrees. In Switzerland people also work out the **average mark**, for example for the school report. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss give long-term means to show whether a month was warmer or colder than usual.

The mean can be shifted a lot by single very large or very small numbers. Such values are called **outliers**. If nine people earn little and one earns a great deal, the average is higher than is true for most of them. Then the **median** is often better, which is the value exactly in the middle of the sorted list.

In science, people often measure several times and take the mean. This makes random **measurement errors** smaller, because deviations upwards and downwards cancel each other out. Statistics about height, income or rainfall also use means. So the mean is one of the most important tools in **statistics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The everyday word for the mean.
The result when you add numbers together.
The value exactly in the middle of a sorted list of numbers.
A value that is very different from all the others.

gewusst: The mean does not have to appear in the list of numbers itself; for 1 and 2, for example, it is 1.5.
In statistics a family sometimes has 1.5 children, even though of course there are no half children.
If you want a better mark in your report, you can work out what mark you need in the next test to raise your average.

teile.einleitung: A Nobel Committee is a group of experts who decide each year who receives a Nobel Prize. A particular institution is responsible for each prize, most of them in Sweden, and for the Peace Prize in Norway. Their work is strictly secret and follows exact rules.
wichtigste: Nobel Committees choose the winners of the Nobel Prizes.
The Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded by the Swedish Academy.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences is responsible for physics and chemistry.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee for the Peace Prize has five members.
Nominations must be submitted by 31 January.
Nominating yourself is not allowed.
The nominations stay secret for 50 years.

abschnitte.text: In his will, Alfred Nobel laid down which institutions would award the prizes. The **Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences** chooses in physics and chemistry, and later the prize in economic sciences was added. The Nobel Assembly at the **Karolinska Institute** in Stockholm decides on physiology or medicine. The **Swedish Academy** awards the literature prize, and the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo the Nobel Peace Prize.

Every year the committees invite selected experts to nominate candidates. These are, for example, professors, former prize winners or, for the Peace Prize, also members of parliaments. Nominations must arrive by **31 January**. Anyone who nominates themselves is not considered.

From February until the autumn, the committees examine the nominations very closely. They get reports from experts all over the world and draw up shortlists. In October they vote, and the decision is announced publicly. A single prize may be shared by at most **three people**, and the Peace Prize can also go to organisations.

Everything to do with the nominations and discussions stays secret for **50 years**. Only after that may researchers look at the documents. So today we know, for example, who was nominated in the 1960s, but not who was on the list in recent decades. The secrecy is meant to protect the committees from outside pressure.

Since 1974, Nobel Prizes have in principle not been awarded to people who have died. In 2011 there was a special case: the medicine prize winner **Ralph Steinman** had died a few days before the announcement, without the committee knowing. The Nobel Foundation decided that he would keep the prize anyway. Linus Pauling is the only person to have received two Nobel Prizes entirely on his own, for chemistry in 1954 and for peace in 1962.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small group of people who carry out a particular task together.
The official proposal of a person for a prize.
An association of respected scholars and experts.
A written assessment by an expert.

gewusst: Every year several hundred nominations arrive for the Nobel Peace Prize.
Mahatma Gandhi was nominated several times but never received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee are chosen by the Norwegian parliament.

teile.einleitung: Neurotransmitters are messenger substances that nerve cells use to send signals to each other. They bridge the tiny gap between two nerve cells, the synapse. Without neurotransmitters we could neither think nor feel nor move.
wichtigste: Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers of the nervous system.
They are stored in synaptic vesicles in the terminal buttons.
An inflow of calcium ions triggers their release into the synaptic cleft.
Ionotropic receptors are ion channels that open directly when a neurotransmitter binds.
GABA is the most important inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.
Acetylcholine is broken down in the cleft by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase.
Using frogs' hearts, Otto Loewi proved the chemical transmission of nerve signals.
SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin and are used as antidepressants.

abschnitte.text: The nervous system consists of billions of **nerve cells**, also called neurons. Within a nerve cell, a signal travels along as an electrical pulse. But between two nerve cells there is a tiny gap that the current cannot jump across. Here **neurotransmitters**, chemical messengers, take over the transmission. The connecting point is called the **synapse**.

At the end of a nerve cell are **terminal buttons**, in which neurotransmitters are stored in small bubbles, the synaptic vesicles. When an electrical signal arrives, calcium ions flow into the terminal button. This makes the bubbles merge with the cell membrane and release their contents into the **synaptic cleft**. The messengers travel across and dock onto **receptors** on the next cell like a key in a lock.

In **ionotropic receptors**, the receptor itself is a channel that opens at once when a messenger docks and lets charged particles through. Metabotropic receptors, on the other hand, work more slowly through a chain of signals in the cell. So that the signal does not keep going for ever, the messenger has to disappear again quickly. Acetylcholine is broken down by the enzyme **acetylcholinesterase**, while other substances are taken back up by the sending cell.

**Glutamate** is the most important excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, and **GABA** the most important inhibitory one. Acetylcholine passes commands from the nerves to the muscles. Dopamine plays a part in movement, motivation and the feeling of reward. Serotonin affects mood, sleep and appetite. Noradrenaline makes the body alert and ready for effort.

In 1921 the pharmacologist **Otto Loewi** carried out a famous experiment with two frogs' hearts. He stimulated the nerve of the first heart, after which it beat more slowly. Then he put the liquid from this heart onto the second heart, and it too slowed down. This proved that nerves pass on their signals with a chemical substance. Loewi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for this in 1936, together with Henry Dale.

Many illnesses are linked to neurotransmitters. In **Parkinson's disease**, nerve cells that make dopamine die, which is why movement becomes difficult. Medicines against depression such as **SSRIs** block the reuptake of serotonin, so that it works for longer. Caffeine also works in the brain, by blocking receptors for a messenger substance that makes you tired.

begriffe.erklaerung: The connecting point between two nerve cells or between a nerve and a muscle.
A docking point on a cell to which only a matching substance can bind.
A tiny bubble in a cell in which substances are stored.
A protein that speeds up chemical processes in the body.
An electrically charged particle, for example calcium or sodium.

gewusst: Otto Loewi is said to have had the idea for his famous experiment in a dream.
The human brain has about 86 billion nerve cells, connected by countless synapses.
Some snake venoms work by blocking receptors for acetylcholine.

teile.einleitung: Mitochondria are tiny parts of our cells that produce energy. That is why they are often called the power stations of the cell. Without them we could neither run nor think.
wichtigste: Mitochondria are parts of the cell called organelles.
They are often called the power stations of the cell.
The energy-rich substance ATP is made in them.
For this cellular respiration they need oxygen.
Carbon dioxide and water are produced in the process.
Muscle cells contain especially many mitochondria.
Mitochondria have their own ring-shaped DNA, a sign that they are descended from bacteria.

abschnitte.text: A mitochondrion is a small **organelle**, a part inside a cell. It is usually only about a thousandth of a millimetre thick and can only be seen with a microscope. Almost all the cells of animals, plants and fungi have mitochondria. The name comes from Greek and means something like thread-grain.

A mitochondrion has two coverings, an outer and an inner **membrane**. The inner membrane is heavily folded; these folds are called **cristae**. The folds make the surface much bigger, just like a crumpled-up sheet of paper. An important part of energy production takes place on this surface.

We eat food, which is broken down into sugar and fat, among other things. In the mitochondria these substances are broken down with oxygen from the air we breathe; this is called **cellular respiration**. It produces the substance **ATP**, a kind of rechargeable battery that the cell can use everywhere. The waste products are carbon dioxide, which we breathe out, and water.

Cells that need a lot of energy contain especially many mitochondria. These include **muscle cells**, heart muscle cells and nerve cells. A cell can contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. If you do endurance sport regularly, you even get more mitochondria in your muscles.

Mitochondria have their own ring-shaped **DNA**, similar to bacteria. They multiply inside the cell by dividing. Researchers believe that over a billion years ago a bacterium got into a larger cell and stayed there. This explanation is called the **endosymbiotic theory** and was made known above all by the biologist Lynn Margulis.

If mitochondria do not work properly, the cells lack energy. This can lead to rare diseases that weaken muscles or nerves. Poisons such as hydrogen cyanide are so dangerous because they stop cellular respiration in the mitochondria. Research on mitochondria therefore helps us understand diseases and ageing better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small part inside a cell with a particular job.
An energy-rich substance that supplies energy in the cell like a rechargeable battery.
The process in which nutrients are broken down with oxygen and energy is produced.
A thin covering that surrounds something and lets only certain substances through.

gewusst: Human red blood cells have no mitochondria, so that they do not use up the oxygen they carry themselves.
Every day a person makes about as much ATP as they weigh, because it is constantly being used up and made again.
As well as mitochondria, plant cells also have chloroplasts, which make sugar using sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Nerve cells, also called neurons, are the cells our body uses to pass on information at lightning speed. They work with tiny electrical signals and chemical messengers. There are about 86 billion of them in the human brain.
wichtigste: The human brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.
Dendrites receive signals from other cells.
The axon is the long extension that passes signals on.
The short electrical signal of a nerve cell is called an action potential.
At rest, a nerve cell has a voltage of about minus 70 millivolts.
The myelin sheath around many axons speeds up the signal.
Glial cells support and supply the nerve cells.

abschnitte.text: A **nerve cell** is a special body cell that can take in, process and pass on information. There are about 86 billion of them in the brain alone, plus many in the spinal cord and the nerves. They report, for example, when we touch something hot, and they control our muscles. Thinking, remembering and feeling also come from nerve cells working together.

The **cell body** contains the nucleus with the genetic information. From it come many short, branching **dendrites**, which receive signals from other cells like branches. A long extension, the **axon**, passes the signals on. The longest human nerve cells reach from the spinal cord to the toes and are about a metre long.

At rest, a nerve cell has a voltage of about minus 70 millivolts, much less than a battery. If it is stimulated strongly enough, it sends out a short signal, the **action potential**. Many axons are surrounded by a fatty covering, the **myelin sheath**. It works like the insulation on a cable and makes conduction much faster, up to over 100 metres a second.

The point of contact between two nerve cells is called a **synapse**. There the signal usually does not jump across directly but is passed on with chemical messengers, the **neurotransmitters**. A single nerve cell can be connected to thousands of others. When we learn, some connections become stronger and others weaker.

The Italian Camillo Golgi invented a staining method that made it possible to see single nerve cells under the microscope. The Spaniard **Santiago Ramón y Cajal** used it to draw thousands of nerve cells and realised that they are separate cells. In 1906 the two shared the Nobel Prize. As well as nerve cells, the brain contains **glial cells**, which support, protect and supply the neurons.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for nerve cell.
The long extension that carries signals away from the nerve cell.
A short, branching extension that receives signals.
The point of contact where a nerve cell passes a signal on to another cell.
A short electrical pulse with which a nerve cell sends a signal.

gewusst: If you laid all of a person's nerve pathways end to end, they would stretch for many thousands of kilometres.
Ramón y Cajal's drawings are so accurate and beautiful that they are still shown in museums today.
An action potential lasts only about a thousandth of a second.

teile.einleitung: MeteoSwiss is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, the national weather service of Switzerland. It measures the weather, makes weather forecasts every day and warns the public about dangerous weather. It also watches how the climate in Switzerland is changing.
wichtigste: MeteoSwiss is Switzerland's official weather service.
It makes weather forecasts every day.
It warns the public about dangerous weather such as storms, gales or heat.
The warnings have 5 danger levels; level 5 means very great danger.
Many measurements come from automatic weather stations.
MeteoSwiss launches weather balloons in Payerne.
Weather radars show where it is raining or snowing at the moment.

abschnitte.text: MeteoSwiss is a **federal office** and belongs to the Federal Department of Home Affairs. Its headquarters are in Zurich, with other sites in Geneva, Locarno-Monti and Payerne. Its roots go back to 1881, when the Swiss Central Meteorological Institute was founded. In German the office is called MeteoSchweiz, in French MétéoSuisse and in Italian MeteoSvizzera.

Automatic **weather stations** are spread all over Switzerland, including on high mountains. Every few minutes they measure temperature, wind, rainfall, humidity and sunshine. In **Payerne** in the canton of Vaud, weather balloons with measuring instruments go up every day and radio back data from high up. On top of this there are satellite pictures, which show clouds from space.

A **weather radar** sends out radio waves that are reflected by raindrops, snowflakes and hailstones. This shows where it is raining or snowing and how heavily. MeteoSwiss runs five radar stations on mountains, for example on the Albis and the Weissfluhgipfel. You can also see the radar pictures in the weather app and on television.

All the measurements go into large computers that calculate with **weather models**. A weather model divides the air into many small cubes and calculates how wind, heat and moisture change in them. Meteorologists check the results and make the forecasts from them. The further into the future a forecast reaches, the less certain it becomes.

In thunderstorms, gales, heavy rain, snow, black ice, heat or frost, MeteoSwiss issues **weather warnings**. The warnings have five **danger levels**, from level 1 for no or low danger to level 5 for very great danger. They are spread via the app, the internet, radio and television. Together with other authorities, they can also be found on the federal natural hazards portal.

MeteoSwiss has been collecting weather data for over 150 years and can therefore show how the **climate** is changing. So we know that it is much warmer in Switzerland today than when measurements began. The office also provides information on pollen for allergy sufferers and on air quality. It also supplies weather data for flight safety at Swiss airports.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the weather and of what happens in the atmosphere.
The science of climate, meaning the weather over long periods.
A device that uses radio waves to detect rain, snow and hail.
A measuring instrument on a weather balloon that sends its data to the ground by radio.

gewusst: Weather balloons from Payerne rise over 30 kilometres high, until they burst in the thin air.
Switzerland's nationwide weather measuring network went into operation at the end of 1863.

teile.einleitung: The cockchafer, also called the May bug, is a brown beetle that buzzes around trees in the evening in spring, especially in May. But it spends most of its life unseen as a larva in the soil. This larva is called a grub and lives in the ground for several years.
wichtigste: Cockchafers are seen especially often in May.
Their wing cases are brown, and their antennae look like little fans.
Adult cockchafers eat the leaves of trees.
The cockchafer's larva is called a grub and lives in the soil.
The grub eats roots and stays in the ground for several years.
A year in which especially many cockchafers fly in an area is called a flight year.
In central Europe there are mainly the common cockchafer and the forest cockchafer.

abschnitte.text: A cockchafer is about 2 to 3 centimetres long. Its **wing cases** are brown, and its head and the shield behind it are usually dark. On the sides of its abdomen it has white, triangular spots. Its **antennae**, which look like little fans, are especially striking; in males they are bigger. At the end of its body the beetle has a pointed extension.

Cockchafers live at the edges of woods, in orchards, parks and in meadows with trees nearby. The adult beetles eat the **leaves** of broadleaved trees such as oaks, beeches, maples and fruit trees. They fly mainly at dusk. After a few weeks they die.

The females lay their eggs in the **soil**. From them hatch fat, whitish, curved larvae, the **grubs**. They eat the roots of grasses, vegetables and trees and grow slowly. In Switzerland their development usually takes three years, and at higher altitudes four. Then they turn into a beetle in the soil, which crawls out in spring.

Because development takes the same length of time for almost all the animals in an area, the beetles there appear in large numbers only every three or four years. Such a year is called a **flight year**. In Switzerland, different flight-year areas are distinguished, such as the Bernese, the Uri and the Basel flight year. In years of mass outbreaks, cockchafers can strip trees almost bare.

In the past, cockchafers and their grubs caused great damage in farming. That is why in Switzerland and Germany the beetles were collected by schoolchildren and farmers, often for a small reward. In the 1950s and 1960s they were greatly reduced with **insecticides**, so that they became rare in many places. Today, organic farming uses among other things a **fungus** that attacks grubs.

The cockchafer is one of the best-known insects in the German-speaking world. It appears in old children's songs and plays a part in the story “Max and Moritz” by Wilhelm Busch, in which Uncle Fritz finds cockchafers in his bed. For a long time the cockchafer was also a popular motif on postcards and chocolate. In recent decades it has become more common again in some areas.

begriffe.erklaerung: The white, curved larva of the cockchafer, which lives in the soil.
The young form of an insect, which looks different from the adult.
The hard front wings of a beetle, which protect the delicate hind wings.
A year in which especially many cockchafers fly in an area.

gewusst: Before taking off, a cockchafer pumps air into its body, which looks as if it were counting.
The fans on a male's antennae are made of seven little leaves, with which it smells scents.
A grub lives in the ground much longer than the adult beetle lives above it.

teile.einleitung: A molecule is a tiny particle made of several atoms that are firmly joined together. Water, sugar, oxygen and even our genetic material are made of molecules. They are so small that a single drop of water contains an unimaginable number of them.
wichtigste: A molecule is a combination of several atoms.
The atoms are joined by covalent bonds.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Molecules can consist of two atoms or of millions.
Molecules are described with chemical formulas such as H₂O.
Molecules are far too small to be seen with a light microscope.
The genetic material DNA is a huge molecule.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny building blocks, the **atoms**. When two or more atoms join firmly together, a **molecule** is formed. The atoms share electrons; this is called a **covalent bond**. A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that still has its properties. The word comes from Latin and means “small mass”.

The best-known molecule is probably **water**, with the formula H₂O. The formula shows that it consists of two hydrogen atoms (H) and one oxygen atom (O). The oxygen we breathe consists of molecules made of two oxygen atoms (O₂). A sugar molecule is much bigger and contains 45 atoms. The carbon dioxide we breathe out has the formula CO₂.

A water molecule is about a third of a millionth of a millimetre in size. So a single drop of water contains more than a thousand billion billion water molecules. But there are also huge molecules, called **macromolecules**. The genetic material **DNA** in a human cell is one such giant molecule; unrolled, it would be about two metres long. Proteins and plastics are also made of long chains of molecules.

Because molecules cannot be seen directly, chemists show them with **models**. In the ball-and-stick model, the atoms are coloured balls and the bonds are sticks. Oxygen is usually shown red, hydrogen white and carbon black. With formulas such as H₂O or CO₂ you can write down which atoms are in a molecule. Today computers also calculate what molecules look like and how they behave.

As early as 1811 the Italian researcher Amedeo Avogadro suggested that gases consist of such combined particles. For a long time it was disputed whether atoms and molecules really exist. Only at the beginning of the 20th century was their existence finally proven, among other things through work by Albert Einstein. Today we know that life consists of countless molecules that react with each other. New medicines are developed by building molecules on purpose.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest building block of a chemical element.
A bond in which atoms share electrons.
A shorthand that shows which atoms a substance is made of, for example H₂O.
A very large molecule made of thousands or millions of atoms.

gewusst: Table salt is not made of molecules but of a lattice of charged particles, the ions.
The scent of a flower comes from tiny scent molecules that fly through the air to our nose.

teile.einleitung: Non-native species, called neobiota, are plants, animals, fungi and other living things that people have brought since 1492 to areas where they did not exist before. Most of them do no harm, but some spread strongly and become a problem. In Switzerland they include, for example, the tiger mosquito and Japanese knotweed.
wichtigste: Neobiota are species that people have brought to new areas since 1492.
Introduced plants are called neophytes, and introduced animals neozoa.
A species counts as invasive if it spreads strongly and causes damage.
In Switzerland, common ragweed must be controlled by law, because its pollen causes strong allergies.
The Asian tiger mosquito has been spreading in Switzerland for some years, first in Ticino.
The quagga mussel multiplies in huge numbers in Swiss lakes and blocks water pipes.
Not dumping garden waste in nature helps against the spread of invasive plants.

abschnitte.text: The word **neobiota** means roughly “new life”. It refers to species that, since Columbus discovered America in 1492, have come to new areas with the help of people. Plants are called **neophytes**, animals **neozoa** and fungi neomycetes. Many of these species, such as the potato or maize, are useful crops today.

Some species were brought on purpose, for example as pretty garden plants or pets. Others travelled as stowaways, for example in ships, containers, car tyres or potting soil. The **quagga mussel** was probably carried from lake to lake on boats. Because of worldwide trade and transport, more species are arriving today than ever before.

A non-native species counts as **invasive** if it spreads strongly and causes damage. It can push out native species, spread diseases or damage buildings. Often it has no natural enemies in its new area. But only a small share of all introduced species actually becomes invasive.

In Switzerland, **common ragweed** must be controlled by law, because its pollen causes severe allergies. Japanese knotweed, with stems like bamboo, grows rampantly on stream banks and damages bank reinforcements. Since about 2007 the **box tree moth**, a moth from East Asia, has been stripping many box trees bare. The Asian tiger mosquito was first found in Ticino and is now spreading north of the Alps too.

Garden waste belongs in the green waste collection or on the compost, not in the woods or by a stream. Boats should be cleaned and dried before they go into another lake. In the garden you can plant native plants instead of invasive species. Since September 2024, some invasive plants such as **cherry laurel** may no longer be sold in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant species that has reached a new area through people.
An animal species that has reached a new area through people; the plural is neozoa.
Spreading strongly and causing damage as it does so.
A species that lives in an area naturally.

gewusst: The potato and the tomato are also neophytes that came to Europe from America.
In lakes, the quagga mussel can form such dense carpets that the pipes of waterworks become clogged.
A single ragweed plant can produce many thousands of seeds.

teile.einleitung: A meta-analysis is a statistical method that combines the results of many individual studies on the same topic. This gives a more reliable answer than a single study can provide. Meta-analyses are especially important in medicine, psychology and educational research.
wichtigste: A meta-analysis is a statistical summary of the results of several studies.
The term was coined by Gene Glass in 1976.
Large studies with precise estimates usually get the most weight.
The typical chart of a meta-analysis is called a forest plot.
A funnel plot helps to spot signs of publication bias.
The measure I² describes how much the results of the individual studies differ from each other.
The organisation Cochrane, founded in 1993, produces systematic reviews on health questions.

abschnitte.text: For many questions there is not just one study but dozens, and their results sometimes contradict each other. A **meta-analysis** collects all the suitable studies and combines their results statistically. The word “meta” here means something like “about”, so it is an analysis of other analyses. The term was coined by the American researcher **Gene Glass** in 1976.

First, following fixed rules, you search for all the studies on a question; this is called a **systematic review**. Then you assess their quality and combine their results. Not all studies count equally: with inverse-variance weighting, large studies with precise estimates get the most **weight**. A random-effects model assumes that the true effects differ somewhat from study to study.

The best-known chart is the **forest plot**. In it, each study appears as a point with a line that shows how uncertain its result is. At the very bottom, a diamond shows the overall result of all the studies. A **funnel plot** helps to spot whether studies may be missing because only studies with exciting results were published.

If studies with disappointing results are not published, **publication bias** arises, and the meta-analysis looks too optimistic. The measure **I²** shows how much the individual studies differ from one another. If it is high, you have to check carefully why the results are so different. Also: if poor studies are combined, the result does not automatically become good.

The organisation **Cochrane** was founded in 1993 and is named after the British doctor Archie Cochrane. It produces systematic reviews on health questions, with thousands of experts worldwide taking part, including from Switzerland. The **PRISMA** guideline sets out how systematic reviews and meta-analyses should be reported. That way others can follow exactly how the work was done.

Meta-analyses help, for example, with the question of whether a medicine works or what side effects it has. In educational research they are used to sum up which teaching methods are especially helpful for learning. Recommendations from health authorities are also often based on meta-analyses. So they are considered especially strong scientific evidence, if they are done carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scientific investigation of a particular question.
A chart that shows the results of all the studies and the overall result.
A distortion because studies with dull results are published less often.
A piece of work that follows fixed rules to find and assess all the studies on a question.

gewusst: Gene Glass developed the meta-analysis partly to show that psychotherapy works on average.
The Cochrane logo is a simplified forest plot.
Some meta-analyses combine over a hundred individual studies.

teile.einleitung: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz are two astronomers from Switzerland who in 1995 discovered the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star outside our solar system. This discovery changed the way we look at the universe. For it the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
wichtigste: Michel Mayor was born in Lausanne in 1942; at the time of the discovery Didier Queloz was his doctoral student.
Both did their research at the University of Geneva.
In 1995 they discovered the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star.
The planet is called 51 Pegasi b and lies in the constellation of Pegasus.
They found it with the radial velocity method.
The measurements were made with the ELODIE spectrograph at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in France.
In 2019 they shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with the cosmologist James Peebles.

abschnitte.text: **Michel Mayor** was born in **Lausanne** in 1942 and became professor of astronomy at the **University of Geneva**. **Didier Queloz** was born in 1966 and was his doctoral student at the beginning of the 1990s. Together they searched for planets around other stars. At the time many experts thought this was almost hopeless. Queloz later also did research at the University of Cambridge in England and at ETH Zurich.

In October 1995, Mayor and Queloz announced the discovery of a planet around the star **51 Pegasi** in the constellation of Pegasus. The planet was given the name **51 Pegasi b**. The star is about 50 light years away from us and quite similar to our Sun. It was the first **exoplanet** found around such a Sun-like star.

You can almost never see a planet around a distant star directly, because the star is far too bright. So Mayor and Queloz used the **radial velocity method**. With its gravity, a planet pulls ever so slightly on its star, so that the star wobbles a little back and forth. This wobble changes the star's light by a tiny amount. With the very precise **ELODIE spectrograph** at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in southern France, they were able to measure this change.

51 Pegasi b did not fit at all with what had been expected. It is a **gas giant** rather like Jupiter, but it orbits its star in only about 4 days. For comparison: Jupiter takes almost 12 years to go round the Sun once. Because the planet is so close to its star, it is extremely hot. Such planets are now called **hot Jupiters**.

In 2019 Mayor and Queloz received half of the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. The other half went to the cosmologist **James Peebles** for his research on the development of the universe. After 1995 a real hunt for exoplanets began, including with instruments that were partly developed in Geneva. By 2025 over 6000 exoplanets had already been confirmed. Today researchers wonder whether there could be life on some of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet that orbits a star other than our Sun.
A measuring instrument that splits light into its colours and examines it closely.
How fast a star is moving towards us or away from us.
A person who writes a large piece of research at a university to gain a doctorate.
The distance that light travels in a year, almost 10 trillion kilometres.

gewusst: 51 Pegasi b also has an official proper name: Dimidium, which means half in Latin, because it is about half as heavy as Jupiter.
The star 51 Pegasi can just be seen with the naked eye on a dark night.
During the first measurements, Queloz first looked for a mistake, because the result was so unexpected.

teile.einleitung: The Mesozoic is the middle era of Earth's history, from about 252 to 66 million years ago. It is the age of the dinosaurs, the pterosaurs and the great marine reptiles. It consists of three periods: the Triassic, the Jurassic and the Cretaceous.
wichtigste: The Mesozoic lasted from about 252 to 66 million years ago.
It is divided into the three periods Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous.
During the Mesozoic the supercontinent Pangaea broke up.
The first mammals and dinosaurs appeared in the Triassic.
Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates to master powered flight.
Flowering plants appeared and spread in the Cretaceous.
At the end of the Cretaceous an asteroid struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.

abschnitte.text: The word Mesozoic means “middle animal era”. It began about 252 million years ago after the biggest mass extinction in Earth's history and ended 66 million years ago. It is divided into three periods: the **Triassic**, the **Jurassic** and the **Cretaceous**. The name Triassic comes from the three-part division of the rocks in Germany, and the name Jurassic from the **Jura mountains** on the border between Switzerland and France.

At the start of the Mesozoic, all the land formed the huge supercontinent **Pangaea**. Over time it broke up, and the continents slowly drifted apart. This is how the Atlantic began to open. A sea called the **Tethys** at times covered large parts of today's Switzerland, which is why many fossilised sea creatures are found in the Jura and the Alps.

The first **dinosaurs** appeared in the Triassic, and in the Jurassic and Cretaceous they became the dominant land animals. Well-known examples are Brachiosaurus, Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus. The **pterosaurs** were the first vertebrates that could actively fly. In the Jurassic the first birds also developed from small predatory dinosaurs.

In the sea lived large reptiles such as the dolphin-like **ichthyosaurs** and the **plesiosaurs**, with four paddles and often a very long neck. There were also countless **ammonites**, relatives of squid with spiral shells, which are common fossils today. The first mammals also appeared in the Triassic; they were mostly small and active at night. In the Cretaceous, **flowering plants** spread.

66 million years ago the dinosaurs died out, except for the ancestors of the birds, along with the pterosaurs, the great marine reptiles and the ammonites. In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez found a striking amount of **iridium**, an element common in asteroids, in the boundary layer between the Cretaceous and the Tertiary. They therefore suspected an impact from space. Later the matching **Chicxulub crater** was found on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.

At **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, exceptionally well-preserved fossils of fish and marine reptiles from the Triassic were found, and the area is a UNESCO World Heritage site. In Frick in the canton of Aargau, many skeletons of the dinosaur **Plateosaurus** were dug up, which can be seen in the Dinosaur Museum in Frick. In Lommiswil near Solothurn, in a former quarry, you can marvel at hundreds of dinosaur footprints from the Jurassic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very long section of Earth's history, divided into periods.
A supercontinent in which all the land masses were once joined.
An ancient sea that lay between the continents in the Mesozoic.
An extinct sea creature with a spiral shell.
The striking of an asteroid or comet on a planet.

gewusst: Birds are the living descendants of the dinosaurs today.
The Jurassic period is named after a mountain range that lies partly in Switzerland.
The Chicxulub crater is about 180 kilometres across and is now mostly hidden under rock and sea.

teile.einleitung: A microwave oven, or microwave for short, is a kitchen appliance that heats food with invisible electromagnetic waves. It does this much faster than a hob or an oven. It was invented thanks to a melted chocolate bar.
wichtigste: Microwaves mainly set the water molecules in food moving, and this makes it warm.
Household appliances usually work at a frequency of about 2.45 gigahertz.
The microwaves are produced by a part called a magnetron.
The engineer Percy Spencer discovered the effect by chance when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket.
A metal mesh in the door keeps the waves inside the appliance.
The turntable makes sure that the food heats up more evenly.
Dishes with a metal rim do not belong in the microwave, because they can give off sparks.

abschnitte.text: Microwaves are **electromagnetic waves**, just like light and radio waves, but invisible to our eyes. In a microwave oven they vibrate about 2.45 billion times a second, which is 2.45 **gigahertz**. A single wave is about 12 centimetres long. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth use the same kind of waves, but with much less power.

Water molecules have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end. The microwaves keep turning these **water molecules** back and forth. The particles rub against each other and produce heat, much as your hands get warm when you rub them together. The waves only go a few centimetres deep, so the inside of large pieces is heated by **heat conduction**.

The heart of it is the **magnetron**, a tube that produces microwaves from electricity. The waves are led into the cooking space and bounced back and forth by the metal walls. The door contains a fine **metal mesh**: the holes are much smaller than the waves, so they cannot get through, but light can. The turntable moves the food because there are warmer and cooler spots in the cooking space.

In the 1940s the American engineer **Percy Spencer** was working on radar equipment for the company Raytheon. He noticed that a chocolate bar in his trouser pocket had melted. Afterwards he tried it with corn kernels, which popped into popcorn. In 1947 the first appliance came onto the market; it was about the size of a fridge and very expensive.

Metal reflects the waves, and **sparks** can form at edges and rims. Eggs in their shells can burst because steam builds up inside them. Frozen food thaws rather slowly, because **ice** absorbs the radiation less well than liquid water. That is why many appliances have a defrost setting that keeps taking short breaks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part in the appliance that produces the microwaves.
How often a wave vibrates per second, measured in hertz.
A billion vibrations per second.
The distance from one wave crest to the next. At 3 gigahertz this is about 10 centimetres.

gewusst: The first microwave oven of 1947 was almost as tall as a man and weighed several hundred kilograms.
You can look in through the door window even though the waves cannot get out, because light has much shorter waves.
A dry plate hardly gets warm in the microwave, because it contains almost no water.

teile.einleitung: A navigation system helps you work out where you are and find the way to a destination. Today most people think of the sat nav in the car or the map app on their mobile phone, which calculate their position using signals from satellites. In the past, people found their way with the stars, a compass and lighthouses.
wichtigste: Satellite navigation works out the position with radio signals from satellites.
The best-known system is GPS from the USA.
Russia runs GLONASS, China BeiDou and Europe Galileo.
A receiver needs at least 4 satellites to work out its position and height accurately.
The distance to a satellite is calculated from the travel time of the radio signal.
Navigation satellites carry atomic clocks, because time has to be measured extremely accurately.
A car sat nav also needs a digital road map to work out a route.

abschnitte.text: Thousands of years ago, sailors were already finding their way by the Sun, the stars and the coasts. The **compass**, which shows the direction of north with a magnetic needle, was invented in China. Later sailors used the **sextant** to measure the angle of the Sun or a star above the horizon and worked out their position from it. At night, lighthouses warned of dangerous coasts.

Today several satellite navigation systems circle the Earth. The American **GPS** was originally built for the military and has been fully working since 1995. In addition there are the Russian **GLONASS**, the Chinese **BeiDou** and the European **Galileo**. The GPS satellites fly at a height of about 20,000 kilometres, and each system uses more than two dozen satellites.

Each satellite constantly sends out a radio signal with the exact time and its position. The receiver measures how long the signal has been on its way, the **travel time**. Because radio waves travel at about 300,000 kilometres a second, they cover 300 metres in just a millionth of a second. That is why extremely accurate **atomic clocks** are needed on board; otherwise the position would be wrong by many metres.

From the distance to one satellite, the receiver only knows that it is somewhere on a huge sphere around that satellite. With three satellites, three such spheres meet at one point; this is called **trilateration**. But because the clock in a mobile phone or sat nav is not as accurate as an atomic clock, a fourth satellite is needed to make up for the clock error. With at least four satellites, longitude, latitude and height can be worked out.

The position alone is not enough to get to a destination. A sat nav needs a **digital road map** in which all the roads, junctions and one-way streets are stored. A computer program searches it for the shortest or fastest route. Many apps also include information on traffic jams and keep adjusting the route.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Navigation systems are found in mobile phones, cars, aircraft, ships and sports watches. In tunnels, narrow mountain valleys or buildings the satellite signal is often weak; then Wi-Fi, mobile networks or motion sensors help. The Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**, runs a network of fixed stations that can be used to correct positions in Switzerland to within a few centimetres. This is used, for example, by surveyors and by farmers with self-driving tractors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A craft that circles the Earth in space.
An extremely accurate clock that measures the vibrations of atoms.
The time a signal takes to get from the transmitter to the receiver.
Working out a position from the distances to several known points.
A measuring instrument used at sea to measure the angle of heavenly bodies.

gewusst: Without Einstein's theory of relativity, GPS would become several kilometres less accurate every day.
Modern mobile phones often receive signals from GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou at the same time.
Migratory birds find their way without technology, using among other things the Earth's magnetic field and the stars.

tz4y4ba.t: National Centre of Competence in Research

teile.einleitung: A National Centre of Competence in Research, NCCR for short, is a large Swiss research network that works on an important topic over many years. In it, groups from different universities research together, for example on planets, quantum physics or robots. NCCRs are funded by the federal government and run by the Swiss National Science Foundation.
wichtigste: An NCCR is a long-term research network on a topic of strategic importance.
NCCRs are run by the Swiss National Science Foundation, SNSF, on behalf of the federal government.
An NCCR can be funded for a maximum of 12 years.
The first series started in 2001.
An NCCR is led by one university, the home institution or leading house.
Researchers propose NCCR topics themselves, whereas the Federal Council sets NRP topics.
As well as top-level research, NCCRs support young researchers and the transfer of knowledge.

abschnitte.text: A **National Centre of Competence in Research** brings together research groups from all over Switzerland on a shared topic. Universities, ETH Zurich, EPFL, universities of applied sciences and research institutes take part. The topics are meant to be especially important for science, the economy or society in Switzerland. The programme is one of the federal government's most important funding tools.

The **Swiss National Science Foundation**, SNSF for short, runs the NCCRs on behalf of the federal government. In a call for proposals, researchers submit their ideas, which are strictly assessed by international experts. In the end, the responsible federal department decides which projects start. An NCCR runs in phases of four years each and can therefore be funded for a maximum of **12 years**.

Every NCCR has a **home institution**, also called the **leading house**, a university that leads and hosts the network. It provides the management and makes sure that the network lives on after federal funding ends. As well as the federal money, the universities themselves and other partners must pay a large part of the costs. This often leads to new professorships or whole research centres.

The NCCR **PlanetS** studies how planets form and looks for planets around other stars; it is led by the University of Bern together with the University of Geneva. The NCCR MARVEL uses computers to develop new materials. Other NCCRs have worked on robotics, quantum physics, climate or the microbiome, the tiny living things in and on the body. Since 2001, new NCCRs have followed in several series, for example in 2005, 2010, 2014 and 2020.

NCCRs should not be confused with the **National Research Programmes**, NRPs for short. For the NRPs, the Federal Council sets a topic on which knowledge is urgently needed, for example the Covid-19 pandemic. NCCRs, on the other hand, start from below: the researchers themselves propose what they would like to work on. What is more, NRPs usually run for much less time than NCCRs.

An NCCR is meant not only to carry out top-level research but also to support young researchers. This includes posts for doctoral students and programmes that support women in science. Another aim is **knowledge transfer**, meaning that results reach companies, schools and the public. That is why new start-up companies have come out of some NCCRs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss National Science Foundation, the most important funder of research in Switzerland.
The university that leads and hosts an NCCR.
A National Research Programme, whose topic is set by the Federal Council.
Passing on research knowledge to the economy and society.
An invitation in which you can apply with a project idea.

gewusst: Researchers from the NCCR PlanetS worked on the space telescope CHEOPS, which studies distant planets.
The SNSF was founded as early as 1952.
Only a small share of the proposals submitted actually become an NCCR in the end.

teile.einleitung: The median is the value that stands exactly in the middle when you put a list of numbers in order of size. In German it is also called the Zentralwert, the central value. It helps to compare numbers fairly, even when single values are extremely large or small.
wichtigste: The median is the middle value of an ordered list of numbers.
In German it is also called the central value.
Before you find the median, you must put the values in order of size.
With an odd number of values, the median is the value in the middle.
With an even number, you take the average of the two middle values.
At least half of the values are less than or equal to the median.
Outliers hardly change the median, but they change the average a lot.

abschnitte.text: The median is an **average** from statistics. It divides an ordered list of numbers into two halves of equal size. At least half of the values are less than or equal to the median, and at least half are greater than or equal to it. The name comes from the Latin word medianus, which means “lying in the middle”.

First you put all the values in order of size, from smallest to largest. So 3, 9, 1, 7 and 5 become 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. With five values, the third stands exactly in the middle, so the median is 5. In the same way, 12, 15, 11, 30 and 14 become 11, 12, 14, 15, 30 after ordering, which gives a median of 14.

With an even number of values, there is no single middle but two **middle values**. Then you work out the average of these two numbers. With 2, 4, 6 and 8, 4 and 6 are in the middle, so the median is 5. Ordered, 7, 3, 10, 3, 8 and 6 become 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, and the median is the average of 6 and 7, which is 6.5.

The well-known **mean**, also called the arithmetic mean, is worked out by adding up all the values and dividing by how many there are. A single very large value, an **outlier**, can shift the mean a lot. This is not the case with the median, which stays stable. In the list 11, 12, 14, 15, 30, the mean is 16.4, even though four of the five numbers are smaller, whereas the median stays at 14.

For wages, the **median wage** is often given, because a few very high wages would distort the mean. According to the Federal Statistical Office, the median wage in Switzerland in 2022 was about 6800 francs a month. The median is also often used for house prices, waiting times or test results. It shows what applies to a typical person.

The median is a special case of **quantiles**, which split a set of data into parts. The quartiles divide the ordered values into four equal parts, and the median is the middle quartile. In a box plot, a common statistical chart, the median is shown as a line in a box. In this way you can see at a glance how the values are spread out.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for the median, the value in the middle.
The sum of all values divided by how many there are, also called the arithmetic mean.
A value that is much larger or smaller than the other values.
The science of collecting and analysing numbers and data.

gewusst: In a list with an even number of values, the median can be a number that does not appear in the list at all.
If a millionaire moves to a small village, the average income rises sharply, but the median hardly changes.

teile.einleitung: Mitochondrial Eve is the most recent common ancestor of all people alive today in a purely maternal line. According to common estimates, she lived about 150,000 to 200,000 years ago in Africa. Researchers did not find her as a fossil, but worked her out from the genetic material of people today.
wichtigste: Mitochondrial Eve is the common ancestor of all people in the maternal line.
She probably lived about 150,000 to 200,000 years ago in Africa.
Mitochondrial DNA is passed on almost only by the mother.
She became known in 1987 through a study by Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking and Allan Wilson.
She was not the only woman of her time, but only her maternal line has survived to today.
The oldest lines belong to haplogroup L, which is found mainly in Africa.
Her male counterpart is called Y-chromosomal Adam.

abschnitte.text: **Mitochondria** are the power stations of the cell, which get energy from food. They have their own small DNA, which in humans has about 16,600 base pairs. This **mitochondrial DNA** is passed on almost only by the mother to all her children. That is why it can be used to trace maternal lines of descent far back, from mother to grandmother to great-grandmother.

In 1987 **Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking and Allan Wilson** of the University of California at Berkeley published a famous study. They compared the mitochondrial DNA of people from different parts of the world. From this they drew a **family tree** whose root lay in Africa. Newspapers gave the common ancestor the name Eve, after the Bible.

The most varied and oldest mitochondrial lines are found today in **Africa**. They belong to **haplogroup L**. All people outside Africa carry lines that developed from one branch of this group. This fits with fossil finds and supports the view that modern humans arose in Africa and spread out from there.

A common misunderstanding is that Eve was the only woman of her time. In reality many thousands of people lived then. But the maternal lines of the other women died **out** over time, for example because a woman had only sons. We still carry genetic material from many of these women, just not in our mitochondria. Eve and **Y-chromosomal Adam**, who is worked out from the paternal line, probably did not live at the same time.

To estimate when Eve lived, the **molecular clock** is used. It is assumed that DNA changes at a roughly steady rate. The more differences two lines have, the longer ago they separated. Because this rate is not known exactly, there is a wide range, usually about 150,000 to 200,000 years. The estimate is checked again and again with new data.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small part of the cell that makes energy and has its own DNA.
A group of people with similar, related DNA lines.
A pair of DNA building blocks, the unit for measuring the length of DNA.
A method of working out from DNA differences when a separation happened.

gewusst: All people alive today carry mitochondrial DNA that goes back to this one woman.
Mitochondrial Eve is not a particular skeleton that could be dug up.
Mitochondrial DNA has also made it possible to link old bone finds to particular groups of people.

teile.einleitung: NEST is a special research building of Empa in Dübendorf near Zurich, where new ideas for sustainable building and living are tested. It works like a set of shelves into which whole flats and offices can be slotted as research modules and swapped again. Real people live and work there while researchers measure how well the new technologies work in everyday life.
wichtigste: NEST is in Dübendorf and belongs to Empa.
The research building opened in 2016.
The abbreviation stands for Next Evolution in Sustainable Building Technologies.
The fixed basic framework is called the backbone.
Research modules, the units, are slotted into the backbone and replaced again.
The unit “Urban Mining and Recycling” shows that all building materials can be reusable.
In the “DFAB House”, digital building with robots and 3D printing was the focus.
The unit “HiLo” stands out for its thin, curved concrete roof.

abschnitte.text: **Empa** is the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology and belongs to the ETH Domain. Since 2016 the research building NEST has stood on its site in **Dübendorf**. The name is the abbreviation for Next Evolution in Sustainable Building Technologies. At the same time the word nest is a reminder of a home.

abschnitte.titel: A building like a set of shelves
abschnitte.text: The heart of it is the **backbone**, a fixed concrete core with several open platforms. It contains the stairs, the lift and all the pipes and cables for water, electricity, heat and data. Individual research modules, called **units**, are slotted into the platforms. When an experiment is finished, a unit can be removed and replaced by a new one.

The unit **Urban Mining and Recycling** is a small flat made entirely of reused or recyclable materials. Nothing is glued; everything is screwed or slotted together so that it can be taken apart again later. The materials used include, for example, pressed building waste and panels made of fungal mycelium. The idea behind it: a house is like a store of materials for the future.

In the **DFAB House**, researchers from ETH Zurich showed how robots and 3D printers can help with building. A construction robot made a curved wall of steel mesh right on site, which was then filled with concrete. The ceiling slabs were made with moulds from a **3D printer**, which makes them light and saves material. The timber parts of the upper floors were also put together by robots.

The unit **HiLo** stands out even from a distance with its curved concrete roof, which in places is only a few centimetres thin. This is made possible by its special shape, which spreads the weight as in a vault. The roof was built on a net of cables and fabric instead of on expensive wooden formwork. HiLo stands for High Performance, Low Emissions, meaning high performance with few greenhouse gases.

In Switzerland, buildings use a large share of the energy and cause a lot of greenhouse gases. At NEST, companies and universities work together to test new materials, windows, heating systems and solar technologies under real conditions. An **energy hub** links the units and studies how electricity and heat can be stored and shared cleverly. What proves itself at NEST can later be used in ordinary houses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The federal research institute for materials and technology.
An exchangeable research module at NEST.
The fixed basic framework of the building.
Acting in such a way that future generations can also live well.
Using buildings as stores of raw materials whose materials are reused.

gewusst: People really do live and work at NEST, and their everyday life gives the researchers valuable data.
The English word backbone means spine.
As well as Empa, the water research institute Eawag, which does research on the same site in Dübendorf, also takes part in NEST.

teile.einleitung: The mole is the unit for the amount of substance, meaning how many particles there are in a portion of a substance. One mole contains about 6.022 · 10²³ particles, an unimaginably large number. Chemists need the mole in order to count atoms and molecules, so to speak.
wichtigste: The mole is the unit of amount of substance, and its symbol is mol.
One mole contains about 6.022 · 10²³ particles.
This number is named after the Italian researcher Amedeo Avogadro.
One mole of water weighs about 18 g.
The molar mass tells you how many grams one mole of a substance weighs.
At 0 °C and normal air pressure, one mole of a gas takes up about 22.4 litres.
Until 2019 the mole was defined using 12 g of carbon-12.

abschnitte.text: Atoms and molecules are so tiny that you cannot count them one by one. So they are grouped into huge packets, rather like buying eggs by the dozen. Such a packet is called a **mole** and contains about 602 sextillion particles. The mole is one of the seven **base units** of the International System of Units, together with the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and candela. The quantity measured in moles is called the **amount of substance**.

The number of particles in a mole is called the **Avogadro constant**. It is named after the Italian scientist **Amedeo Avogadro**, who did research on gases at the beginning of the 19th century. He suggested that equal volumes of different gases under the same conditions contain the same number of particles. The exact number could only be measured much later.

Every substance has a **molar mass**, the weight of one mole in grams. Carbon has 12 g/mol, so 2 moles of carbon weigh 24 g. Oxygen gas, O₂, has 32 g/mol, so 64 g of oxygen is exactly 2 mol. Water, H₂O, consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, and one mole weighs about 18 g. That is roughly as much as a large gulp of water.

For gases there is a handy rule: at 0 °C and normal air pressure, one mole of a gas takes up about **22.4 litres**. This volume is called the **molar volume** and is the same for almost all gases. It is roughly the contents of two large buckets of water. In this way you can work out from the volume of a gas how many particles are in it.

The mole was added to the International System of Units as a base unit in 1971. For a long time it was defined like this: one mole contains as many particles as there are atoms in **12 g of carbon-12**. Since 20 May 2019 the mole has had a new definition, and the Avogadro constant has an **exactly fixed value** of 6.02214076 · 10²³ per mole. At the same time the kilogram, the ampere and the kelvin were also redefined. In Switzerland the institute METAS makes sure that these units are put into practice exactly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that states how many particles are in a portion of a substance.
The number of particles in a mole, about 6.022 · 10²³.
The mass of one mole of a substance, given in grams per mole.
A particle made of two or more atoms firmly joined together.
One of the seven basic units of the International System of Units.

gewusst: If you spread a mole of grains of sand evenly over Switzerland, it would make a layer many kilometres high.
Chemists celebrate 23 October as Mole Day, because Avogadro's number ends in 10²³.
There are said to be more molecules in a glass of water than there are stars in the observable universe.
